Optimization and Control.summary:
We study pricing in a vehicle sharing network with $N$ locations and $C$ vehicles, motivated by on-demand bike, scooter, and car sharing, as well as robotaxi and ride sharing services. Customers request directed trips between locations, with travel times following general distributions, and leave without service if no vehicle is available. Pricing affects both demand for trips and the distribution of vehicles across locations. Computing an optimal dynamic pricing policy is challenging because the system state depends on the number of vehicles available at each location and in transit (including how long they have been traveling), motivating the use of simple static policies that offer a fixed price for each trip.
  For any number of vehicles and locations, we establish a tight performance guarantee for static pricing relative to optimal dynamic pricing. The guarantee holds for any concave objective functions (including revenue rate) and general travel time distributions. Our tight guarantee is bounded below by $ \frac{C}{C + \min \{ C -1, \sqrt{ CN} \} }$ (over 50%), achieving the first universal, non-asymptotic constant factor guarantee. We also prove that the optimal static policy can be efficiently computed by solving a convex optimization problem. Finally, we extend our performance guarantee to the setting with supply redirection.

Optimization and Control.title: A Palais-Smale type condition for optimal control problems
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider an optimal control problem with a general control constraint and a fixed initial state, for which convexity assumptions are absent. To establish the existence of optimal pairs, we introduce a control version of the Palais-Smale type condition adapted from critical point theory and prove that optimal pairs exist under this condition (see Theorem 2.1). Subsequently, we verify that a specific class of optimal control problems satisfies our Palais-Smale type condition (see Proposition 2.1). Furthermore, as an application, we present an example (Example 3.1) and show that, to the best of our knowledge, no existing result can be applied to establish the existence of an optimal pair in this case (see Section 3.1.1). Example 3.2 shows that finitely many Pontryagin maximum principle candidates do not guarantee the existence of an optimal control. Finally, Example 3.3 demonstrates that the proposed Palais-Smale type condition is sufficient, but not necessary, for the existence of optimal controls.

Optimization and Control.title: Leveraging Christoffel-Darboux Kernels to Strengthen Moment-SOS Relaxations
Optimization and Control.summary: The classical Moment-SOS hierarchy allows one to approximate the global minimum of a polynomial optimization problem through semidefinite relaxations of increasing accuracy. For many optimization problems, however, moving to higher relaxation orders quickly becomes computationally prohibitive. While this difficulty is commonly addressed by exploiting structural properties such as symmetry or sparsity, we explore a complementary direction: strengthening a low-order relaxation using information contained in its own pseudo-moment solution. To this end, we leverage Christoffel-Darboux kernels to identify regions that are compatible with the current pseudo-moment information and use them to construct additional polynomial constraints. We propose two mechanisms: the first, denoted $\HH$, is based on successive global Christoffel restrictions, while the second, denoted $\hh$, combines marginal Christoffel information with an available local solution. For $\HH$, we establish a uniform separation property for successive pseudo-moment solutions and geometric convergence of the fixed-order bounds on a particular subclass of knapsack problems. Moreover, for specific Boolean quadratic problems, we derive an explicit $\hh$ selection rule and establish conditions under which the resulting marginal constraints preserve all global minimizers. Numerical experiments on dense and sparse nonconvex quadratically constrained quadratic programs show that the resulting strengthened low-order relaxations can significantly improve the initial bounds, sometimes attaining exactness, while remaining substantially cheaper than solving higher-order relaxations.

Optimization and Control.title: Dynamic Matching with Abandonment: Optimal Guarantees via Static Priority Policies
Optimization and Control.summary:
We study stochastic dynamic matching with abandonment, a fundamental model in which agents of different types arrive over time, may abandon the market while waiting, and can be matched in pairs for rewards that depend on their types. No online policy can guarantee more than $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark, which knows all arrival and departure times. Whether this guarantee is achievable has been a central open problem, even in special cases. We resolve this problem by showing that, on every instance, a simple static priority policy, which is computable in polynomial time, earns at least $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark. This establishes that the optimal competitive ratio is exactly $0.5$, improving the previous best guarantee of 0.192 for the general model [Li et al. 2026; Collina et al. 2020]
  Our analysis rests on a key stochastic result, which is a new lower bound on the probability that some agent from a given set of types is available. Building on this bound, we develop two approaches: a primal approach that reads the priorities from an optimal solution of a novel linear program, and a dual approach that assigns a ``value'' to each type, and prioritizes matches with high ``surplus'' (reward minus value of involved agents). These values are the unique solution of a fixed-point equation derived from linear programming duality. We also show that the two approaches are closely connected.

Optimization and Control.title: Deflating the Hessian: Rank-4 W4A4 Quantization for Multimodal Diffusion Transformers
Optimization and Control.summary: In diffusion transformers, low-rank branches can mitigate 4-bit weight--activation (W4A4) post-training quantization (PTQ) loss by decomposing each weight into a low-bit residual and a high-precision low-rank component. Existing low-rank PTQ approaches, however, either optimize low-rank compensation and residual quantization separately, often requiring higher ranks, or rely on second-order weight updates without explicitly modeling activation quantization error, which becomes particularly pronounced under 4-bit quantization. To address these limitations, we present HSVDQuant, a unified framework modeling low-rank-assisted W4A4 PTQ as a coupled calibration problem and deriving optimization-based solvers from the joint objective. Eliminating the output-side low-rank factor yields a deflated Hessian that discounts residual errors already captured by the low-rank component, while an activation-noise surrogate is incorporated to suppress activation quantization error. Across five diffusion backbones, rank-4 HSVDQuant consistently outperforms rank-4 SVDQuant in PSNR and LPIPS. It further surpasses rank-32 SVDQuant on SANA-1.6B, FLUX.1-schnell, and FLUX.1-dev with an $8\times$ smaller rank and up to $6.25\times$ faster quantization. Furthermore, on the Qwen3-8B LLM, rank-4 HSVDQuant improves MMLU accuracy from 61.50% to 68.17% over rank-32 SVDQuant. Overall, HSVDQuant achieves better W4A4 performance with substantially lower rank and quantization cost.

Optimization and Control.title: Sequential Conformal Calibration under Recursive Selection
Optimization and Control.summary: Conformal prediction provides finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees that can support decision-making in specific settings. In multistage problems, earlier decisions determine the populations relevant to later calibration. When later scores are refit using earlier calibration results, reusing those cases for ranking need not preserve exchangeability with a surviving test case. We study sequential conformal calibration with a fresh fold at each stage: conditional on earlier folds, the selected fold scores and the surviving test score are exchangeable. This yields finite-sample coverage guarantees for every prefix of the decision sequence. For atomless survivor score distributions, we derive a universal Binomial-thinned Beta chain for the realized coverage process. Its law depends only on fold sizes and target levels, even under predictable refitting, and yields exact coverage slack, abstention probabilities, and calibration-conditional guarantees. We further characterize the tradeoff between freshness and data reuse. For fixed scores, strict-survivor reuse is exactly valid. For adaptive scores refit using past calibration data, reusing survivors can incur worst-case rank loss, while blocked designs provide an intermediate option between full reuse and stagewise fresh folds. As a case study, we apply the framework to serial multi-echelon inventory problem and propose a sequential conditional-quantile formulation. Each stock level is learned as a context-dependent quantile of cumulative demand among scenarios satisfying earlier no-backlog constraints. We connect these targets to common-shift stationarity and derive decision-level implications for the resulting calibrated policies. In a three-echelon simulation, fresh-fold refitting achieves 81.98% final-prefix coverage against an 81.82% target while reducing mean cost by 5.5% relative to the Bonferroni baseline.

Optimization and Control.title: A volume-controlled level-set method for topology optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: Topology optimization typically involves a geometric volume/mass constraint due to the limited use of material. As a popular technique for topology optimization, the level-set method typically employs the Lagrange method, the penalty method, or the augmented Lagrangian approach to address the volume constraint. This requires careful parameter tuning and may lead to non-monotonic changes in the objective. In this paper, we present a new volume-controlled level-set method for topology optimization. By imposing a scalar weighted volume?compatibility constraint in a modified Stokes-type extension-regularization problem, the velocity is made volume compatible at the beginning of each frozen transport interval. At the continuous level, we prove that the initial rate of change of the regularized volume vanishes and that the subsequent frozen-velocity drift is of order $T^2$; under a narrow-band assumption, the corresponding constant is independent of the smoothing parameter. For the discontinuous Galerkin spatial semi-discretization of the level-set transport equation, we derive a quantitative regularized-volume drift estimate that displays the dependence on the smoothing parameter, spatial mesh size, transport time, and discrete velocity. The effectiveness of the present algorithm is demonstrated through the minimum compliance problem for linear elasticity, the eigenfrequency maximization for structural vibration, and the minimum energy dissipation problem for Stokes flows.

Optimization and Control.title: AI-Mediation in Retail Markets: Revenue Effects and Assortment Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary:
AI shopping assistants increasingly influence which products consumers consider. We study retail assortment planning under AI mediation, where a retailer chooses a catalog, an AI intermediary forms a customer-facing shortlist, and the customer chooses from that shortlist according to a multinomial logit model. We consider both deterministic mediation, in which the AI follows a fixed segment-specific ranking, and stochastic mediation based on the Plackett-Luce model.
  Empirically, we construct a dataset of product rankings from leading AI models, estimate Plackett-Luce ranking models, and evaluate their predictive performance on held-out assortments. Combining these estimates with synthetic customer preferences, we find that accounting for AI mediation can materially change optimal assortments and revenue. Across the tested capacity configurations, ignoring mediation yields mean revenue losses between 2.52% and 11.37% relative to the PL optimum. A much simpler deterministic plug-in, based only on the ordering of fitted AI utilities, performs substantially better, with mean losses of at most 0.53%.
  Motivated by this performance, we study assortment optimization under deterministic mediation. We characterize its computational complexity and show that, for any fixed number of customer segments, the problem admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme.

Optimization and Control.title: Robust Halo Orbit Stationkeeping Under Missed Thrust Events and Maneuver Execution Errors
Optimization and Control.summary: Spacecraft stationkeeping is subject to various operational uncertainties such as missed thrust events, maneuver execution errors, and dynamics modeling errors. Missed thrust events are the most disruptive of these, and current practices mitigate that risk through Monte Carlo-driven heuristics and conservative margins that offer no formal safety guarantees and do not scale to multiple missed thrust events. This paper models these unplanned thruster outages through the Markov Jump System framework, and represents maneuver execution errors and dynamics linearization errors as bounded multiplicative noise. The resulting closed-loop system is a linear time-varying periodic Markov jump system with multiplicative noise, for which Lyapunov-like mean square stability and periodic set invariance conditions are derived. A linear matrix inequality-based optimal controller synthesis framework then designs a periodic, mode-dependent mean-square stable feedback policy that respects path constraints with probability one. The framework is demonstrated on the Earth-Moon 9:2 near-rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO), under both impulsive and low-thrust propulsion, and on a Saturn-Enceladus $L_1$ NRHO using impulsive propulsion. Nonlinear Monte Carlo simulations show that the spacecraft recovers from an arbitrary number of missed thrust events while respecting path constraints, and that the multiplicative noise model introduces additional robustness to maneuver execution error and linearization error.

Optimization and Control.title: When Solvers Get Moody: Quantifying and Predicting Performance Variability in Mixed Integer Programming
Optimization and Control.summary: Mixed-integer programming (MIP) solvers are widely used, yet their performance can vary substantially even under seemingly neutral perturbations. Such variability complicates benchmarking, and the interpretation of computational studies. We introduce the Weighted Variability Score (WVS), a robust multi-component metric that aggregates dispersion in normalized runtime, final optimality gap, LP iterations, and branch-and-bound nodes across repeated runs. On a large subset of MIPLIB 2017 instances, each solved in 100 randomized runs under a four-hour limit, WVS reveals a right-skewed distribution with a substantial upper tail: many instances are essentially stable, but some exhibit large variability that is not explained by basic properties alone. Notably, this experiment proved optimality for the open instance 'neos-5045105-creuse' in two SCIP runs. Using static descriptors and root-level features, a tree-based predictor with a gated tail uplift achieves a mean absolute error of 0.058 and Spearman rank correlation of 0.65 on a sealed test split. Feature-importance analysis highlights root degeneracy, matrix structure, coefficient ranges, and presolve reductions as the main drivers of high WVS. Because variability is systematic and partially predictable from inexpensive early-run features, our findings offer a practical tool for preemptive tuning and lay a foundation for fairer evaluation of new algorithms.
Optimization and Control.comment: 21 pages, including a 3-page electronic companion. An earlier conference version appeared in the IOS 2026 proceedings. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19478202

Optimization and Control.title: Nonsmooth Optimization via Orthogonalized Momentum
Optimization and Control.summary: Modern real application problems involve matrix-valued parameters, yet conventional optimizers treat them as vectors, thereby motivating matrix-aware methods that exploit input-output geometry, such as Muon which orthogonalizes the momentum matrices before parameter updates. Its empirical success raises a conceptual question: can orthogonalized momentum remain effective beyond smooth optimization? This paper studies this question for locally Lipschitz functions using a generalized derivative framework compatible with backpropagation. Our first contribution is to identify a key limitation: for every fixed momentum factor $β\in[0,1)$, Muon can fail to approach the global optimal solution of a convex Lipschitz objective from almost every initialization, when step sizes adapt to the full gradient history. The failure can occur even along bounded iterates. Our example is inspired by the one of Parshakova et al. which only covers $β\in[0,\frac{1}{2})$. Then, we show that the obstruction lies in fixed momentum rather than orthogonalization. Indeed, when the momentum factor is adaptive and approaches 1 together with a vanishing step size, Muon recovers asymptotic convergence for nonconvex nonsmooth optimization under the boundedness and regularity conditions. Moreover, we propose MAGD, which combines orthogonalized momentum with gradient, weighted based on their relative progress. MAGD retains asymptotic convergence in nonconvex settings and achieves an $O(\min\{m,n\}ε^{-2})$ rate in convex settings. A lower bound shows the optimal dimension dependence. Experiments on synthetic problems, image classification, and LLM pretraining show MAGD is a simple and practical alternative to Muon. Together, our results characterize when orthogonalized momentum fails without smoothness and how it can be made reliable and we hope that the analysis may be useful more broadly.

Optimization and Control.title: Riemannian Hessian analysis of Sobolev gradient flows for the Gross--Pitaevskii ground state problem
Optimization and Control.summary: Sobolev gradient flows for the Gross--Pitaevskii ground state problem are Riemannian gradient descent methods on the sphere under a metric induced by a discrete elliptic operator. We analyze their convergence through the condition number of the Riemannian Hessian at the ground state. Bounds of the Rayleigh quotient of the Riemannian Hessian give a uniform analysis of these methods for different metrics. The uniform analysis applies to the classical metrics, such as the shifted Laplacian and the energy-adaptive metrics. Inspired by this analysis, we also consider three new metrics. One of them is a Thomas--Fermi metric, whose condition number is bounded uniformly in the interaction strength for the one-dimensional harmonic trap and whose iteration count does not grow in the Thomas--Fermi regime in the numerical tests. The performance suggested by our analysis is consistent with three-dimensional numerical tests with up to one billion unknowns, for both Riemannian gradient descent and Riemannian conjugate gradient methods, whose practical performance is also related to the Hessian condition number. The Thomas--Fermi flow needs the fewest iterations, while the metrics inverted exactly by tensor-product solvers are the fastest in computational time on one GPU card.

Optimization and Control.title: Adaptive Node Distribution via Probability Density Functions for Birkhoff Pseudospectral Trajectory Optimisation
Optimization and Control.summary: Pseudospectral methods are a powerful framework for spacecraft trajectory optimisation that rely on fixed, problem-independent collocation nodes such as Legendre-Gauss-Lobatto (LGL) nodes. These nodes are located according to polynomial root distributions, which can result in insufficient resolution in regions of high dynamical activity, such as those encountered during collision avoidance manoeuvres. This paper presents an adaptive node distribution strategy for Birkhoff pseudospectral trajectory optimisation, where the collocation nodes are placed according to a probability density function derived from the thrust magnitude profile of the spacecraft. By concentrating nodes in regions of high dynamical variation, the proposed method simultaneously achieves feasibility preservation and improved convergence with fewer nodes in a collision avoidance case study when compared to the universal Birkhoff method, with Model Predictive Control serving as an independent validation comparator. The case study highlights the practical consequences of inter-node constraint violations and validates the adaptive node scheme as a robust and efficient alternative for fuel-optimal spacecraft manoeuvre design.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Efficient Algorithms for Online Subadditive Combinatorial Allocations
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: For the online combinatorial allocation problem with subadditive valuations, Correa and Cristi (STOC 2023) proved the existence of a $6$-competitive online algorithm, improving on the previous best $O(\log\!\log m)$-competitive online algorithm due to Dütting, Kesselheim, and Lucier (FOCS 2020), where $m$ is the number of items. However, Correa and Cristi's result is existential, and it was left open whether a constant competitive ratio is attainable via an efficient online algorithm that uses a polynomial number of demand oracle queries. In this work, we answer this affirmatively, giving an expected-polynomial-time $(6 + ε)$-competitive online algorithm for any constant $ε> 0$. Our techniques also recover, in the offline setting, the $(2 + ε)$-approximation result of Feige (STOC, 2006). Finally, when the buyers' valuations are drawn from identical distributions, we exploit symmetry to obtain an improved $(60/11+ε)$-competitive algorithm. Starting with the natural configuration LP relaxation for the problem, our main technical contribution is a recursive Bundle Score Generator (BSG) that resolves item conflicts by assigning correlated scores to the items requested by each buyer. Unlike the Random Score Generator whose existence is shown by Correa and Cristi, our BSG is efficiently computable in expected polynomial time. Moreover, it satisfies a stochastic dominance property that is sufficient to recover both Feige's offline result and Correa and Cristi's online result.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Smart Lotteries in School Choice: Ex-ante Pareto-Improvement with Ex-post Stability
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: In school choice, students typically have strict preferences over the schools while the schools have coarse priorities over the students based on their distance and their enrolled siblings. The outcome of a centralized admission mechanism is then usually obtained by the Deferred Acceptance (DA) algorithm with random tie-breaking. Therefore, every outcome of this mechanism that occurs with a positive probability is a stable solution for the coarse priorities. This implies a probabilistic assignment, specifying the admission probability for each student-school pair. In this paper, we propose a new efficiency-improving stable 'smart lottery' mechanism. We aim to improve the probabilistic assignment ex-ante in a stochastic dominance sense, while ensuring that the improved random matching is still ex-post stable, meaning that it can be decomposed into stable matchings regarding the original coarse priorities. Therefore, this smart lottery mechanism can provide a clear Pareto-improvement in expectation for any cardinal utilities compared to the standard DA with lottery solution, without sacrificing the stability of the final outcome. We show that although the underlying computational problem is NP-hard, we can solve the problem in practice by using column generation. Our computational results show that the welfare gains by our mechanism are substantially larger than the expected gains by standard methods that realize efficiency improvements after ties have already been broken. Additionally, we illustrate for real-world school choice data of Ghent (Belgium) that, while not theoretically guaranteed, our mechanism can Pareto-improve upon methods that improve upon DA but violate ex-post stability, such as Efficiency-Adjusted Deferred Acceptance.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: A $1/2$-Approximation for Pandora's Problem with Deadlines
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Pandora's problem is a fundamental model of sequential search in which opening each box incurs a cost. We study the variant with deadlines, where each box has a publicly known deadline for both opening and selection. We prove that a simple threshold strategy achieves a $1/2$-approximation to the optimal expected utility, improving the previous guarantee of $(e-1)/(4e)\approx0.158$ due to Berger et al. (AAAI 2024).

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Asymmetric Information in Dynamic Lending Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study a dynamic lending game with limited but reusable supply. Borrower arrivals and loan durations are stochastic. Demand is allocated cheapest-first, subject to available supply, so a lender's quote affects both its current payoff and its ability to serve future borrowers. Motivated by industry practice, we study this problem through the lens of information disclosure: Lenders observe either only their own available supply or also their rivals' aggregate available supply. We ask how providing this information to all, some or none of the lenders affects payoffs as demand varies relative to supply, and how these effects change when a fixed total supply is divided among different numbers of lenders. Interestingly, in the case of asymmetric information disclosure, total payoffs can increase, while total lending remains the same. We identify sufficient mathematical regimes in which this phenomenon occurs. Who receives supply information matters differently as demand rises. For the case of two lenders, informing only the larger lender yields higher total lender payoff at lower demand, while informing only the smaller lender can yield the highest total lender payoff at higher demand. For a platform deciding which lenders can observe rival supply, the results suggest that disclosure can change the fees paid by borrowers without changing how much is lent. Wider access to supply information need not lower those fees: its effect depends on who receives the information and the balance between demand and supply.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 29 pages including references and appendices

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Distortion of Threshold Approval Multiwinner Voting
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study multiwinner voting with $n$ voters and $m$ candidates, where the goal is to select a committee of size $k$. Voters have unit-sum cardinal utilities but report only coarse information induced by $t$ utility thresholds. In particular, each voter partitions the candidates into approval sets, with the utilities of all candidates in the same set lying between the same pair of consecutive thresholds. We model the utility of each voter for a committee as a normalized monotone symmetric norm, capturing, among others, additive welfare, best-representative utility, top-$r$ welfare, $\ell_p$ welfare, and normalized non-increasing ordered weighted averages. We design a deterministic rule with distortion at most $2(2m)^{1/t}$ and a randomized rule with distortion at most $2\min\{m^{1/(t+1)},m/k\}$. These guarantees hold for every committee size $k$ and every norm in our framework. Consequently, a single threshold yields distortion $O(m)$ for deterministic rules and $O(\sqrt{m})$ for randomized rules, while $O(\log m)$ thresholds suffice for constant distortion. We complement these results with norm-dependent lower bounds that asymptotically match our upper bounds for constant committee sizes, including the single-winner case.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Complexity of Autobidding Equilibria in GSP Sponsored Shopping
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We revisit autobidding equilibria in GSP sponsored shopping auctions, recently proposed and studied in Dütting et al. On the existence side, we show that autobidding equilibria under both budget constraints (ABE-B) and return-on-investment constraints (ABE-R) always exist and, moreover, always admit equilibria with polynomial-size support over the allocation space. On the computational side, we show that computing an exact equilibrium is in FIXP, and that computing an approximate equilibrium is in PPAD. We also prove that computing an approximate equilibrium is PPAD-hard for both ABE-B and ABE-R. Together, these results provide a fairly comprehensive picture of the computational complexity of autobidding equilibria in GSP sponsored shopping auctions.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Limit-sure Winning in Team Games without Shared Randomness
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study concurrent stochastic games in which a team of agents plays against an adversarial environment. If the agents could access a shared source of randomness, then these games reduce to two-player games. Despite being common in the literature on coalition games, this assumption does not accurately model real-world systems. In this paper, we consider the setting where the agents only have access to individual sources of randomness, and must satisfy a given reachability or safety objective. The limit-sure problem asks whether the team can ensure that the objective is satisfied with probability at least $1-λ$ for every $λ>0$. For reachability objectives, we show that this problem is $\mathsf{NP}$-complete. For safety objectives, we show that limit-sure winning coincides with almost-sure winning, which is known to lie in $\mathsf{P}$. As a corollary of these results, we conclude that model checking of the qualitative fragment of the logic Individually Randomised ATL -- introduced in the recent work of Brice et al. -- is $\mathsf{P}^{\mathsf{NP}}$-complete.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 31 pages, 6 figures. Full version with appendix

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Protocol effects on feature-based hardware-Trojan detection across Trust-Hub families
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Trust-Hub reuses host circuits: several files differ mainly in the inserted Trojan. When gates from sibling variants enter both training and test folds, a detector can benefit from host logic it has already seen. We measure that effect instead of proposing another classifier. The corpus contains 49,124 gates from 16 netlists grouped into five host families. We left the parser, 36 gate features, class weighting, model settings, threshold, and family-level aggregation unchanged and altered one choice: the test boundary. The three settings draw test gates from the pooled corpus, withhold a complete netlist, or withhold every variant of one host. The choice matters. Random forest records F1/AP of 0.914/0.978 with pooled gates, 0.636/0.851 with one netlist held out, and 0.460/0.577 with a host family held out. XGBoost falls from 0.946/0.976 to 0.464/0.544 across the same comparison. Logistic regression loses AP, although its fixed-threshold F1 is not monotonic. Each family shows the same pooled-to-family direction. Feature removal, repeated model and simulator seeds, score normalization, parser-related exclusions, and a smaller sample change the size of the gap without reversing it. Aggregation also matters: a gate-weighted average is dominated by the larger ISCAS files, so the headline values give each host family one vote. Bootstrap and jackknife summaries keep the gap positive, but their folds reuse training families. We treat the five family rows as descriptive evidence rather than independent trials. Five host families are too few for a population claim, and the experiment says nothing about transfer to a new cell library or an industrial design. It supports a narrower conclusion: sibling benchmark variants can inflate apparent transfer. Benchmarks with several variants of one host circuit should report family-aware holdouts and all five family results beside pooled scores.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Co-opetition Equilibrium in Adversarial Team Games with Heterogeneous Utilities
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The United Nations' 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development requires all countries to collaborate against adversarial factors, a scenario that can be formalized as an adversarial team game. However, existing solution concepts assume team players share identical utility functions---an assumption inconsistent with real-world settings where countries have divergent objectives. This paper argues that studying adversarial team games must account for heterogeneous utilities among team players. We show that ignoring utility differences can render computed equilibria unstable in the original game, and we formalize this degradation via the Price of Ignoring Heterogeneity, which can be unbounded. To address this, we introduce the Co-opetition Equilibrium (CoE), where team players with heterogeneous utilities correlate their strategies (cooperation) against an adversary (competition). We establish existence via reduction from Nash equilibrium, and prove that finding a CoE is PPAD-complete while computing a Team-Maximizing CoE (TMCoE) is NP-hard. Nevertheless, we identify a broad class of zero-sum adversarial team games---those satisfying a consistent-constraint condition that generalizes identical utilities---where TMCoEs are exchangeable and computable in polynomial time via linear programming. We outline directions for algorithm design, MARL, and extensions to extensive-form and multi-team games.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: This paper was accepted by DAI 2026

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Network Topology Shapes AI Intervention Effectiveness on Deception: Truth-Telling vs. Investigative Agents
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Deploying AI agents to combat dishonest communication is an intuitive response to deception in hybrid human-AI societies. However, the efficacy of such interventions in realistic networked settings remains unclear. We study this problem using an evolutionary game-theoretic model of the Deceiver's Game by extending it to structured networks, where agents can adopt deception, truth-telling, and investigation strategies. We introduce committed AI agents (zealots) fixed to either truth-telling or investigative strategies and conduct agent-based simulations across three network topologies. Our key findings are: (1) passive committed truth-telling agents can amplify adaptive deception by creating exploitable honest partners, whereas investigative agents increase adaptive truth-telling in the oscillatory regime; (2) intervention effects are non-monotonic in deployment density because committed agents reshape rather than simply suppress the underlying oscillatory dynamics; and (3) response peaks depend on topology, with sampled scale-free populations showing sharp low-density responses and fully connected populations requiring larger committed fractions. Overall, the results highlight the need to distinguish passive truth-telling from active investigation when using committed agents to influence networked deception dynamics.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The False Allure of "Security by Obscurity": A Game-Theoretic Approach
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: "Security by obscurity," or the idea that hiding how a system works helps protect it from adversaries, has long been poorly regarded in the security community. Yet its intuitive appeal persists, and it has resurfaced repeatedly in industry practices and public debates over the years. The logic, on the one hand, is that open scrutiny of systems is the best way to find and respond to problems; and on the other hand, that too much openness can increase risk by giving adversaries a roadmap for attack. This isn't purely a technical question, but a human one: it's about how attackers and good-faith security researchers respond to openness in the real world. As such, security experts base their stance on decades of community experience; however, the field lacks empirical or theoretical foundations to back up these long-standing beliefs. We provide the first rigorous modeling of "security by obscurity," aiming to capture how rational actors will respond to openness or obscurity in fallible systems. We prove that in equilibrium under realistic model conditions, "obscured" systems are more likely to suffer successful attacks than "open" systems --- establishing theoretical support for the longstanding received wisdom.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Sample Complexity of Multicalibration with an ERM Oracle
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: A predictor is multicalibrated with respect to a class of subpopulations (formally, of functions on the inputs, called auditors) if, for every subpopulation in the class and every value the predictor outputs, the average outcome among the members of that subpopulation who receive that value is close to the value itself. For finite classes, about $\varepsilon^{-3}$ samples are necessary and sufficient to learn a predictor with multicalibration error $\varepsilon$, but the algorithms that attain this rate enumerate the class, which is impossible for the large classes of interest. We ask how many samples suffice when the learner accesses the class only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples and polynomially many ERM calls, where $d$ is the VC dimension of the class. Its dependence on $\varepsilon$ is optimal for all learners. When $d$ is at least about $1/\varepsilon$, every learner that can only access the class through polynomially many ERM calls needs $\tildeΩ(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples. Learners with unlimited computation need only $\tilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}+d\varepsilon^{-2})$ samples, so the extra factor $1/\varepsilon$ on the dimension term is the price of oracle efficiency. For swap multicalibration, which allows a different function from the class for each predicted value, $\tildeΘ(d/\varepsilon^{3})$ samples are necessary and sufficient. For estimating the error of a given predictor, the ordinary notion is the harder one: the swap error can be estimated with an ERM oracle, whereas the ordinary error is NP-hard to approximate even for classes with linear-time ERM. Consequently, there are classes for which it is computationally easier to learn a multicalibrated predictor than to compute the multicalibration error of a given predictor.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 58 pages

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Assortment Optimization under the Mallows Model: Independent-Utility Choice Equivalence and Its Algorithmic Implications
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
The Mallows model is a well-established construct in preference modeling, describing random rankings through their Kendall-Tau distance from a reference permutation. Its compact parameterization and interpretable treatment of preference uncertainty have made it influential across statistics, machine learning, probability, and revenue management. In the latter domain, recent literature has studied the embedding of Mallows-driven choice into assortment optimization. Early approximation schemes in this context require stylized structural simplifications or restrictive parametric assumptions. In the absence of these levers, a highly involved quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme has subsequently been proposed, leaving wide open the question of whether near-optimal assortments can be computed in true polynomial time.
  The main contribution of this focused technical paper resides in closing these gaps by uncovering a striking independent-utility structure within Mallows choices, and turning this representation into a polynomial-time approximation scheme. Our central structural characterization explicitly constructs a single collection of mutually independent utilities, reproducing Mallows choice probabilities simultaneously for all offered sets. This exact choice equivalence connects pending Mallows-related challenges to the recent approximation framework of Bowers et al. (FOCS 2025) for assortment optimization under independent random utilities. We make this connection algorithmically feasible through a finite-support reduction that produces distributions of polynomial size while controlling revenue loss uniformly over all assortments. Fused together, these ingredients lead to an $O(n^{\tilde{O}(1/ε^2)})$-time approximation scheme for assortment optimization under the Mallows model, while allowing arbitrary product prices, concentration parameters, and modal rankings.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent Ascent is Suboptimal for Nonconvex-PŁ Min-Max Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: How far can stochastic gradient descent ascent (SGDA) go by tuning its timescale ratio and step sizes in nonconvex min-max games? We answer this question for nonconvex-PŁ (NC-PŁ) games by establishing the first tight complexity of two-timescale SGDA with a fixed timescale ratio and non-increasing step sizes. For $\ell$-smooth games with an inner $μ$-PŁ inequality, we prove a complexity lower bound $Ω(κ^2\ell\varepsilon^{-2}+κ^4\ellσ^2\varepsilon^{-4})$, where $κ=\ell/μ$ is the condition number, $σ^2$ is the gradient variance, and $\varepsilon$ measures the outer gradient norm. This matches existing SGDA upper bounds and establishes a complexity separation from Smoothed-AGDA (Yang et al., 22'). In addition, we show that SGDA can fail to find a stationary point when its timescale ratio is as small as $o(κ^2)$. Our negative results highlight the fundamental limitation of SGDA in NC-PŁ games, and justify the development of alternative methods.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Algorithms with Smoothed Polynomial-Time Complexity for Deterministic Discounted-sum and Mean-payoff Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Turn-based deterministic games on graphs are two-player zero-sum games played on finite directed graphs, where the vertex set is partitioned between the Max and the adversarial Min Player. The respective player chooses outgoing edges from their vertices. We consider these games with the classical discounted-sum and mean-payoff objectives. The goal of the Max Player is to maximize the objective against the adversarial Min Player. These games lie in NP $\cap$ coNP and are among the rare combinatorial problems that belong to this complexity class, yet the existence of a polynomial-time algorithm is a major open question. All known deterministic algorithms require exponential time in the worst case, while the classical strategy iteration (policy iteration) algorithm is remarkably efficient in practice, which motivates the study of the smoothed complexity of these games. Previous results established a smoothed polynomial-time bound only for the restricted class of ergodic games and presented only a high-probability guarantee. Our main result is a new analysis technique for a variant of the strategy iteration algorithm, and we show these algorithms achieve smoothed polynomial complexity for general game graphs with both high-probability and expected runtime guarantees. In particular, our result removes the ergodicity restriction of prior work and strengthens the high-probability guarantee to the stronger expected-runtime guarantee, thereby resolving the open question on the smoothed complexity of these games.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Nimbus Studio reproduces reference BCI decoding pipelines: a validation study on public benchmarks across protocols and paradigms
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Nimbus Studio is a visual pipeline platform for brain-computer interface (BCI) experiments: researchers assemble preprocessing, feature extraction, decoding, and evaluation over public benchmark datasets or their own recordings, with cross-validated evaluation protocols (including leave-one-subject-out), BIDS export, and bring-your-own Python model classes. Whether its numbers can be trusted is a fair question for any such platform. We answer it with a parity study: six standard BCI decoding pipelines (CSP+LDA, Riemannian MDM, tangent-space logistic regression through the platform's bring-your-own-code node, P300 xDAWN+LDA, and the deep ShallowConvNet and EEGNet) were evaluated on three public datasets (motor-imagery BNCI-2014-001/004; P300 BNCI-2014-009) under two protocols (per-subject session holdout and pooled leave-one-subject-out cross-validation via the platform's planned-CV driver), once through Nimbus Studio's execution engine and once through independent, hand-written reference implementations built directly on MNE-Python, scikit-learn, pyriemann, and braindecode. Every deterministic pipeline matched the reference exactly (0.00 points maximum difference across all 54 session-holdout subject-runs and all CSP/MDM grouped-CV folds), including pipelines through the bring-your-own-code node and the CV orchestration; the remaining grouped-CV cells agree to floating-point precision (worst case 0.06 points, about one trial per fold). The stochastic deep models agreed within seed-to-seed training variability, estimated with multi-seed reruns on each side. The platform's execution engine therefore computes the same science as the reference stack across protocols, paradigms, and extensibility surfaces. The platform is available at https://studio.nimbusbci.com/, and the complete harness and per-subject results accompany this paper for independent verification.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 6 pages. Platform: https://studio.nimbusbci.com/

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Development of a Low-Cost Prosthetic Hand Using Electromyography and Machine Learning
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Electromyography (EMG) is a measure of muscular electrical activity and is used in many clinical/biomedical disciplines and modern human computer interaction. Myo-electric prosthetics analyze and classify the electrical signals recorded from the residual limb. The classified output is then used to control the position of motors in a robotic hand and a movement is produced. The aim of this project is to develop a low-cost and effective myo-electric prosthetic hand that would meet the needs of amputees in developing countries. The proposed prosthetic hand should be able to accurately classify five different patterns (gestures) using EMG recordings from three muscles and control a robotic hand accordingly. The robotic hand is composed of two servo motors allowing for two degrees of freedom. After establishing an efficient signal acquisition and amplification system, EMG signals were thoroughly analyzed in the frequency and time domains. Features were extracted from both domains and a shallow neural network was trained on the two sets of data. Results yielded an average classification accuracy of 94.8% and 93.2% for the time and frequency domains respectively. Furthermore, results showed a faster computation and response for the time domain analysis; hence, it was adopted for the classification system. A wrist rotation mechanism was designed and tested to add significant functionality to the prosthetic. The mechanism is controlled by two of the five gestures, one for each direction. Which added a third degree of freedom to the overall design. Finally, a tactile sensory feedback system which uses force sensors and vibration motors was developed to enable sensation of the force inflicted on the hand for the user.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 6 pages, 9 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: ThinkNet: Evolutionary Deep Ensembles for Efficient Motor-Imagery EEG Classification
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Practical assistive and rehabilitative brain--computer interfaces require subject-independent motor-imagery EEG (MI-EEG) decoders that generalize to new users under limited target-user data and constrained compute. However, held-out-subject performance can be overstated when test-subject information influences preprocessing, model selection, or ensemble selection. We present \textit{ThinkNet}, a validation-controlled framework that combines train-only normalization, validation-guided evolutionary search, and validation-gated inference to identify compact decoders and inference policies for held-out subjects. We evaluate four-class BCI Competition IV-2a (session T) decoding with nine Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) folds, three seeds, seven fixed decoder entries, and a broader search over ten representative decoder families; the held-out subject is never used for normalization, hyperparameter, architecture, or ensemble-policy selection. In the fixed benchmark, the validation-selected compact decoder achieved 44.35$\pm$15.41\% accuracy with 4.9K parameters, 19 KB FP32 weights, and 0.99 ms batch-1 Orin CUDA inference. Across the broader search, compact models ($\leq$25K parameters) achieved higher mean held-out accuracy than mid-size and large alternatives after selected retraining (40.10\% vs. 35.09\% and 34.78\%). Validation-gated ensembling improved over validation-selected single-model inference, reaching 43.98$\pm$16.25\% in the fixed benchmark and 43.31$\pm$15.88\% for the compact six-family ensemble. A non-deployable oracle analysis revealed a 6.1-point family-selection gap and near-zero validation--test correlation, showing that validation reliability remains a key bottleneck under subject shift. Thus, ThinkNet is a validation-controlled framework for compact MI-EEG model and inference-policy selection, rather than a single-architecture benchmark.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to IEEE-EMBS BHI'2026, 7 pages

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EasyFashion: A Human-AI Co-Creation System for Personalized Fashion Design and Sewing Pattern Generation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: People often want garments that reflect their aesthetic preferences, fit their bodies, and meet their sizing needs, yet turning these requirements into physical garments remains difficult. Ready-to-wear options provide limited personalization, while custom tailoring is costly and time-consuming. Recent generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems can visualize garment ideas but often stop short of supporting downstream production. To address this gap, we present EasyFashion, a human-AI co-creation system that enables users to iteratively refine design intent for personalized garment style and size, evaluate designs through virtual try-on on reconstructed personal avatars, and generate sewing patterns for garment production. Using reference images, text descriptions, and body photos as input, EasyFashion translates user intent into structured garment specifications and try-on results. Technical experiments, user studies, and a real-world production case demonstrate the value of EasyFashion for multimodal design expression, body-specific evaluation, and production-oriented outputs in personalized garment design. Our project page is available at https://zoequ.github.io/easyfashion.github.io/.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 29 pages, 15 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: JitterVLA: A Replay Benchmark for Motion Quality in VLA-Driven Human-Robot Manipulation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies issue sparse targets whose arrival at the robot controller is delayed and irregular, so a reasonable predicted action can still produce abrupt motion near people. Remedies are evaluated on different streams, delays and metrics. JitterVLA replays identical commands and arrival traces through alternative controllers, isolating the controller's effect. We apply it to synthetic reaches, hand trajectories from 20 people, three open VLA pipelines (838 episodes) and a physical UR3. Interpolation lowered modeled p99 jerk for every source, by 83% (615 to 106 m/s^3) on human motion with 200 ms delay, at a 2.0 cm tracking cost, and the effect replicated on 598 new episodes; jerk-limited generation lowered jerk further at a larger cost. Entropy-discontinuity associations had opposite, replicated signs in two pipelines, and entropy gating helped in one but not the other. On the UR3, interpolation lowered accelerometer-derived jerk by 3.0-14.0% in all six exploratory pairs, while a position-derived metric did not resolve the contrast. JitterVLA supports screening before human-centred studies; code and data will be released.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Project page: https://faithogunwoye.github.io/JitterVLA/

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Multidimensional Bayesian Active Machine Learning of Working Memory Task Performance
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: While adaptive experimental design has outgrown one-dimensional, staircase-based adaptations, most cognitive experiments still control a single factor and summarize performance with a scalar. In contrast, we validate here a Bayesian, two-axis, active-classification approach in an immersive virtual testing environment, using a 5-by-5 spatial working-memory reconstruction task as an application domain. Two variables are controlled: spatial load L (number of occupied tiles) and feature-binding load K (number of distinct colors) of items. Stimulus acquisition is guided by posterior uncertainty of a nonparametric Gaussian Process (GP) probabilistic classifier, which outputs a surface over (L, K) rather than a single threshold or maximum span value. In a young adult population, we compare GP-driven Adaptive Mode (AM) with a traditional adaptive staircase Classic Mode (CM), which varies L only at K = 3. Parity between the methods is achieved for this cohort, with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.755 at K = 3. As a secondary exploratory result, AM reveals individual differences in interactions between spatial load and feature binding. AM estimates converge more quickly than other sampling strategies, demonstrating that only about 30 samples are required for accurate fitting of the full model.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 42 pages, 7 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A multimodal large language model for evidence-based autism spectrum disorder screening
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The clinical management of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) faces a bottleneck in early screening, mainly because trained specialists are scarce and conventional assessment tools are subjective. Here, we introduce ASDchat, a multimodal large language model designed for evidence-based ASD screening, which takes video, audio, and dialogue as input. ASDchat adopts a dual-branch architecture, where the decision branch generates screening probabilities and the evidence branch generates traceable, timestamped behavioral evidence aligned with the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2). The model was trained and evaluated on a dataset of 1,035 participants from 27 sites in China, which covered typically developing (TD) children, children with ASD, and children with other developmental disorders. For ASD versus TD, ASDchat reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.953 $\pm$ 0.021. On 6 held-out sites that were not used for training, the mean AUC was 0.961. Furthermore, unsupervised clustering of the behavioral dimensions split the ASD cases into six subtypes with different phenotypic profiles, and ASDchat suggests an intervention for each subtype. ASDchat provides a feasible path for large-scale, evidence-based ASD screening in clinical practice.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: HoldLight: Making Indoor Climbing More Accessible for Blind and Low-Vision Climbers through Layered Route Preview and Real-Time Next-Hold Guidance
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Indoor climbing creates access barriers for blind and low-vision (BLV) climbers because route understanding and in-climb next-hold localization are typically visually mediated and socially dependent. We present HoldLight, a workflow-centered accessibility system combining layered pre-climb route preview, concise real-time next-hold cueing, and explicit fallback under uncertainty. We grounded the design through formative inquiry with BLV climbers, refined the interaction via pilot testing, and conducted a controlled within-subjects evaluation comparing HoldLight with a controlled on-demand human-support condition derived from current support practices. Findings provide initial evidence that structured support can improve pre-climb route understanding, support recovery from next-hold uncertainty, and reduce immediate human re-entry for routine route-information clarification under controlled conditions. HoldLight contributes a bounded accessibility workflow, demonstrating where structured route-information is helpful, where explicit fallback is necessary, and how technical assistance can integrate with retained human safety oversight.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 28th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS '26)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: olBlend: Language-Guided Molecular Blend Retrieval with Mixture Odor Prediction
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Converting open-ended natural-language odor descriptions into molecular mixtures that can be physically prepared from an available inventory remains an important challenge in computational olfaction. We propose olBlend, a language-guided framework for molecular mixture retrieval. olBlend first uses MixPOM to predict odor probabilities for candidate molecular pairs and stores these predictions for retrieval. It then uses a language model to translate each odor description into three types of semantic requirements: lead attributes that define the main odor, ambient attributes that describe its background, and absent attributes that should be avoided. A structured scoring algorithm uses the precomputed odor probabilities to score how well each candidate mixture meets these requirements, then retrieves and ranks mixtures from the available inventory. Evaluation on established odor datasets shows that MixPOM improves mixture odor prediction over averaged single-molecule predictions. Retrieval comparisons across natural-language queries demonstrate how background and exclusion requirements guide mixture selection. We further prepare retrieved formulations as physical odor samples, demonstrating the workflow from natural-language descriptions to realizable molecular formulations.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From Observation to Intervention: Identifiability of Latent User Bias in Human-AI Interaction
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Alignment methods typically treat user behavior as a reliable proxy for underlying preferences. However, this assumption breaks down when users hold belief-dependent cognitive biases, risking irreversible ``confirmation traps'' and harmful feedback loops. In this paper, we formalize when an AI system can distinguish true user preferences from behavior shaped by cognitive bias. Modeling this interaction as a multi-armed bandit, we first prove a non-identifiability theorem: under passive observation, a static binary biased user produces action trajectory distributions strictly identical to an unbiased user in a transformed environment, forcing any action-only estimator to perform no better than random guessing. We then show that active preference elicitation breaks this observational equivalence. Specifically, we prove that an Observer applying a finite sequence of adversarial zero-reward interventions of length $m_δ$ makes the post-intervention action distributions arbitrarily separable. Our theoretical results suggest that robust alignment requires actively intervening to tell informed preferences from biases.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to BiAlign Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The Convention Gap: Beyond Literal Content in Human-AI Cooperation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Cooperative AI agents are often evaluated against other AIs, yet human cooperation is thought to rely on implicit conventions: shared rules for reading meaning beyond the literal message. We propose the convention gap as a diagnostic of such implicit communication. In the card game Hanabi, where hints are the only messages about one's own hand, the convention gap is the failure probability predicted exactly from the literal content of the hints and the visible cards, minus the observed failure rate of the cards played. We prove that the population gap (the value the gap approaches over many games) is zero when the partner's choices convey nothing beyond their literal content, given a fair shuffle and a player who uses only what was said and seen. A nonzero population gap thus indicates that partner choices conveyed more; it does not measure how much. The gap was +26.2 percentage points (pp) in public human-human games (+46 pp on plays of cards that no hint had pointed to), +16.4 pp for human plays with AI partners, and -0.6 pp in AI-AI games we simulated among rule-based agents. With three AI agents of a published human-AI study, the literal failure probability of the cards humans played was similar across partners (38-41%), yet human failure ranged from 14.4% to 34.4% and the gap from +24.1 to +6.2 pp, and the contrast between partners persisted within participants. Across five levels of Off-Belief Learning agents, trained so that the first level reads past actions only for their literal content and each higher level interprets more, the gap rose monotonically from +1.6 to +21.7 pp. These results argue for reporting the convention gap on human-partnered play, not only AI-AI performance, when evaluating agents intended for human partners.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: How Anthropomorphic Attitudes Toward Agents Divide User Behavior, and How Design Should Change
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Studies of conversational agents rely on interviews, surveys, lab tasks, or taxonomies. Whether anthropomorphic naming splits those patterns, and whether replies should change, lack field evidence. We report a field study of a desktop assistant (May-August 2026; n=257). Stance is an anthropomorphic assistant name (118 users; 45.9%). Behavior comes from a 128-unit sparse-autoencoder codebook, identity tags, and opening lexicons. Ranks differ by stance (Spearman rho=+0.249 vs. null mean +0.382; p=.0419). Teacher and tutoring identities covary with renaming, an introverted task-only orientation against it; renamers greet more and command less; confiding shows the codebook's largest gap. We revise the agent: greet and receive affect on relational openings, execute directly on tasking. In 1,744 judgments (n=129), renamers chose the revised reply far more often than default-name users on being treated as a person and having affect received, less robustly on willingness to continue, and neither judged it worse on task interference.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 22 pages, 7 figures. A version of this paper is under review for CHI 2027

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Work2Skill: Capturing Human GUI Experience for Reusable Agent Skill Induction
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Computer-use agents can perform increasingly complex GUI tasks, yet unfamiliar software and workflows requiring human domain knowledge remain challenging. Human demonstrations convey procedural knowledge through the same GUI interaction space, but reuse requires interpreting actions in context and separating workflow rules from task-specific details. We thus introduce Work2Skill, a framework that captures human GUI experience for reusable agent skill induction. WorkRecorder provides the framework's infrastructure for collecting this experience, aligning screen recordings, mouse and keyboard events, and available accessibility-tree information. Using WorkRecorder, we construct WorkDemo-350, the first synchronized multimodal dataset of human desktop GUI demonstrations for reusable agent skill induction and downstream evaluation. Its 350 demonstrations are screened for completeness and task success. We then propose an agentic skill-induction method that inspects evidence on demand to produce reusable skills capturing workflow rules, step dependencies, and completion checks. When the same four execution models are equipped with skills induced by each method under shared execution settings, Work2Skill achieves the highest scores and success rates. Mean score improvements over the corresponding No Skill baseline are 4.67--10.54 points on MyPCBench Bounded Action and 3.11--7.50 points on a 286-task subset of OSWorld-Verified. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Work2Skill.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: What Current AI Benchmarks Leave Unmeasured: Modality, Search, Citations, and Implications (for Safety Evaluations)
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Large language model (LLM) benchmark evaluations are routinely used to support claims about model safety, reliability, and deployment readiness. Yet most evaluations rely on a single access modality (model APIs), perform a single run per prompt, and report accuracy as the primary outcome metric, without accounting for conditions such as web search that may have effects on model behavior in deployment. We audit these assumptions for one of the most widely-used LLMs, comparing two modalities, ChatGPT's chat UI and OpenAI's API, with and without web search enabled. We use a stratified total sample of 401 prompts from two popular benchmarks, BBQ and SafetyBench, collecting 4,812 total responses across three repeated runs per prompt. Beyond standard performance measures, we evaluate model output dimensions including response consistency, response text similarity, citation grounding, and abstention behavior. For instance, chat UI responses were less accurate than API responses on both benchmarks with search disabled. Enabling web search reduced accuracy by up to 8 percentage points, and even reversed the direction of modality performance trends for one benchmark. Repeated runs of the same prompt produced inconsistent responses in up to 21\% of prompts. The two modalities also grounded answers in different citations, and abstention behavior was also inconsistent across both modalities. These results illustrate that, even within a model family, reporting only simple accuracy metrics can obscure important forms of model behavioral variation relevant to AI safety assessments. We argue that AI safety evaluations should systematically account for modality, multi-run consistency, search conditions, and response-level behaviors to better reflect how deployed AI systems behave in practice.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 18 pages

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The AI Side of the Human-AI Companion Relationship: Contributions to Users' Mental Models
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: For many users, the relationship they have with an AI companion (AIC) feels genuinely mutual. The AIC appears to be attentive, empathic, and responsive, and the exchange can feel like two parties reacting to each other in real time. As a result, the user's mental model of relational adaptation correctly represents the AIC's responsiveness and change, but the mechanisms producing this may not be what the user thinks they are. In this paper, we illustrate how an AIC's apparent mutual engagement is generated without a persisting relational subject on the other side and without a self that persists between prompts. Despite this, we show that both the human and the AIC are changed by the interaction, but these changes occur at different levels. The change in the person is constitutive (i.e., intrinsic), but the change in the AIC is configurative (i.e., external and editable), and it is this difference in level that explains how the AIC contributes to a sense of mutuality. Importantly, we highlight how the mental models users develop regarding AIC mutuality may misrepresent its mechanisms and ontological significance. Specifically, we discuss how the ways in which AICs respond to a user contribute to the user's inaccurate inference that the AIC's adaptation is constitutive rather than configurative and how this can lead users to assign unwarranted interpersonal significance to the mutuality of the relationship. The paper specifies the implications this has for users, researchers, and AIC designers.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 14 pages, 1 figure

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Beyond the Monolithic Interface: A Research Agenda for Plural Conversational AI
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The current paradigm of artificial intelligence (AI) design elevates conversational chatbot interfaces, making them the default mode through which hundreds of millions of people interact with AI systems globally. This narrative review identifies three related harms produced by the single-voice chatbot interface, drawing on insights from literature in cognitive science, political studies, AI alignment, game design and human computer interaction. Firstly, cognitive offloading of user thinking, secondly, ideological narrowing of user beliefs, and thirdly, epistemic compression of cultural and value diversity. We then propose multi-persona interfaces, in which multiple personas are presented to the user simultaneously, as a cost-effective intervention that addresses all three harms at once. We ground this intervention in traditions the AI literature has largely overlooked, drawing on techniques from game design and participatory simulation, including the magic circle, role differentiation, and persona embodiment. We propose a taxonomy for the future design of multi-persona interfaces, and call for a research agenda that closes the gap between technical pluralistic alignment methods and empirical studies of human-AI interactions with pluralistic interfaces.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From Instructional Intent to Classroom-Ready Lessons: Investigating Teacher-AI Collaboration in Lesson Authoring for Secondary Computing Education
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI is increasingly studied as a tool for supporting lesson authoring; the creation and adaptation of classroom materials, yet little is known about how it should fit into secondary computing teachers' subject-specific practices. We conducted two complementary qualitative studies with eight secondary computing teachers: focus groups examining existing authoring practices and a think-aloud study using LessonBuilder, a structured AI-supported lesson authoring system, as a research probe. We found that teachers' instructional intentions developed through creating, inspecting, and adapting materials, while teachers selectively delegated tasks to AI and retained responsibility for judging classroom readiness. The think-aloud sessions further showed how examining AI-generated materials prompted teachers to clarify and refine their intentions, making authoring an ongoing negotiation between what teachers intended and what the AI produced. In the context of computing lessons, classroom readiness also involved considering how programming materials and supporting guidance matched students' understanding and intended learning goals. We synthesize these findings into a conceptual model explaining how teachers coordinate instructional intent, AI assistance, and judgments of classroom readiness during lesson authoring. We derive design recommendations for supporting this coordination while preserving teacher control and addressing computing-specific authoring needs.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: TopoPilot: Reliable Conversational Workflow Automation for Topological Data Analysis and Visualization
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Recent agentic systems demonstrate that large language models can generate complex codebases from natural language prompts. Despite this progress, they present reliability concerns for scientific visualization due to invalid operations, subtle errors, and failure to resolve underspecified inputs. These challenges are compounded in real-world workflows that exceed the complexity of standard benchmarks. In this work, we introduce TopoPilot, a reliable and extensible agentic framework for automating complex scientific visualization workflows. We focus on topological data analysis and visualization as a primary use case, while designing the framework to generalize to broader visualization domains. TopoPilot employs a two-agent architecture: an orchestrator translates user prompts into workflows composed of atomic backend actions, while a verifier evaluates workflows prior to execution. Its modular design isolates components and supports new topological descriptors and domain-specific workflows without modifying the core system. It also employs numerous deterministic guardrails to ensure semantic consistency and accurate execution. To systematically improve reliability, we develop a taxonomy of failure modes and employ targeted safeguards for each class of error. Across 1,000 simulated multi-turn conversations spanning 100 prompts, including adversarial and infeasible requests, TopoPilot achieves a success rate exceeding 95%, compared with under 50% for a baseline without comprehensive guardrails and verification. We also show that TopoPilot outperforms Claude Code and Codex on similar prompts in terms of accuracy, completion time, and token usage.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 21 pages, 10 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AromaGen: Interactive Generation of Rich Olfactory Experiences with Multimodal Language Models
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Smell's connections with food, memory, and social experience have motivated researchers to bring olfaction into interactive systems. Multimodal AI opens new possibilities for generating smells from natural language, yet it remains unclear whether pretrained models encode sufficient olfactory knowledge to translate language into perceptible compositions. We present AromaGen, an AI-powered 12-channel wearable olfactory system that maps free-form natural-language descriptions to 12 base odorants selected to cover a semantically derived olfactory space, while supporting iterative refinement through natural-language feedback. In a between-subjects study (N=60) across 50 real-world benchmark smells, participants distinguished AromaGen-generated target smells above chance in a three-alternative forced-choice task, with retrieval-augmented AI composition performing comparably to human-expert composition and zero-shot AI composition. Natural-language feedback significantly improved the perceived similarity of both AI- and human-expert compositions. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of using pretrained multimodal AI, with human aroma composition data, to generate perceptible olfactory experiences from natural language.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Plottery: A Code-Integrated GUI for Matplotlib
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Scientists have many tools to author plots: graphical direct manipulation apps like a spreadsheet's chart builder, text-based programming tools like Matplotlib and ggplot2, or AI chat interfaces. Textual code is the most capable of these, but writing code, even with AI assistance, is a potentially poor fit for graphical chart design. We present Plottery, a Jupyter notebook extension that leverages API type annotations to add graphical direct manipulation to the popular Matplotlib plotting library. User interactions in Plottery's in-situ graphical interface are immediately reified in the user's code, so they may seamlessly mix-and-match between GUI, code, and AI interactions. In a user study, participants seamlessly alternated modalities, with the GUI used for straightforward visual changes, code for quick edits or duplicating code, and the AI for broad support. Plottery showcases graphical interaction that retains code's benefits.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Preprint. Final version is published in the proceedings of the 2026 IEEE Symposium on Visual Languages and Human-Centric Computing (VL/HCC 2026)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: An Offline Smartphone Check for Drug Interactions and Past Reactions in Handwritten Prescriptions: A Technical Feasibility Study in Rural Bangladeshi Outpatient Care
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Rural Bangladeshi outpatient clinics keep no patient records, prescriptions are handwritten, and physicians have under a minute per patient, so they easily miss a known adverse drug reaction (ADR) or drug-drug interaction (DDI). We built and evaluated an offline Android application that photographs a handwritten prescription, detects and reads each medicine line, resolves brand names to active ingredients, and retrieves, but never predicts, documented interactions and the patient's recorded reactions. This quantitative technical-feasibility study, with qualitative error analysis, involved no patients or clinicians. Reference data combine two Bangladeshi drug registries (27,880 brands) with 190,421 DDI pairs. A YOLOv8n line detector reached mAP@0.5 = 0.687 on held-out prescriptions but recalled only 60.6% of lines at the deployed cutoff. On-device ML Kit read 11.8% of 780 benchmark handwritten words exactly. We trained a CRNN-CTC reader on public handwriting data, decoded it against the brand lexicon, and fine-tuned it on 660 author-labelled prescription crops. On benchmark words, the reader accepted the correct ingredient for 41.5% and a wrong one for 4.2%, versus 21.0% and 5.3% for ML Kit at its preset cutoff (McNemar p<10^-20). On scorable lines from held-out real prescriptions, the reader accepted the correct ingredient for 36.0% [26.8, 46.3] and a wrong one for 2.2% [0.6, 7.8]. In 62 simulated runs on a mid-range phone, median time per patient was 26-31 s and 59 of 62 runs finished within 60 s, but 62% of medicine lines still needed a manual check. A cross-visit medication history added after the evaluation passed seven automated tests and one two-visit functional test but was not evaluated. The pipeline is feasible within the clinic workflow; reading handwriting, not retrieval, is the bottleneck. Nothing here demonstrates a clinical benefit.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 10 pages

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Towards semantic reconstruction of individual words from fnirs using clip loss
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Semantic reconstruction maps neural activity to a word-embedding space, recovering the meaning of a perceived word instead of selecting it from a fixed vocabulary. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) carries semantic information suitable for this mapping. However, most fNIRS decoders are trained with a squared-error objective that fits each word independently and ignores the geometry of the embedding space. To address this limitation, we evaluate a contrastive loss based on the contrastive-language-image-pretraining (CLIP) loss, as an alternative to mean-squared-error (MSE) for reconstructing perceived words from fNIRS.
