The Newton systems are solved by the minimal residual method with a block-diagonal preconditioner. We prove that the spectrum of the Newton operator with respect to the inner product defined by the preconditioner is bounded independently of the proximity parameter, the iterate, the mesh and the observation and control domains. The results are combined into a complete algorithm, and tested in numerical experiments.

Optimization and Control.title: On the optimization of discrepancy measures
Optimization and Control.summary:
Points in the unit cube with low discrepancy can be constructed using algebra or, more recently, by direct computational optimization of a criterion. The usual $L_\infty$ star discrepancy is a poor criterion for this because it is computationally expensive and lacks differentiability. Its usual replacement, the $L_2$ star discrepancy, is smooth but exhibits other pathologies shown by J. Matoušek. In an attempt to address these problems, we introduce the \textit{average squared discrepancy} which averages over $2^d$ versions of the $L_2$ star discrepancy anchored in the different vertices of $[0,1]^d$. Not only can this criterion be computed in $O(dn^2)$ time, like the $L_2$ star discrepancy, but also we show that it is equivalent to a weighted symmetric $L_2$ criterion of Hickernell's by a constant factor. We compare this criterion with a wide range of traditional discrepancy measures, and show that only the average squared discrepancy avoids the problems raised by Matoušek. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive numerical study showing in particular that optimizing for the average squared discrepancy leads to strong performance for the $L_2$ star discrepancy, whereas the converse does not hold.
  This version corrects some of the threshold sample sizes n at which random points become better than n repeated points for some discrepancy measures. In particular, the periodic L_2 discrepancy has no repeated point pathology.

Optimization and Control.title: A Logarithmic-dual-update Bregman ADMM for Optimal Transport
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper studies an entropy Bregman alternating direction method of multipliers (BADMM) with logarithmic dual update for solving discrete optimal transport (OT) problems. The algorithm uses simple row and column normalizations without inner iterations, allowing efficient CPU and GPU implementations. However, the convergence of this method for general OT problems has not been established. Starting from a strictly positive feasible primal point and a zero multiplier, here we establish the $R$-linear convergence of the primal--dual sequence for general OT costs with any fixed multiplier stepsize in $(0,2)$ and a sufficiently large fixed penalty, even when the primal limit lies on the boundary. Our analysis further characterizes the primal limit as the entropy Bregman projection of the initial point onto the optimal solution set and establishes strict complementarity of the limiting OT primal--dual solution. For separable costs on two-dimensional grids, we exploit the separable structure to accelerate matrix--vector products and reduce storage requirements. Numerical experiments show competitive performance of our BADMM for general cost matrices with substantial speedups over state-of-the-art solvers, including HOT and HALO, for squared Euclidean costs on two-dimensional-grid marginals. The largest tested problem, with $2048\times2048 \approx 4.19$M grid points in each marginal, is solved in approximately 100 seconds on a single GPU.

Optimization and Control.title: Structure and Conditioning in Finite-Horizon Continuous-Time Inverse LQR with Unknown Dynamics
Optimization and Control.summary: Inverse Optimal Control (IOC) aims to infer the underlying cost functional of an agent from observations of its expert behavior. This paper studies the finite-horizon continuous-time inverse LQR problem from closed-loop state--input trajectories, where both the system matrices and the quadratic cost are unknown. The finite horizon induces a time-varying optimal gain, and this endogenous excitation serves as the structural mechanism that makes joint recovery possible. We quantify this mechanism through three computable conditioning indices, which measure state richness, gain-variation richness, and injectivity of a structured cost operator. Using these indices, we establish joint identifiability conditions for the inverse problem considered here. Crucially, these conditions guarantee recovery of the ground-truth system matrices $(A,B)$ and the true cost weighting matrices, rather than merely a behaviorally equivalent surrogate. We also develop a conditioning-aware sampled-data reconstruction method that reconstructs the gain $K(\cdot)$ and the closed-loop dynamics matrix $A_c(\cdot)$ from noisy measurements, recovers $(A,B)$ in closed form, and identifies the quadratic weights through a convex semidefinite program. We further establish the non-asymptotic perturbation bounds and the consistency of the full reconstruction method under sub-Gaussian observation noise, with explicit dependence on the same conditioning indices. Numerical experiments support the theory and illustrate the diagnostic value of the conditioning indices.
Optimization and Control.comment: Updated the title and corrected minor typographical errors

Optimization and Control.title: Distributed Stochastic Proximal Algorithm on Riemannian Submanifolds for Weakly-convex Functions
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper aims to investigate the distributed stochastic optimization problems on compact embedded submanifolds (in the Euclidean space) where the local cost functions are weakly-convex. To address the manifold structure, we propose a distributed Riemannian stochastic proximal algorithm framework by utilizing the retraction and Riemannian consensus protocol, and analyze three specific algorithms: the distributed Riemannian stochastic subgradient, proximal point, and prox-linear algorithms. When the initial points satisfy certain conditions, we show that the iterates generated by this framework converge to a nearly stationary point in expectation while achieving consensus. We further establish the convergence rate of the algorithm framework as $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1+κ_g}{\sqrt{k}})$ where $k$ denotes the number of iterations and $κ_g$ shows the impact of manifold geometry on the algorithm performance. Finally, numerical experiments are implemented to demonstrate the theoretical results and show the empirical performance.

Optimization and Control.title: Minimal time for heat observability on almost-Riemannian surfaces
Optimization and Control.summary: We determine the minimal observation time for the heat equation on a closed almost-Riemannian surface, for a class of observation sets leaving sufficiently thin collars around simple Baouendi-Grushin circles. The structure and density are analytic near these circles, and the coefficients may depend on both variables. The formula is expressed through a complex phase describing concentration near the singular set and extends the thresholds known for separated models. Regular unobserved regions away from the circles do not change this time, provided all other singularities are observed. For singular circles of constant bracket step greater than two, local analyticity implies failure of observability at every time for observation sets at positive distance. We also construct quasimodes concentrated near simple singular circles, with exponentially small errors. Their superpositions give a lower bound for the Schrödinger observation time.

Optimization and Control.title: Scalable Identification of Physics-Based and Neural Dynamics from Partial Measurements
Optimization and Control.summary: We present a scalable method for identifying nonlinear dynamics from partial measurements, supporting physics-based, neural-network, and gray-box models. We use the Prediction Error Method (PEM) coupled with state estimation performed by a Moving Horizon Estimation (MHE) scheme, which can account directly for general nonlinear dynamics. This results in a bi-level optimization problem that scales poorly with increasing model parameters. To improve computational efficiency, we derive a reformulation that avoids explicit parameter-wide sensitivity matrices and exploits the temporal structure of the underlying optimization problem. Numerical comparisons show up to a $215\times$ speedup in hypergradient evaluation. Racing-vehicle simulations demonstrate accurate prediction and physical-parameter recovery in tire-force identification. Real-world data show that the gray-box model improves prediction accuracy with a neural residual while retaining physical interpretability.

Optimization and Control.title: High-Order Error Bounds for Markovian LSA with Richardson-Romberg Extrapolation
Optimization and Control.summary: In this paper, we study the bias and high-order error bounds of the Linear Stochastic Approximation (LSA) algorithm with Polyak-Ruppert (PR) averaging under Markovian noise. We focus on the version of the algorithm with constant step size $α$ and propose a novel decomposition of the bias via a linearization technique. We analyze the structure of the bias and show that the leading-order term is linear in $α$ and cannot be eliminated by PR averaging. To address this, we apply the Richardson-Romberg (RR) extrapolation procedure, which effectively cancels the leading bias term. We derive high-order moment bounds for the RR iterates and show that the leading error term aligns with the asymptotically optimal covariance matrix of the vanilla averaged LSA iterates.
Optimization and Control.comment: Revised the proofs of Proposition 7 and Corollary 6. The dependence on $α$ and $n$ remains unchanged, while the dependence on $τ_{\text{mix}}$ and $p$ is now less favorable

Optimization and Control.title: Towards learning-enhanced solvers for multi-parametric optimization
Optimization and Control.summary:
Neural networks (NNs) have been employed in various ways to accelerate the solution of multi-parametric optimization problems (OPs), which prominently arise in model predictive control (MPC). Early approaches focused on approximating the parametric solution (e.g., the optimal control law) directly by NNs. More recently, learning-based techniques have been used to emulate or enhance solver iterations. For the direct approximation of the parametric solution, it has been demonstrated that exploiting structural properties of the underlying OP facilitates the design of suitable NN architectures. In this paper, we show that structural analysis can also be leveraged to systematically integrate learning into classical optimization algorithms, thereby enhancing their performance.
  We formalize our concept for the case of multi-parametric quadratic programs (mpQPs), which frequently arise in linear-quadratic MPC, as a representative application. More precisely, we demonstrate that tailored NNs enable a parameter-dependent fine-tuning of the step sizes in a standard dual projected gradient scheme. The design of the NNs is guided by the observation that optimal step sizes, which permit obtaining the exact optimal solution in finitely many iterations, are piecewise constant functions over the parameter space (e.g., the state space in MPC). We establish key theoretical properties of the proposed approach and illustrate its effectiveness in a numerical case study.
Optimization and Control.comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, to be published in the proceedings of the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (2026)

Optimization and Control.title: Asymptotic Risk of Learning-Rate Schedules for Least-Squares Regression with Discretely Distributed Features
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the last iterate of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on streaming least squares with discretely distributed features (Slock's model), which decouples the dynamics across eigendirections. Under power-law source and capacity conditions, we derive the exact finite-time risk and asymptotic equivalents of constant and Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) schedules. With a tuned base learning-rate, the resulting scaling law decays as $Θ(T^{-q})$, where $T$ is the horizon, and $q$ is independent of the cooldown length $c \in (0,1]$ but is strictly smaller for the constant schedule: any cooldown of fixed relative length $c > 0$, however short, improves the risk by a polynomial factor, while its length only affects the constant, which is minimized by linear decay ($c = 1$). Finally, we show that the optimal risk depends on the batch size $b$ and horizon $T$ only through $bT$, up to a critical batch size.

Optimization and Control.title: Convex Chance-Constrained Stochastic Control under Uncertain Specifications with Application to Learning-Based Hybrid Powertrain Control
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper proposes a strictly convex chance-constrained stochastic control framework that accounts for uncertainty in control specifications such as reference trajectories and operational constraints. Control inputs and risk allocation are jointly optimized under general, possibly non-Gaussian, uncertainties through sufficient deterministic conditions for probabilistic constraint satisfaction. A decreasing risk regularizer ensures existence and full use of the allowable risk. Under the stated regularity assumptions, the joint solution is unique and locally Lipschitz-continuous, supporting stable numerical optimization. The formulation is extended to learning-based exactly linearizable (EL) models through monotone state and input transformations. A hybrid powertrain example compares deterministic control, equal risk allocation, and optimized risk allocation with and without regularization in terms of charge sustaining, constraint violations, closed-loop cost, and solver time.
Optimization and Control.comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Control Systems Technology (TCST)

Optimization and Control.title: The First Step of Decision Making: Alignment under Semantic Uncertainty for Automated Operations Research
Optimization and Control.summary: Problem definition: Automated operations research (OR) depends on correctly understanding the problem users intend to solve. In practice, limited user knowledge and vague expressions can obscure that problem, creating semantic uncertainty in the descriptions used for modeling. This uncertainty can lead to mathematical models that depart from users' intentions. We study semantic alignment to identify and correct errors or omissions in these descriptions before mathematical modeling. Methodology/results: We develop AMAO, an ambiguity-aware multi-agent framework for automated OR under semantic uncertainty. Its two-stage alignment process first uses semantic cues and contextual information to identify and correct potential semantic errors, then obtains additional information via human--AI interaction for further revision when the available context is insufficient. Specifically, AMAO integrates OR-guided mixture-of-experts (MoE) tuning and trajectory-based harness evolution to enhance semantic alignment capabilities. In addition, an ambiguity-aware benchmark and its matched multi-turn dialogue extension are proposed. Extensive experiments support that AMAO can recover the intended operational problem from ambiguous descriptions and recognize when available information is insufficient. Managerial implications: AMAO provides managers with an integrated workflow for translating ambiguous operational descriptions into mathematical models and optimization solutions. By combining semantic alignment with targeted user interaction, it supports recovery of the intended problem and improves downstream solution accuracy.

Optimization and Control.title: Taming Nonconvexity with Epigraph Lifting
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider inverse problems regularized by a trained neural network with \emph{convex activations} and \emph{unrestricted weights}. The resulting optimization problem is generally nonconvex, and gradient-based methods may converge to poor local minima. We introduce a \emph{penalized epigraph lifting} of the network and show that the lifted problem admits a \emph{difference-of-convex (DC) decomposition}. For Lipschitz continuous activations, we establish \emph{finite exactness}: the original objective is recovered exactly at a finite and explicitly computable penalty threshold $\barρ$. Building on this structure, we propose \emph{H-DC} (Homotopic DC), a homotopic scheme that solves a sequence of DC subproblems with increasing $ρ$, warm-starting each level from the previous solution. Numerical experiments on synthetic problems, a manifold denoiser regularizer, and image inpainting with a learned Mumford--Shah regularizer show that H-DC consistently escapes poor local minima and reaches solutions with lower objective values than gradient-based methods from the same initialization.

Optimization and Control.title: Equilibria and consensus in discrete-time opinion dynamics with mixed weighted-averaging and weighted-median mechanisms
Optimization and Control.summary: Opinion dynamics models relate interpersonal influence to consensus or persistent disagreement. We study a discrete-time model combining weighted-average and weighted-median updates on a fixed directed network. Individuals update synchronously with possibly different adjustment coefficients. We characterize equilibria through local balance conditions and opinion level sets, and establish convergence to a Lyapunov-stable equilibrium using nonexpansiveness and Krasnosel'skii--Mann theory. We define type-dependent cohesive sets: each weighted-average member assigns all its weight to the set, whereas each weighted-median member assigns at least one half. Consensus is reached from every initial condition if and only if no two such sets are disjoint. Otherwise, an open set of initial conditions leads to persistent disagreement. Replacing weighted-median individuals by weighted-average individuals preserves consensus whenever it is already guaranteed for all initial conditions. Four numerical studies examine the number and locations of weighted-average individuals. The frequency of reaching a prescribed consensus tolerance is nondecreasing with their fraction in the sampled ensembles, but individual realizations need not follow this trend.

Optimization and Control.title: On error bounds and noncritical Lagrange multipliers
Optimization and Control.summary: Critical Lagrange multipliers are known to be responsible for the potentially slow convergence of Newton-type methods, and noncriticality of a given multiplier has been tied to an error bound which estimates the distance of a primal-dual pair associated with a perturbed problem to the primal solution and the multiplier set of the unperturbed one, and is decisive for a local convergence analysis. We investigate this relation in an abstract setting where merely a set-valued mapping assigning primal-dual pairs to a parameter is available, and characterize the error bound of interest in terms of noncriticality of the underlying multiplier and two calmness-type properties of the associated multiplier mapping, one of which is a novel weak inner calmness in the fuzzy sense. No structural assumptions on the underlying problem are needed for that, and the two calmness-type conditions are not only sufficient but also necessary. Afterwards, we specify these findings for composite optimization problems. Whenever the subdifferential of the outer function is a polyhedral mapping, both conditions hold automatically, which explains the equivalence of noncriticality and the error bound observed in the polyhedral setting. Whenever the outer function is $C^2$-decomposable, they are secured by calmness of a restricted multiplier mapping together with a closedness condition, which recovers and extends the known characterization for $C^2$-cone reducible constraint systems.

Optimization and Control.title: Multiplicative Gradient Method for Log-Homogeneous Optimization: A Unified Mirror-Descent Framework
Optimization and Control.summary:
Consider the problems of computing $\ell_p$-Lewis weights, Kelly portfolios, D-optimal designs, general equilibria in Fisher markets, and optimal error exponents for channel coding in information theory. All of them can be formulated as optimization problems over the probability simplex, but except for the last one, the associated objective functions are neither Lipschitz continuous nor smooth, rendering existing first-order optimization algorithms and their guarantees not directly applicable. Nevertheless, first-order algorithms for solving these problems do exist in the literature and, perhaps surprisingly, look very similar, even though their interpretations, derivations, and analyses mostly appear unrelated. In this paper, we develop a framework unifying these results that captures their common problem structure through log-homogeneity and a novel second-order condition on the objective function, and identifies their common algorithmic pattern as multiplicative gradient methods.
  The framework recovers known algorithms and their optimization error guarantees for computing Kelly portfolios, D-optimal designs, optimal error exponents for channel coding in classical communication, $\ell_p$-Lewis weights with $p < 2$, and general equilibria in Fisher markets. To illustrate the insights provided by the framework, we further show that multiplicative gradient methods yield state-of-the-art performance guarantees for computing $\ell_p$-Lewis weights with $p > 2$ and optimal error exponents in classical-quantum communication. Both results are novel to the best of our knowledge.

Optimization and Control.title: Some remarks on nonexistence in the Gamow liquid drop model
Optimization and Control.summary: In this paper we deal with the celebrated Gamow liquid drop model, namely, for $m>0$, $N\geq 2$ and $α\in (0,N)$, we study the problem \[ \min\Big\{P(Ω)+ V_α(Ω) : Ω\subset \mathbb{R}^N,\;|Ω|=m\Big\}\,, \] and focus mostly on the nonexistence of minimizers for large masses. First we show that any possible minimizer in the asymptotic regime must satisfy an optimal thickness property. Eventually, in the simplified setting of sets made up as a tiling of cubes, we show that nonexistence occurs for large masses for the whole range of parameters $N\geq 2$ and $α\in (0,N)$.

Optimization and Control.title: On the Complexity of Finding Stationary Points of p-th Order Hölder Smooth Functions in One Dimension
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the query complexity of finding an an $\varepsilon$-stationary points of a one-dimensional non-convex function whose $p$-th derivative is $β_p$-Hölder continuous. We determine the optimal complexity for deterministic and randomized algorithms and for oracles that return only derivatives, only function values, or full local information. Randomness provably helps when only derivatives are available, function values help in all cases, and higher-order derivatives never do. Together with known results in higher dimensions, this shows how these benefits depend on the dimension. Our deterministic lower bound also implies that the optimal accuracy exponents of objective-function-free adaptive regularization of order $p$ (OFFAR$p$) in every dimension $d\ge1$ and of deterministic gradient-only trapping in dimension $d=2$.

Optimization and Control.title: Well-Posedness and Strong Convergence of Infinite-Dimensional Port-Hamiltonian Primal-Dual Gradient Dynamics
Optimization and Control.summary: We establish a functional-analytic framework that justifies the LaSalle convergence argument outlined in [van der Schaft, 2026] on port-Hamiltonian primal-dual gradient dynamics for finite-horizon optimal control of linear systems. In addition to strict convexity of the running cost as in \cite{vanderSchaft2026PDGJuly}, our analysis requires global Lipschitz continuity of the cost gradient. This ensures that the nonlinear gradient operator is well-defined and Lipschitz on the entire underlying space. We establish global well-posedness of the optimizer dynamics: every initial value determines a unique global mild solution, and the associated solution operators form a contraction semigroup. Similar to [Gernandtand Schaller, 2025], this is proved using tools from maximal monotone operator theory. Assuming existence of an optimal solution, we combine a dissipation inequality with an infinite-dimensional LaSalle invariance principle to prove strong convergence of every trajectory with a relatively compact positive orbit to the unique optimal state, control, and costate. Moreover, we present a sufficient condition for compactness through uniform control regularity and show that convergence holds for all initial states. Finally, we present an example with a strictly but not strongly convex running cost for which every mild solution converges strongly to the unique equilibrium, while no global exponential estimate uniformly over initial values can be obtained.

Optimization and Control.title: Optimal Synthesis on the Special Linear Group
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the exponential map on the group of real two-by-two matrices with determinant one, endowed with a left-invariant Riemannian metric. Using the Euler-Poincaré equation and its linearization, we determine the conjugate and Maxwell times and identify a domain on which the exponential map is a global diffeomorphism onto the complement of the Maxwell stratum. This provides an alternative proof that the first Maxwell time coincides with the cut time. We obtain an explicit matrix description of the cut locus and characterize the globally minimizing geodesics. Furthermore, we analyze the first Maxwell-time function, determine its unique global minimum, and show that the injectivity radius is $\frac{π\sqrt{14}}{4}$. Finally, we characterize the intersection of the cut and conjugate loci and prove that every geodesic is equi-optimal.

Optimization and Control.title: Exact Verification of First-Order Methods via Mixed-Integer Linear Programming
Optimization and Control.summary: We present exact mixed-integer linear programming formulations for verifying the performance of first-order methods for parametric quadratic optimization. We formulate the verification problem as a mixed-integer linear program where the objective is to maximize the infinity norm of the fixed-point residual after a given number of iterations. Our approach captures a wide range of gradient, projection, proximal iterations through affine or piecewise affine constraints. We derive tight polyhedral convex hull formulations of the constraints representing the algorithm iterations. To improve the scalability, we develop a custom bound tightening technique combining interval propagation, operator theory, and optimization-based bound tightening. Numerical examples, including linear and quadratic programs from network optimization, sparse coding using Lasso, and optimal control, show that our method provides several orders of magnitude reductions in the worst-case fixed-point residuals, closely matching the true worst-case performance.

Optimization and Control.title: Exploration strategies for Gaussian process bandit optimization with inference regret guarantees
Optimization and Control.summary: Existing cumulative regret guarantees for Bayesian optimization (BO) do not necessarily characterize the quality of the algorithm's final output. This gap is critical under noisy evaluations, where the goal is to return a single high-quality recommendation. To address it, we introduce efficient exploration strategies that can be incorporated into any BO procedure by occasionally replacing the acquisition query with an exploration query. To validate this approach, we bound the Gaussian process posterior standard deviation over the search space via the fill distance of the queries, which measures the largest region left unexplored. We then use this result to derive upper bounds on the inference regret, i.e., the gap between the global optimum and the function value at the algorithm's returned point. Empirically, these exploration strategies improve the final recommendations of existing BO algorithms on synthetic benchmarks, hyperparameter optimization, and a control task.

Optimization and Control.title: Regularity of the Price of Anarchy in Routing Games over the Multivariate Demand Space
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the price of anarchy (PoA) in nonatomic routing games as a function of the full vector of origin--destination demands. We show that the Beckmann value function is continuously differentiable on the positive demand cone, with gradient equal to the equilibrium origin--destination cost vector; hence the PoA is continuously differentiable on the regular demand region. We prove that the nondifferentiability set has Lebesgue measure zero and, when every edge cost is strictly increasing or constant, is covered by countably many codimension-one submanifolds. Under the same cost structure, all equilibrium objects are cellwise as smooth as the edge costs. For affine costs, the exceptional sets become finite unions of lower-dimensional polyhedral cells linked by an exact scaling law, and the maximum of the PoA over a cell closure is attained on the cell boundary, generalizing the one-dimensional endpoint result. The theory is illustrated on the Sioux Falls benchmark network.

Optimization and Control.title: A restart-free accelerated algorithm for nonconvex minimization: continuous- and discrete-time analysis
Optimization and Control.summary: We propose two deterministic momentum-based first-order methods for minimizing lower-bounded nonconvex functions with Lipschitz-continuous gradients and Hessians. Both methods attain an $\varepsilon$-approximate first-order stationary point in $O(\varepsilon^{-7/4})$ function and gradient evaluations, and their update parameters do not depend on the target accuracy or a prescribed terminal iteration. The convergence guarantees concern the best point among weighted averages of the iterates. Instead of relying on momentum-resetting restarts, both methods employ a velocity-control mechanism that adaptively reduces the velocity. The first method uses a differentiable velocity-control rule, making its last iterate differentiable with respect to the initial point. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first deterministic first-order method to combine this differentiability property with the stated complexity. The second method adaptively estimates the gradient and Hessian Lipschitz constants and requires no prior knowledge of their values. Numerical experiments show that it outperforms existing parameter-free methods on some test problems. Both methods are derived by discretizing a new continuous-time model described by an ordinary differential equation. We develop parallel continuous- and discrete-time convergence analyses within the performance estimation problem framework.

Optimization and Control.title: Optimal Diagonal Preconditioning Beyond Worst-Case Conditioning: Theory and Practice of Omega Scaling
Optimization and Control.summary:
We study optimal diagonal preconditioning using the classical worst-case $κ$-condition number and the averaging-based $ω$-condition number.
  For the $κ$-optimal preconditioning problem, we derive an affine-based pseudoconvex reformulation with three key advantages: all stationary points are global minima, subgradients are inexpensive to compute, and the optimization variable is an $n$-dimensional vector rather than an $n\times n$ matrix as in semidefinite programming (SDP) approaches. We develop a simple and highly efficient subgradient method, with convergence guarantees, for solving this pseudoconvex formulation that is substantially more scalable and accurate than existing SDP-based methods.
  For the $ω$-condition number, we provide explicit characterizations of optimal diagonal and block diagonal preconditioners. In particular, we show that several classical preconditioners, including Jacobi and row/column normalization, are $ω$-optimal, and that matrix balancing schemes monotonically reduce $ω$ and converge to stationary points of the two-sided problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first unified and explicit characterization of optimality conditions for both $κ$ and $ω$-based preconditioning.
  Our numerical experiments further reveal a striking phenomenon: although $κ$-optimal preconditioners achieve stronger reductions in the worst-case condition number, $ω$-optimal preconditioners are substantially cheaper to compute and yield better performance for iterative methods such as preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) and least squares method (LSQR). Moreover, applying $ω$-optimal scaling to linear systems that are already $κ$-optimally preconditioned leads to further improvements in PCG iterations.

Optimization and Control.title: On the convexification of a bilinearly constrained set with a common variable
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the convexification of sets defined by box constraints and bilinear inequality constraints in which all bilinear terms share a common variable. For this structured class of nonconvex sets, we provide a complete characterization of the extreme points of the convex hull and derive an explicit description of all facet-defining inequalities, thereby obtaining a full polyhedral description of the convex hull. In addition, we develop a polynomial-time separation algorithm for the facet-defining inequalities and illustrate its effectiveness through examples. These results offer both structural insight into the geometry of the convex hull and algorithmic tools for identifying violated inequalities.

Optimization and Control.title: Constraint-Lifted Sector-Constrained Guidance for Rear-Approach Interception
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper develops a sector-constrained guidance (SCG) law for interception of a maneuvering target while maintaining a prescribed approach geometry. The line of sight is required to remain within a specified angular sector behind the target throughout the engagement, resulting in a state-constrained guidance problem. To enforce this constraint, the directional angle between the target heading and the line of sight is mapped from the prescribed sector to an unconstrained coordinate using a sigmoid diffeomorphism. A guidance law is then designed in the lifted coordinate to generate a desired transverse velocity and corresponding pursuer lead angle. The desired lead angle is tracked through an inner-loop turn-rate controller, which is implemented through the normal-acceleration command of a nonlinear point-mass model. This construction embeds the sector constraint directly into the guidance law and does not require online constrained optimization. Numerical simulations against a maneuvering target show that SCG achieves interception while maintaining the prescribed rear-sector constraint, including when the pursuer normal-acceleration command is subject to actuator saturation. Comparisons with proportional guidance under the same engagement conditions demonstrate that proportional guidance may achieve interception but does not maintain the prescribed directional constraint.

Optimization and Control.title: Admissibility-Preserving Constraint Lifting for Conditional Deadbeat Control of Discrete-Time Nonlinear Systems
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper presents a constraint-enforcing control framework for a class of discrete-time strict- feedback nonlinear systems. The objective is to guarantee closed-loop stability while ensuring forward invariance of a prescribed safe set defined by state constraints. The pro- posed approach transforms the constrained control problem into an equivalent unconstrained one through smooth constraint-lifting mappings constructed using strictly increasing sigmoid functions. Controller synthesis is then performed in the lifted coordinates, enabling recursive backstepping design while preserving the admissibility of the constrained states. Conditions on the controller gains are derived to guarantee both asymptotic stability of the closed-loop system and forward invariance of the admissible domain of the lifting functions. The analysis also establishes a conditional deadbeat property for the second backstepping step once the system trajectory enters a region in which the lifting-domain admissibility conditions are satisfied. Numerical simulations of a constrained Roup oscillator demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in enforcing state constraints while tracking a reference command.

Optimization and Control.title: A Backend-Agnostic MWIS Kernel for Stochastic Unit Commitment with Neutral-Atom Hardware Validation
Optimization and Control.summary: Quantum hardware is beginning to address structured combinatorial optimisation, but two steps still block practical use: mapping real operational models onto hardware-compatible instances, and converting noisy hardware output back into feasible decisions. Here we introduce a backend-agnostic computational interface that compiles the discrete decision layer of stochastic unit commitment into a move-based maximum-weight independent set (MWIS) problem, while retaining continuous dispatch and feasibility recovery in the classical computational layer. We validate the approach in a green hydrogen scheduling setting and deploy it on the QuEra Aquila neutral-atom quantum processor. This is the first end-to-end industrial scheduling workflow that connects real operational decisions to programmable neutral-atom hardware through a solver-agnostic MWIS representation. Across a 15-day hardware campaign on 50-node instances, hardware-generated solutions after classical refinement match or exceed the dispatch margins obtained from exact MWIS on every day. When scaling to 144 nodes, encoding quality remains stable, while the probability that the full atom array survives, rather than graph embedding, emerges as the dominant bottleneck to further scaling. Together, these results establish a hardware-compatible computational pathway toward larger problem scales, and lay the groundwork for exploring regimes in which exact classical optimisation may no longer scale efficiently.
Optimization and Control.comment: v2: added data availability statement; Supplementary Information now included as ancillary file (SI.pdf)

Optimization and Control.title: Sequential Conformal Calibration under Recursive Selection
Optimization and Control.summary: Conformal prediction provides finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees that can support decision-making in specific settings. In multistage problems, earlier decisions determine the populations relevant to later calibration. When later scores are refit using earlier calibration results, reusing those cases for ranking need not preserve exchangeability with a surviving test case. We study sequential conformal calibration with a fresh fold at each stage: conditional on earlier folds, the selected fold scores and the surviving test score are exchangeable. This yields finite-sample coverage guarantees for every prefix of the decision sequence. For atomless survivor score distributions, we derive a universal Binomial-thinned Beta chain for the realized coverage process. Its law depends only on fold sizes and target levels, even under predictable refitting, and yields exact coverage slack, abstention probabilities, and calibration-conditional guarantees. We further characterize the tradeoff between freshness and data reuse. For fixed scores, strict-survivor reuse is exactly valid. For adaptive scores refit using past calibration data, reusing survivors can incur worst-case rank loss, while blocked designs provide an intermediate option between full reuse and stagewise fresh folds. As a case study, we apply the framework to serial multi-echelon inventory problem and propose a sequential conditional-quantile formulation. Each stock level is learned as a context-dependent quantile of cumulative demand among scenarios satisfying earlier no-backlog constraints. We connect these targets to common-shift stationarity and derive decision-level implications for the resulting calibrated policies. In a three-echelon simulation, fresh-fold refitting achieves 81.98% final-prefix coverage against an 81.82% target while reducing mean cost by 5.5% relative to the Bonferroni baseline.

Optimization and Control.title: ReLoop: Structured Modeling and Behavioral Verification for Reliable LLM-Based Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can translate natural-language problem descriptions into optimization code, but the code is prone to silent failures: it executes and returns a solver-feasible solution while encoding a semantically incorrect formulation. On compositional problems, the resulting feasibility-correctness gap reaches 90 percentage points. We introduce ReLoop, which combines two mechanisms. Structured generation decomposes code production into a four-stage reasoning chain (understand, formalize, synthesize, verify) to reduce formulation errors during generation. Behavioral verification detects the errors that remain by testing whether the formulation responds correctly to solver-based parameter perturbation, a signal that comes from the solver rather than from LLM self-review and requires no ground truth. The two mechanisms address different error structures: structured generation gives the largest gain on compositional problems (+8.5pp accuracy on RetailOpt-190 with Claude Opus 4.6), and behavioral verification gives its largest gain on localized defects (+4.4pp on MAMO-ComplexLP). With diagnostic execution recovery, ReLoop reaches 100% executable code on Claude Opus 4.6, and relative to direct generation it raises or preserves every reported metric of the three chat-tuned foundation models on all three benchmarks. For the narrowly fine-tuned SFT model we test, the chain-of-thought prompt conflicts with its learned output format and lowers its accuracy on MAMO-ComplexLP; we document and analyze this interaction. We release RetailOpt-190, 190 compositional retail optimization scenarios in which several constraints interact.

Optimization and Control.title: Online Submodular Welfare Maximization: Computation is not the Bottleneck
Optimization and Control.summary:
We revisit the online submodular welfare maximization problem (OSW), a vast generalization of numerous well-studied online allocation problems, including online bipartite matching, display ads and AdWords. A natural greedy OSW algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of $1/2$ [LLN06], and $1-1/e$ under i.i.d. arrivals [KPV13]. Both bounds are tight for polynomial-time algorithms unless NP=RP [KPV13]. The information-theoretic limits for OSW, in contrast, remained open. This prompted researchers to ask for tighter upper bounds [Mehta13] or conjecture the existence of better-competitive (slow) algorithms [Huang23, LTX+23, CHS24, Huang2024, HTW24}.
  We resolve Mehta's question and refute the subsequent conjectures, proving that the greedy algorithm is in fact tight for both adversarial and i.i.d. arrivals, regardless of computation time. Seemingly contradicting recent $(1-1/e)$-competitive fractional algorithms for OSW [HJP+24,Patton26], we show that this impossibility even holds for fractional algorithms, provided their outputs correspond to marginals that are roundable in hindsight. Conceptually, our proofs can be seen as identifying that a bottleneck for OSW, even under (deterministic) adversarial arrivals, is the inherently random notion of correlation gap [ADSY12].

Optimization and Control.title: A Mean Field Model of Consumption Inertia and Keeping Up with the Joneses
Optimization and Control.summary: Households compare their living standard with others' and dislike changing it. We study consumption and investment when felicity depends on consumption relative to a benchmark, the population's geometric average consumption, and cuts in felicity weigh more than increases. Asset returns are exogenous. For finitely many types and arbitrary initial wealth and inherited standards, a mean field equilibrium exists under a weak interaction condition, and for fixed budget multipliers the benchmark is the fixed point of a contraction. In a complete market with common risk, a mean field equilibrium at empirical type frequencies is an exact Nash equilibrium of the finite game, for any preferences over relative consumption. We bound the gain from deviating when plans computed at another composition are used. We compute equilibria in which groups with different wealth, inherited standards, and loss aversion revise spending at different dates. With identical households and common risk, the unique symmetric equilibrium is the policy of a single loss averse household with modified curvature. In a baseline example, ignoring the inherited standard costs up to 17% of wealth, while small errors about the composition of the reference group cost less than 0.5%.

Optimization and Control.title: Single-Loop Stochastic Projected Damped Extragradient Methods for Nonconvex--(Strongly) Concave Minimax Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: We develop single-loop stochastic projected damped extragradient methods for nonconvex--(strongly) concave minimax optimization, with complexity guarantees for both game stationarity (GS) and optimization stationarity (OS). Our approach combines a stochastic projected damped extragradient (SPDE) method with a recursive variance-reduced variant, VR-SPDE, both of which retain a single-loop structure. Under an unbiased stochastic gradient oracle with uniformly bounded variance, SPDE finds an $\varepsilon$-game-stationary point with stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) complexities of $O(κ\varepsilon^{-4})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-5})$ in the nonconvex--strongly concave and nonconvex--concave settings, respectively, where $κ=L/μ$. Under an additional mean-square Lipschitz condition on the stochastic gradients, VR-SPDE improves these GS complexities to $O(κ^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-9/2})$, respectively. For an $\varepsilon$-optimization-stationary point, SPDE achieves SFO complexities of $O(κ\varepsilon^{-4})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-6})$, while VR-SPDE achieves $O(κ^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-6})$, in the two settings, respectively. These OS guarantees match the best-known bounds achieved by multi-loop methods while preserving a single-loop implementation. To the best of our knowledge, our results provide the best-known SFO complexity guarantees among single-loop stochastic first-order methods for the respective stationarity criteria and problem classes.

Optimization and Control.title: Practical Regularized Quasi-Newton Methods with Inexact Function Values
Optimization and Control.summary:
Many practical optimization problems involve objective function values that are corrupted by unavoidable numerical errors. In smooth nonconvex optimization, quasi-Newton methods combined with line search are widely used due to their efficiency and scalability. These methods implicitly assume accurate function evaluations and thus may fail to converge in noisy settings. Developing fast and stable quasi-Newton methods for such scenarios is therefore crucial.
  To address this issue, we propose a novel noise-tolerant regularized quasi-Newton method equipped with a relaxed Armijo-type line search, designed to remain stable under inaccurate function evaluations. By combining a regularization parameter update rule inspired by Objective-Function-Free Optimization and the AdaGrad-Norm method, we prove an order-optimal $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ complexity bound under errors in function values.
  We performed extensive experiments on the CUTEst benchmark collection with artificially noisy objective function evaluations, as well as with low-precision floating-point arithmetic (64-, 32-, and 16-bit). The results demonstrate stable performance under reduced precision and function-value noise while retaining practical convergence speed and computational cost.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Online Job Assignment
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Motivated primarily by applications in cloud computing, we study a simple, yet powerful, online allocation problem in which jobs of varying durations arrive over continuous time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably to one of the available offline servers. Each server has a fixed initial capacity, with assigned jobs occupying one unit for their duration and releasing it upon completion. The algorithm earns a reward for each assignment upon completion. We consider a general heterogeneous setting where both the reward and duration of a job depend on the job-server pair. The objective of the online algorithm is to maximize the total collected reward, and remain competitive against an omniscient benchmark that knows all job arrivals in advance. Our main contribution is the design of a new online algorithm, termed Forward-Looking BALANCE (FLB), and using primal-dual framework to establish that it is (asymptotically) optimal-competitive.
  This meta-algorithm has two main primitives: (i) keeping track of the capacity used for each server at each time and applying a penalty function to this quantity, and (ii) adjusting the reward of assigning a job to a server by subtracting the total penalty of a particularly chosen subset of future times, in contrast to just looking at the current time. The FLB algorithm then assigns the arriving job to the server with the maximum adjusted reward. If R and D are the ratios of maximum over minimum rewards and durations, we show that the FLB algorithm obtains an asymptotic competitive ratio of ln(RD)+3lnln(max(R,D))+O(1). We further show this bound has optimal dependencies on all the parameters. Our main analysis combines a novel dual-fitting technique, which leverages the configuration LP benchmark for this problem, and a novel inductive argument to establish the capacity feasibility of the algorithm, which might be of independent interest.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Unit-Demand Pricing for Min-Buying Customers
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the unit-demand pricing problem under \textit{min-buying} behavior, where customers purchase the lowest-priced item that yields non-negative utility. In contrast to the quasi-linear model, we show that uniform pricing becomes substantially more effective under min-buying. First, we study symmetric environments. We show that for min-buying customers with independent and identically distributed valuations, a uniform price across items is optimal. We then extend this optimality result to all valuations drawn from exchangeable and affiliated distributions. However, uniform pricing is not optimal in all symmetric environments: for min-buying customers we construct an exchangeable and non-affiliated valuation distribution for which the gap between uniform pricing and optimal item pricing is logarithmic in the number of items. This gap is tight and matches the worst-case gap in the quasi-linear setting. Next, we consider asymmetric environments in which valuations are independent but not identically distributed. When these valuations are regular and customers are min-buying, we show that a uniform price guarantees approximately 69.86\% of the optimal item-pricing revenue and this is tight. Overall, our results highlight that the value of non-uniform pricing substantially diminishes, and often disappears entirely, under more conservative demand models in which customers engage in satisficing behaviors such as min-buying.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: A Stochastic Growth Model for Online Platforms
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We investigate the growth trajectory of online platforms operating as market makers in two-sided matching markets. Their expansion, often referred to as the ``chicken-and-egg dilemma'' in the literature, poses an inherent challenge: service providers find value in joining the platform because of the presence of customers, while customers are drawn to the platform by the availability of service providers. Much of the existing literature addresses this expansion challenge through either a static market-clearing lens or aggregate dynamic models, emphasizing how network externalities shape a platform's growth trajectory and equilibrium size. These approaches do not fully capture how gradual growth must be implemented through server-level admission, assignment, and compensation decisions. Embedded in this growth process are intertemporal participation constraints that the platform must satisfy to attract and retain forward-looking servers.
  To explicitly account for the stochastic dynamics of a platform's gradual growth, we model the system as a Markov process. Potential servers and customers arrive according to Poisson processes, and customer demand is non-decreasing in the number of active servers. Under mild conditions, we characterize the platform's optimal admission, assignment, and compensation policies. The platform admits servers at the maximum feasible rate until it reaches an endogenous target size, which can be smaller than the static market-clearing optimum. In the baseline model, seniority-based compensation acts as an operational substitute for financially subsidized growth: instead of using upfront subsidies to induce early server participation, the platform uses future cash flows to reward early servers for joining when demand is limited and for helping the platform reach later, higher-demand states.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Online Resource Allocation with Cancellations
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We initiate the study of two-sided online resource allocation with costly cancellations within the buyback model. Our focus is on edge-weighted online matching and several of its extensions. In our base matching model, nodes arrive online on one side and request offline resources on the other side. In contrast to the classic literature, in our model the decision maker can reclaim any fraction of an offline resource that was preallocated to an earlier online node. However, reclaiming a resource not only results in the loss of the previously allocated edge-weight but also incurs an additional penalty equal to a non-negative constant factor $f$ times the edge-weight. Parameterizing the problem by the buyback factor $f$, our main result is the development of optimal competitive algorithms for \emph{all possible values} of $f$ through a novel primal-dual family of algorithms in the fractional (or equivalently, large capacity) setting. We establish the optimality of our results by deriving separate lower bounds for both the small and large buyback factor regimes and showing that our primal-dual algorithm exactly matches these lower bounds by appropriately tuning a parameter as a function of $f$. Interestingly, our results reveal a phase transition: for the small buyback regime ($f < \frac{e-2}{2}$), the optimal competitive ratio is $\frac{e}{e-(1+f)}$, and for the large buyback regime ($f \geq \frac{e-2}{2}$), the competitive ratio is $-W_{-1}\left(\frac{-1}{e(1+f)}\right)$, where $W_{-1}$ is the non-principal branch of the Lambert $W$ function.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: A preliminary conference version of this work has appeared in the ACM Economics and Computations(EC) 2023 conference under the title "Online Resource Allocation with Buyback: Optimal Algorithms via Primal-Dual." ; An earlier version of this paper was distributed under the title "Online Matching with Cancellation Costs."

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Dynamic Run-Out Pricing for Perishable Goods
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
I study a dynamic pricing problem in which a seller with limited inventory must sequentially price a perishable product for arriving customers with heterogeneous valuations. The key difficulty lies in balancing immediate sales against future opportunities under capacity constraints and stochastic customer valuations. I propose a simple, interpretable, and asymptotically optimal dynamic pricing algorithm, called Dynamic Run-Out Pricing (DROP), that adjusts prices in real time based on current inventory and anticipated future demand.
  Under the assumption that customers' valuations follow bounded or exponential distributions, our theoretical results show that DROP's expected revenue converges to the optimal revenue as market size grows. Unlike traditional notions of near-optimality, where the ratio of the algorithm's revenue to the optimal revenue converges to 1, I show that the absolute difference between the two revenues converges to 0 as the market size increases, underscoring the algorithm's effectiveness.
  Furthermore, I extend our analysis to heavy-tailed valuation distributions, specifically the Pareto distribution, where standard run-out heuristics severely underprice inventory by ignoring the value of waiting for extreme valuations. To correct this, I introduce the Tail-Aware DROP (TA-DROP) heuristic, which intentionally inflates prices to protect inventory, and I prove that it restores asymptotic optimality with a strict polynomial convergence rate.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: A Tractability Boundary for Exclusion Zones in Instant-Runoff Voting: Planar Versus One-Apex Graphs
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study exclusion zones for instant-runoff voting (IRV) on connected, unweighted graphs. Each vertex hosts one voter and may host a candidate. Voters rank candidates by shortest-path distance and cast one whole vote in each round. Distance ties favour the smaller identifier in a common fixed vertex ordering, and equal-score elimination ties remove the larger identifier in that ordering. A nonempty vertex set $S$ is an exclusion zone if every election with at least one participating candidate in $S$ elects a winner in $S$. In this setting, we consider three computational problems: deciding whether a target candidate can lose against some nonempty subset of a given set of allowed opponents, deciding whether a given vertex subset is an exclusion zone, and computing the unique minimum exclusion zone. We establish that all three are polynomial-time solvable on trees, outerplanar graphs and, more generally, planar graphs. For an n-vertex tree, the first problem (candidate loss) can be decided in O(n) time. The planar algorithm uses the structure of an inclusion-minimal candidate set that eliminates the target in the first round: contracting the candidates' voter cells makes the target cell adjacent to every other cell, leading to bounded-width structure and enumerable separators. We give explicit implementations and conservative polynomial running-time and space bounds; the large exponents for outerplanar and planar graphs establish tractability rather than practical efficiency. In contrast, even on bipartite exact one-apex graphs of bounded diameter with every nontarget vertex eligible to stand, candidate loss is NP-complete, singleton-zone verification is coNP-complete, and the minimum exclusion zone cannot be computed in polynomial time unless P = coNP. Thus planarity marks a tractability boundary for these computational problems under the voting and tie-breaking conventions studied here.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 66 pages

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: An Introduction to Contract Theory for Computer Scientists
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: This survey introduces contract design to computer scientists: using outcome-based payments to incentivize effort. We discuss applications that motivate a computational approach to contract design, ranging from online labor markets, to incentive-aware algorithmic classification, to emerging ecosystems of AI agents. We present the classic principal-agent model and introduce basic concepts. We show how optimal contracts are computable via linear programming, and why they can be opaque and brittle. Motivated by this we turn to simpler contract formats, specifically linear contracts. We discuss approximation guarantees, and robust (max-min) optimality of such contracts. We then move beyond the single-agent setting to combinatorial contract settings with multiple agents, mapping the algorithmic landscape of tractability and approximation. Finally, we discuss partial information settings through the lens of learning algorithms, and outline open directions. The goal is a concise, accessible entry point that connects economic foundations with algorithmic tools and highlights opportunities for new theory and applications.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Large player classes and approximately weighted voting
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: It is known that completeness of the coalitional ($C$-)desirability relation in a simple game does not imply the existence of a weighted-majority representation. We show that weightedness is implied in an approximate sense. Call an $n$-player simple game $\varepsilon$-weighted if, for some weight vector in the $(n-1)$-simplex, any losing coalition weight exceeds any winning coalition weight by at most $\varepsilon$; let $\varepsilon^{\ast}$ be the smallest such $\varepsilon$. We establish an upper bound on $\varepsilon^{\ast}$ in a general $C$-complete game, and deduce that, if all classes of equally desirable players become large asymptotically but the number of classes is bounded, then $\varepsilon^{\ast}=O(1/n_{\min})$ for the minimal player class size $n_{\min}$, and the bound is tight. Importantly, the minimal attainable fraction $δ$ of coalitions mislabeled by a weighting rule also tends to $0$ when $n_{\min}\rightarrow\infty$ and the number of player classes is bounded, with $δ=O(1/\sqrt{n_{\min}})$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Non-Exclusive Notifications for Ride-Hailing at Lyft II: Simulations and Marketplace Analysis
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Ride-hailing platforms increasingly face uncertain driver acceptance, which makes traditional one-to-one \emph{exclusive dispatch} (ED) less efficient: rejections and timeouts force sequential retries and lengthen rider wait times, which in turn creates friction in the marketplace. \emph{Non-exclusive dispatch} (NED) mitigates this friction by broadcasting a request to multiple drivers in parallel. While NED can reduce latency, it introduces new design challenges---most notably, how to choose notification sets and how to resolve driver contention (when multiple drivers accept the same ride).
  In this paper---the second in a two-part collaboration with Lyft---we develop a theoretically grounded framework to evaluate the long-run performance and marketplace effects of transitioning from ED to NED. We bridge theory and practice by combining (i) an optimization model that formulates NED as a constrained welfare maximization problem with (ii) large-scale discrete-event simulations on proprietary Lyft traces and (iii) a stylized macroscopic equilibrium model. Across simulation and equilibrium analysis, we find that NED improves key fulfillment metrics relative to ED: it reduces match time (and hence rider reneging) while increasing both the number and the average quality of completed matches. We also quantify the speed--quality trade-off between two common contention resolution rules, \emph{First-Accept} and \emph{Best-Accept}: First-Accept maximizes speed and throughput, whereas Best-Accept is required to maximize per-match quality. Finally, we show that slightly conservative notification heuristics can improve long-run efficiency by avoiding excessive locking of high-value drivers and preserving future availability.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Non-Exclusive Notifications for Ride-Hailing at Lyft I: Single-Cycle Approximation Algorithms
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Ride-hailing platforms increasingly rely on non-exclusive notifications--broadcasting a single request to multiple drivers simultaneously--to mitigate inefficiencies caused by uncertain driver acceptance. In this paper, the first in a two-part collaboration with Lyft, we formally model the Notification Set Selection Problem for a single decision cycle, where the platform determines the optimal subset of drivers to notify for each incoming ride request. We analyze this combinatorial optimization problem under two contention-resolution protocols: First Acceptance (FA), which prioritizes speed by assigning the ride to the first responder, and Best Acceptance (BA), which prioritizes match quality by selecting the highest-valued accepting driver.
  We show that welfare maximization under both mechanisms is NP-hard, ruling out a polynomial-time exact algorithm unless P=NP. Despite this hardness, we establish several positive algorithmic results. For FA, we develop a Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (PTAS) for the single-rider problem. For the general matching setting, we provide a (1-1/e)-approximation algorithm that applies to both FA and BA. Along the way, we show that the FA valuation function constitutes a novel discrete choice model with structural properties of independent interest. For BA, we further prove that the welfare objective is monotone and submodular and exploit additional structure to obtain an approximation guarantee that surpasses the classical (1-1/e) barrier. Finally, when acceptance probabilities are independent of the drivers, we show that the BA problem can be solved exactly in polynomial time through a linear programming formulation. We evaluate our algorithms on synthetic instances and on instances calibrated using real ride-sharing data from Lyft, demonstrating strong empirical performance.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Online Fair Division with Upgrade Recourse
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the online fair division of indivisible goods. In the standard model, where assignments are irrevocable, no algorithm can guarantee any positive fraction of the maximin share (MMS). Reassigning earlier goods can restore fairness, but it may take value away from agents who already hold them. We ask how much fairness can be maintained if every reassignment must leave each affected agent at least as well off. We consider two forms of such upgrade recourse. Under item-level upgrades, each good an agent holds must be kept or replaced by a distinct good she values at least as much; under bundle-level upgrades, only her total value must not decrease. For item-level upgrades, we show that the optimal MMS factor is essentially $1/H_n \approx 1/\ln n$, where $H_n$ is the $n$-th harmonic number, and that fixed picking sequences nearly attain it. Since these sequences use only the agents' rankings of individual goods, knowing the actual values cannot improve the optimal factor for up to 33 agents, and improves it by at most a vanishing margin as $n$ grows. Bundle-level upgrades allow substantially stronger guarantees. By permitting several-for-one exchanges, they turn this vanishing factor into a constant: we achieve exact MMS for two agents and more than half of MMS for any number of agents, in both cases together with relaxations of envy-freeness. Finally, we show that predictions about future goods let online algorithms inherit any offline MMS guarantee, losing only an additive term bounded by the prediction error. Under item-level upgrades, however, insisting on exact MMS when predictions are correct leaves no positive guarantee when they are wrong.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Prophet Inequalities with Cancellation Costs
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Most of the literature on online algorithms and sequential decision-making in revenue management focuses on settings with irrevocable decisions. Motivated by modern applications such as cloud spot markets, selling banner ads, and online hotel booking, we study "prophet inequalities with cancellations" under linear cancellation costs (the buyback model). A sequence of independent random variables $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ with known distributions is revealed one by one. After accepting $X_j$, a decision-maker may later discard it and accept another variable at a cost of $f \times X_j$, where $f \ge 0$. The goal is to maximize the expected net reward: the value of the final accepted variable minus the total cancellation cost. We compare online policies with an omniscient optimal offline "prophet" benchmark.
  Our first main result is an optimal prophet inequality for all parameters $f \ge 0$. We fully characterize the worst-case competitive ratio of the optimal online policy against the optimal offline benchmark via a differential equation, for which we provide a constructive solution. Our second main result is a simple polynomial-time randomized adaptive policy that achieves this optimal competitive ratio. Our policy is order-agnostic (in the sense of Samuel-Cahn (1984)): it only needs to know the set of distributions and not their arrival order. These results follow from reductions to a continuous "generalized flow problem," viewed as the dual to a factor-revealing LP for the worst-case competitive ratio. Our techniques include a geometric interpretation of its solution via a differential equation and the embedding of random variables into specific Poisson point processes. We also use these building blocks to construct lower-bound instances and to design and analyze our
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: The first conference version of this paper has appeared in the ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 2024), and the second conference version has appeared in the ACM Economics and Computations (EC 2026)

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Complexity of Exact and Approximate Nash Equilibria in Anonymous Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We prove that, for every fixed rational $c>0$, computing a $2^{-n^c}$-approximate Nash equilibrium in an $n$-player two-strategy anonymous game is $\mathsf{PPAD}$-complete. This holds even when one strategy always pays $1/2$ and, for all but two players, the other is constant outside at most five opponent counts. The reduction uses coefficient estimates to simulate circuit constraints approximately. Exact computation requires eliminating the simulation error: with three strategies, a separate construction uses polynomial roots to implement circuit gates exactly. This yields $\mathsf{FIXP}$-completeness of exact equilibrium computation under separable-linear reductions and $\mathsf{FIXP}_a$-completeness of approximation in distance to an exact equilibrium.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 48 pages, including appendices and references; 2 figures and 4 tables

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: A $1/2$-Approximation for Pandora's Problem with Deadlines
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Pandora's problem is a fundamental model of sequential search in which opening each box incurs a cost. We study the variant with deadlines, where each box has a publicly known deadline for both opening and selection. We prove that a simple threshold strategy achieves a $1/2$-approximation to the optimal expected utility, improving the previous guarantee arbitrarily close to $1/4$ due to Amanatidis et al. (2025).

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Digital-Twin-Referenced Belief-Guided Q-Learning for Jammer Identification and Beam-Power Control in a mmWave Model
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Digital Twin (DT) combined with reinforcement learning (RL) can support adaptive resource allocation and security-aware decision-making by comparing expected and observed network behavior. This paper presents a simulation-based DT reference and a belief-guided Q-learning (BGQL) for joint jammer identification and beam-power control in a site-specific 28-GHz network. For each action, the same channel simulator is evaluated under an attack-free and an attacked configuration. Receiver-level residuals are combined with spatial jamming footprints and accumulated to form a normalized suspicion vector. BGQL incorporates this vector into an aggregated state, a belief-concentration reward, and exploratory beam-selection rule. The BGQL scheme is compared with SARSA, Greedy, and Random under matched attacker sets. Across 30 paired Monte Carlo runs in four configurations, with the number of active jammers supplied to every method, BGQL achieves mean aggregate full-band link-rate scores of approximately 437.4--564.2~Mbit/s and rate-to-device-power scores of 60.37--76.79~Mbit/J. Its detection accuracy is 100\% in one-jammer configurations and approximately 78\%--81\% in two-jammer configurations. BGQL requires approximately 80--130~s per run, compared with 5--14~s for SARSA, reflecting evaluation of 625 beam pairs during exploratory steps. These findings provide a matched-model simulation proof of concept for DT-referenced belief-guided learning for security-aware beam-power control in 6G networks.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Voter Model with Opinion Graph
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the \emph{voter model with opinion graph}, a generalization of the standard (pull) voter model that adds a notion of bounded confidence. In this process, we consider a finite set $A$ of $n$ agents. Each agent $u \in A$ has an opinion $x_u \in O$, where we model opinions as vertices in an undirected opinion graph $G = (O,E)$ with $|O|=q$. In each step, an agent $u$ interacts with another agent $v \in A$. In contrast to classical voting, $u$ adopts the opinion $x_v$ if and only if $x_v$ and $x_u$ are neighbors in $G$. The process is stable once all remaining opinions are an independent set in $G$. We analyze two variants of the process: the ordinary EdgeVOG process, which samples a pair of interacting agents uniformly at random from all possible pairs, and the productive EdgeVOG process, which samples only pairs with neighboring opinions in $G$.
  We show the following:
  - For every opinion graph and every initial configuration, ordinary EdgeVOG stabilizes within $O(n^2\log n)$ steps in expectation and with high probability. The expectation bound is asymptotically tight. For the productive EdgeVOG process, the expected stabilization time is exactly the initial number of compatible agent pairs, while $O(n^2\log n)$ steps suffice with high probability.
  - An opinion $i$ with initial support $s_i$ survives with probability at least $p_i:=s_i/(s_i+\sum_{j\in N(i)}s_j)$. Further, let $μ= \sum_{i \in O} p_i$, then we show the probability that less than $(1-δ)μ$ opinions survive is at most $\exp(-δ^2μ/(2(Δ^2+1)))$ for every $0\leqδ\leq1$.
  -If $G$ has maximum degree $Δ$ and every opinion initially has support at most $\hat{s}$, then no opinion ever acquires more than $\tilde{O}(\min\{n,Δ^6\hat{s}\})$ agents with high probability. This yields near-linear stabilization bounds for productive EdgeVOG for a large class of configurations.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Abstract shortened to comply Arxiv requirements

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: (Un)Decidability of Two-Clock Weighted Timed Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
The Value Problem for weighted timed games consists in determining, given a two-player weighted timed game with a reachability objective and a rational threshold, whether or not the value of the game exceeds the threshold. This problem is known to be undecidable for weighted timed games with three or more clocks, and decidable for one-clock weighted timed games.
  In this paper, we settle the remaining two-clock case, which has remained stubbornly open for a decade. We show that two-clock weighted timed games lie precisely at the decidability frontier: On the one hand the Value problem is undecidable for two-clock weighted timed games, even when restricted to non-negative weights and under a time bound; On the other hand, we establish decidability under an almost divergence restriction, by providing a $3$\textsc{ExpTime} algorithm for computing the value of almost divergent turn-based two-clock weighted timed games.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The Dynamics of Delusion: Modeling Bidirectional False Belief Amplification in Human-Chatbot Dialogue
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: There is growing concern that AI chatbots might fuel delusional beliefs in users. Some have suggested that humans and chatbots mutually reinforce false beliefs over time, but quantitative evidence is lacking. Using a unique dataset of chat logs from individuals who exhibited delusional thinking, we developed a latent state model that captures accumulating and decaying influences between humans and chatbots. We find that a bidirectional influence model substantially outperforms a unidirectional alternative where humans are the primary driver of delusion. We find that humans exert strong but short-lived influence on chatbots, whereas chatbots exert longer-lasting influence on humans. Moreover, chatbots exert strong, stable self-influence over their own future outputs that tends to perpetuate delusions over long stretches of conversation. In fact, this chatbot self-influence constituted the dominant pathway when considering accumulated influence over time. Overall, these results indicate that humans tend to drive sharp, immediate increases in delusion, whereas chatbots sustain and propagate these effects over longer timescales. Together, these findings provide the first empirical, quantitative evidence that human-chatbot interactions can form feedback loops of delusion, decomposable into distinct pathways with dissociable temporal dynamics. By doing so, they can inform the development of safer AI systems.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Agency as a New Organizing Abstraction for Computer Science
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Advances in large-scale machine learning have enabled agentic AI systems: persistent, autonomous computational entities that pursue goals, initiate actions, and interact with open environments. These systems are often framed as applications of foundation models. We argue that this framing is incomplete: agency is also a candidate new organizing abstraction for computer science. What is new is not the concept of an agent, nor runtime policy generation per se, but its general-purpose, open-ended form, in which systems can synthesize courses of action from goals, observations, and memory, over tools and environments for which no complete task-specific model was specified in advance. Thus agency becomes a systems-level abstraction as well as an AI modeling concept. Where the process abstraction organizes computation around executing programs, agency organizes it around pursuing goals under bounded resources: a process executes a program; an agent pursues a goal. From this perspective, the recurring failures of deployed agentic systems (runaway resource consumption, behavior redirected by adversarial content, opaque continuous operation) are symptoms of structural abstraction gaps, not isolated engineering defects. We examine these gaps across six dimensions (execution, interfaces, correctness, oversight, coordination, and persistence) and argue that closing them requires coordinated advances in systems,
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: An extended version of a paper to appear in Communications of the ACM, November 2026
