Differential Geometry.comment: Substantially revised and shortened; title changed. Proofs simplified, references updated, and exposition reorganized to emphasize the reference curvature technique. The connection between Theorem B and the question of Chang, Gursky, and Yang is clarified

Differential Geometry.title: On the Structure of the Cut Locus in Certain Classes of Warped Product Manifolds
Differential Geometry.summary: In this paper, we determine the structure of the cut locus for a class of complete warped product manifolds $M=(R^1\times S^1,dt^2+m(t)^2dθ^2)$, where the warping function $m(t)$ is positive and even, under the assumption that there exists a positive number $t_1$ such that the Gaussian curvature is nonpositive on the domain $t^{-1}\left((t_1,\infty) \right)$ and is decreasing along the subarc $t^{-1}([0,t_1])\capθ^{-1}(0)$ of the upper half meridian.

Differential Geometry.title: Curvature equivalence for Legendre curves in the unit tangent bundle over Euclidean plane
Differential Geometry.summary: The Legendre curve in the unit tangent bundle over Euclidean plane is a plane curve with a moving frame. We have the (Legendre) curvature of the Legendre curve, and the existence and uniqueness theorems for the curvature are valid. In this paper, we introduce an equivalence relation for Legendre curves called the curvature equivalence. We investigate properties of the curvature equivalence and give local and global classifications of Legendre curves under the curvature equivalence.

Differential Geometry.title: Holomorphic Bisectional Curvature on Total Spaces of Holomorphic Vector Bundles
Differential Geometry.summary: We study complete K$ä$hler metrics with prescribed signs of holomorphic bisectional curvature on total spaces of holomorphic vector bundles over compact complex manifolds. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions in the nonnegative and strictly negative cases, characterized respectively by unitary flatness and Griffiths negativity of the bundle, together with the corresponding curvature conditions on the base. We also obtain a global metric splitting in the nonnegative case, rule out strictly positive curvature over positive-dimensional bases, and construct counterexamples to the converse in the nonpositive case.

Geometric Topology.title: A Sharp Lower Bound for Integral Menger Curvature
Geometric Topology.summary:
We prove that round circles $C_L$ are the unique minimisers of integral Menger curvature among embedded closed $C^1$ curves $γ$ of prescribed length $L$ for every $p\geq 2$, i.e. $M_p(C_L) \leq M_p(γ)$, with equality if and only if $γ$ parametrises a round circle. The proof combines a three-point symmetrisation, an analysis of diagonal truncations, and the periodic Wirtinger inequality. For $p>3$, known self-avoidance and regularity results extend the minimisation result to closed rectifiable curves without assuming embeddedness or smoothness, provided the length of the curve image equals $L$.
  In particular, $M_p$ detects the unknot and is basic for $p>3$, thereby answering a question posed repeatedly in the literature.

Geometric Topology.title: Overlap-Helly theorems
Geometric Topology.summary: In this paper we introduce a generalization of Helly's theorem closely connected to Bárány-Gromov overlap theorems (also called selection lemmas). Our main result implies both the topological colorful Helly of Kalai and Meschulam and Karasev's topological centerpoint theorem. We further investigate the topological fractional Helly theorem from this overlap perspective, and show an overlap theorem for dense complexes (a continuous second selection lemma for tame maps).

Geometric Topology.title: The inf spectrum of moduli space
Geometric Topology.summary: Given a surface of genus $g \geq 2$, its inf spectrum is the ordered multiset of inf lengths of curves on the surface, the infimum being over all hyperbolic metrics. We show that the inf spectrum has exponential growth with coefficients that only depend on g, improving the earlier double exponential upper bound. The proof involves developing a number of tools including the process of "thickening" a surface and the notion of model surfaces. These tools may be of independent interest.

Geometric Topology.title: Exotic S^2 x S^2 candidates that are just fake
Geometric Topology.summary: We show that two infinite families of homology $S^2\times S^2$'s presented in \cite{FPS, AP}, originally proposed as exotic candidates, are aspherical. In particular, none of these manifolds is an exotic $S^2\times S^2$. We prove this by reconstructing them from aspherical building blocks, following Edmonds. The same arguments apply to and rule out further candidates for simply connected exotica. We also give counterexamples to the conjecture that Luttinger surgery preserves symplectic asphericity.
Geometric Topology.comment: 15 pages. v2 addresses questions received about symplectic asphericity under Luttinger surgery (Theorem 2) and the existence of metrics of strictly negative sectional curvature on these examples (Addendum 13)

Geometric Topology.title: Non-isotopic surfaces in $T^4\#(S^2\times S^2)$: an example
Geometric Topology.summary: We prove that there exist infinitely many embedded tori with a common geometric dual in $T^4\#(S^2\times S^2)$ that are homotopic, diffeomorphic, but not isotopic to each other, even after arbitrary many external stabilizations. These surfaces are obtained by applying the Norman trick to a fixed immersed surface, using non-homotopic tubing arcs. The isotopy classes of these surfaces are distinguished by homotopy classes of the 2-handles (relative to the boundary) in the complement of the image of the $0$- and $1$-handles.
Geometric Topology.comment: 18 pages, comments are welcomed. Version 2: added references

Geometric Topology.title: Symplectic four-manifolds and hyperbolic $π$-orbifolds
Geometric Topology.summary: We construct closed symplectic 4-manifolds admitting the structure of hyperbolic $π$-orbifold, addressing LeBrun's conjecture. Our simplest example has Euler characteristic $304$, is tessellated by $64$ copies of the right-angled hyperbolic $120$-cell and admits a four-fold branched covering over a product of two surfaces of genus $4$.

Geometric Topology.title: Continuum-many discontinuous actions of $\operatorname{SL}_{n+1}(\mathbb{Q})$ on manifolds
Geometric Topology.summary: For any $n\geq 1$, we construct a continuum of non-conjugate actions by homeomorphisms of $\operatorname{SL}_{n+1}(\mathbb{Q})$ on the $n$-sphere $S^{n}$ that do not extend to a continuous action of $\operatorname{SL}_{n+1}(\mathbb{R})$. We do this by adapting a blow-up construction of Bowden and Mann. We motivate studying these actions and note down some related observations.

Geometric Topology.title: A Counterexample to Three Conjectures of Luo
Geometric Topology.summary: We give a single counterexample to Conjectures 1--3 as stated in Luo's paper: a minimal two-tetrahedron triangulation of the lens space L(3,1) with a null-homotopic loop edge. The proof uses quadrilateral matching equations, an explicit calculation of shape parameters, and known results on volume maximization.

Geometric Topology.title: Homotopy Self-Equivalences of Manifolds
Geometric Topology.summary: Hambleton and Kreck described the group of based homotopy self-equivalences of a closed oriented $4$-manifold by a commutative braid of exact sequences built from bordism groups and the Postnikov $2$-type. We construct the analogous braid for closed oriented $BO\langle n+1\rangle$-manifolds $M$ of dimension $2n$ or $2n-1$ whose fundamental group is finite or infinite cyclic and which satisfy one condition on the action of $π_1$ on the homotopy of the fibre of $M\to P_n(M)$. We compute $\operatorname{Aut}_\bullet(S^1\times S^{m-1})\cong(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$ for $m\ge4$, and $\operatorname{Aut}_\bullet(S^3\times S^3)\cong(\mathbb{Z}/12)^2\rtimes SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ with the standard action modulo $12$. Further, $\operatorname{Aut}_\bullet(S^3\times S^4)\cong(\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/24)\rtimes(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$ has order $192$, that $\operatorname{Aut}_\bullet(S^4\times S^4)\cong D_4\times\mathbb{Z}/2$ has order $16$, and that for connected sums of $r\ge2$ copies of $S^3\times S^3$ the kernel contains a subgroup $(\mathbb{Z}/12)^{2r}$ on which the permutations of the summands act non-trivially. For $S^p\times S^p$ the kernel is a sum of two copies of $π_{2p}(S^p)$ modulo Whitehead products with $ι_p$, and the image is determined by an obstruction on the Whitehead square. In particular $\operatorname{Aut}_\bullet(S^5\times S^5)$ is isomorphic to the theta subgroup of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ and $\operatorname{Aut}_\bullet(S^7\times S^7)$ is an extension of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ by $(\mathbb{Z}/120)^2$.

Geometric Topology.title: One boundary, infinitely geometries
Modular fusion categories with trivial Torelli group actions
Geometric Topology.summary: In this paper, we study modular fusion categories whose mapping class group representations are trivial on the Torelli groups, with particular emphasis on the congruence properties of the resulting representations of $\mathrm{Sp}(2g, \mathbb{Z})$. We prove that, for any $g \ge 3$, the Torelli group is contained in the kernel of the genus-$g$ mapping class group representation $ρ_g$ associated with a modular fusion category $\mathcal{C}$ if and only if $\mathcal{C}$ is pointed. This refines the corresponding result in \cite{MW25}. We also characterize the modular fusion categories for which the genus-$2$ Torelli group is contained in $\ker ρ_2$; in particular, categories with isotropic adjoint subcategories belong to this class. Finally, we give a complete classification of modular fusion categories with isotropic adjoint subcategories, and determine the groups $G$ satisfying $\mathcal{Z}(\mathrm{Vect}_G)$ is 2-Torelli trivial but $\mathcal{Z}(\mathrm{Vect}_G)_{\mathrm{ad}}$ is not isotropic are precisely 2-Engel groups of nilpotent class 3.
Geometric Topology.comment: Added Section 4 on 2-Torelli triviality and 2-Engel groups

Geometric Topology.title: Gröbner Bases for Alexander Fitting Ideals of Links
Geometric Topology.summary: Multivariable Alexander theory produces Fitting ideals without preferred generators. After fixing a coefficient field and a monomial order, we represent these ideals by reduced Gröbner bases of their polynomial contractions, obtaining Alexander--Gröbner invariants of links. Over \(\mathbb Q\), for the maximal free-abelian coefficient system of a connected compact oriented \(3\)-manifold whose nonempty boundary is a disjoint union of tori, we deduce determinant-divisor reciprocity from Blanchfield duality. We compute these invariants for torus links and low-crossing links, and we determine \(\AG_2\) for a two-component pretzel family.
Geometric Topology.comment: 18 pages, 2 figures. In this revision, I revised some minor errors

Geometric Topology.title: An $SL_2(\mathbb{R}) $-Casson invariant and Reidemeister torsions
Geometric Topology.summary: We define an $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$-Casson invariant of closed 3-manifolds. We also observe procedures of computing the invariants in terms of Reidemeister torsions. We discuss some approach of giving the Casson invariant some gradings.
Geometric Topology.comment: This manuscript has been withdrawn by the author because the arguments, as presented, are not sufficiently precise

Optimization and Control.title: Nonlinear Feedback Control in High Dimensions using the Polynomial-Polynomial Regulator
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider the problem of computing Taylor approximations to the optimal feedback law and value function for infinite-horizon finite-dimensional nonlinear optimal control problem---also known as Al'brekht's method. The scalability of existing Al'brekht-based approaches to computing approximate solutions to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation associated with the optimal control problem has been severely limited by computational resources. The computational time issue has been partially mitigated by recent works leveraging tensor-structure to develop efficient numerical methods. However, RAM requirements still have remained a major hindrance to scaling beyond state dimensions of a few hundred or low thousands. We propose an acceleration to compute the expensive higher-order terms in a reduced space, mitigating the curse of dimensionality. A fast and scalable \textsc{Matlab} implementation is provided open-source for general purpose use, with the ability to accommodate arbitrary polynomial nonlinearities in the control-affine state equation, as well as polynomial state-dependence in the cost function, and the ability to handle systems in generalized form with a non-identity mass matrix, such as finite element models. Combined with the exploitation of sparsity and modern low-rank Riccati solvers, this permits computing approximations to polynomial feedback laws based on Al'brekht's method in hundreds of thousands of states.

Optimization and Control.title: Comparing Socially-Equitable Renewable Energy Budget Allocation MDP Policies in Mature and Emerging Economies
Optimization and Control.summary: Equitable renewable-energy planning is a sequential decision problem, but the decision variables available to a public planner differ sharply between mature and emerging economies. In the former the government largely builds generation, while in the latter it steers private investment through incentives and quotas. We formulate socially-equitable renewable-energy budget allocation as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and, using a single problem-agnostic solver interface, compare the same policies across the two settings: eight U.S. cities (a mature economy) and West Java, Indonesia (an emerging economy). The results show that across both settings, a receding-horizon value-iteration policy dominates. In the U.S., it reaches 66% renewable penetration while cutting the underserved low-income population by 96% versus a random baseline. In West Java it closes the low-access gap while crowding in about seven times the private capital of a naive market-chasing heuristic. More interestingly, this heuristic, which is mildly sub-optimal in the U.S., could yield catastrophic outcomes in Indonesia, by underserving every low-access region, because chasing attractive markets and serving the underserved diverge once the planner acts through private developers.

Optimization and Control.title: An Efficient, Lean 4 Verified Necessary and Sufficient Condition for Membership in Pedigree Polytopes
Optimization and Control.summary: The set \(P_{n}\) consists of the characteristic vectors of pedigrees, which are combinatorial encodings in one-to-one correspondence with Hamiltonian cycles. For \(n \geq 4\) and \(τ_{n} = \binom{n}{3}-1\), the Membership Problem for the Pedigree Polytope (M3P) asks whether a given vector \(X \in \mathbb{Q}^{τ_{n}}\) belongs to \(\mathrm{conv}(P_n)\). This paper gives a complete account, with the full proof statements and machine-verified Lean~4 certificates, of the necessary and sufficient (\NS) condition established in Chapter~5 of \emph{Pedigree Polytopes: New Insights on Computational Complexity of Combinatorial Optimisation Problems} (Arthanari, 2023): membership of $X$ in $\mathrm{conv}(P_n)$ is characterised by the feasibility, at every stage $k=4,\dots,n-1$, of a recursively constructed layered network, together with, when needed, a multicommodity flow problem $\mathrm{MCF}(k-1)$ achieving its maximum possible flow $z_{\max}$. We present the construction, the \NS{} condition itself, and the proofs of this characterisation, together with the resulting polynomial-time algorithm for M3P. Both directions of the \NS{} condition --- sufficiency and necessity (the multicommodity-flow feasibility argument of the book's Chapter~5) --- are machine-verified in Lean~4/Mathlib4 with zero unresolved \texttt{sorry}s in either dependency chain. The \NS{} characterisation therefore follows directly from the two machine-checked implications. The complete Lean~4 project is publicly available. A companion introductory article (arXiv:2507.09069) presents the same material for a broader readership, without the Lean~4 verification; the present paper adds full statements, proof sketches, and the complete machine-checked certificates.
Optimization and Control.comment: 23 pages, 1 Table giving Lean~4 files and their corresponding results in $\emph{Pedigree Polytopes} \cite{arthanari2023book}$

Optimization and Control.title: Two Linear Programs are Better than One
Optimization and Control.summary:
The extension complexity $\operatorname{xc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$ is the minimum number of facets of a polytope that projects onto it. Motivated by the complexity of neural networks, Hertrich and Loho introduced the virtual extension complexity $\operatorname{vxc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$, which is the minimum of $\operatorname{xc}(Q) + \operatorname{xc}(R)$ among all polytopes $Q$ and $R$ such that $P+Q=R$. We show the following results pertaining to virtual extension complexity.
  First, we resolve the core open problem on the topic by showing the virtual extension complexity can be exponentially smaller than extension complexity. Second, we show there are matroid base polytopes with exponential virtual extension complexity by adapting a semi-algebraic counting argument by Hrubeš that extends the counting arguments of Rothvoss. Finally, we show that the maximum virtual extension complexity of a polygon with $n$ vertices is $Θ(\sqrt{n})$. This resolves an analogue of a question on extension complexity of Fiorini, Rothvoss, and Tiwary in 2011 in the case of virtual extension complexity.

Optimization and Control.title: The $p$-Bures-Wasserstein distance via $3\times3$ block matrices (with application to $p$-Bures-Wasserstein barycenters)
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the $p$-Bures-Wasserstein distance $D_p(A,B)=(\mathrm{tr}\,A^p+\mathrm{tr}\,B^p-2\|A^{1/2}B^{1/2}\|_p^p)^{1/2}$ on positive semidefinite matrices; it equals the Bures-Wasserstein distance for $p=1$, and the Hilbert-Schmidt distance for $p=2$. We prove that $D_p$ is a metric for every $1\le p\le2$, by proving a stronger 2014 conjecture of Lin and van den Driessche on $3\times3$ block matrices. Our main tool is a partition inequality for Schatten norms, proved by complex interpolation. We also characterize Fréchet means for $D_p$ by a fixed-point equation and prove geometric convergence of the associated iteration.
Optimization and Control.comment: 20 pages; 4 appendices; one synthetic experiment included

Optimization and Control.title: Tight Complexity of Muon under Heavy-Tailed Noise
Optimization and Control.summary: A growing lesson from neural network optimization is that optimizer design should respect how the model is parametrized. The layerwise input-output structure of neural networks motivates Muon and Scion, whose updates also support hyperparameter transfer. At the same time, stochastic gradient noise in deep learning is often far from sub-Gaussian and may exhibit heavy tails. These observations have shaped recent algorithmic principles for training neural networks, yet their joint theoretical consequences are underexplored. In particular, it is unclear what dimension dependence is unavoidable for gradient-based methods when the problem class is defined using an input-output norm and the stochastic gradient noise is heavy-tailed, and if higher-order smoothness can accelerate optimization. We study these questions through nonconvex smooth stochastic optimization over $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ equipped with general norms and under $p^\mathrm{th}$-moment heavy-tailed noise, where the goal is to achieve an $ε$-stationary point in the dual norm. Our first contribution is a dimension-dependent lower bound: when $\max\{m,n\}$ is large enough, any method using only the stochastic gradients requires $Ω(\min\{m, n\}ε^{-\frac{3p-2}{p-1}})$ oracle calls for the problem class defined by the spectral norm, which is a common input-output matrix norm. We prove that a batched Muon method with the spectral norm can achieve the matching upper bound of $O(\min\{m, n\}ε^{-\frac{3p-2}{p-1}})$. To exploit higher-order smoothness, we propose a transported Muon method and improve the bound to $O(\min\{m, n\}ε^{-\frac{5p-3}{2p-2}})$ when the norm is spectral and the Hessian is Lipschitz. Finally, we incorporate practical heuristics into our transported method and evaluate it across multiple architectures and model sizes, showing its compatibility with neural network training.

Optimization and Control.title: Entropy-Regularized Mean-Field Games with Average-Reward Criterion: Span-Seminorm Contractions and Model-Free Learning
Optimization and Control.summary: We study stationary discrete-time mean-field games with finite state and action spaces under the average-reward criterion, with an entropy-regularized objective and population-dependent dynamics and rewards. Under a minorization condition, the soft Q-operator is a span-seminorm contraction for the full transition kernel, so relative value iteration does not require the minorizing measure. When the Lipschitz constant of the kernel is below the minorization mass and the temperature exceeds an explicit threshold, the equilibrium fixed-point operator is a contraction: an equilibrium exists, its population distribution is unique, and a fixed-point iteration converges to it geometrically. We then learn the equilibrium model-free from a simulator, combining soft Q-learning at a fixed population distribution with an empirical transition kernel. We prove a finite-sample bound for soft Q-learning in the span seminorm, with temperature-independent constants, and derive convergence rates for the learned population distribution and policy. A congestion-aware routing game illustrates the results.

Optimization and Control.title: On the Convergence of Constrained Gradient Method
Optimization and Control.summary: The constrained gradient method (CGM) has recently been proposed to solve convex optimization and monotone variational inequality (VI) problems with general functional constraints. While existing literature has established convergence results for CGM, the assumptions employed therein are quite restrictive; in some cases, certain assumptions are mutually inconsistent, leading to gaps in the underlying analysis. This paper derives rigorous and improved convergence guarantees for CGM under weaker and more reasonable assumptions, covering strongly convex optimization problems, as well as VI problems under both strongly monotone and general monotone settings. Preliminary numerical experiments are provided to verify the validity of CGM and demonstrate its efficacy in addressing such problems.

Optimization and Control.title: Cosm: orchestrated collective dynamics give rise to rapid computational search at the solution frontier
Optimization and Control.summary: We introduce Collective Switched Motion (Cosm), a heuristic optimization framework based on orchestrated collective dynamics. Cosm organizes the objective into conflict-minimized subobjectives and activates them sequentially, temporally separating competing local influences. The interplay of switching and local interactions among variables, supplemented by structured correlated perturbations, gives rise to collective search behavior including coordinated cluster motion. Using this framework, we develop and test a solver for sparse Ising optimization. On G64, a large sparse instance with a highly heterogeneous degree distribution from the longstanding Gset Max-Cut benchmark suite, Cosm establishes a new best-known cut of 8753. On large random-graph instances G61 and G70, whose best-known cuts of 5799 and 9595 have been difficult for prior heuristics to attain, a vectorized CPU implementation of Cosm reliably reaches these cuts with times-to-target of 15 s and 2.4 s, respectively. Cosm also heuristically attains the certified optimum of G81, the largest Gset instance (a 20,000-variable two-dimensional spin glass), along with those of G72 and G77. Tests on planted-solution spin-glass benchmarks suggest more favorable empirical scaling than that previously reported for seven compared solvers. Cosm demonstrates that, from simple interacting elements and a new form of orchestration, effective search can emerge.
Optimization and Control.comment: Updated framing, presentation, and comparisons with prior work

Optimization and Control.title: Quantum ordinal optimization under a fixed comparison budget
Optimization and Control.summary: Ordinal optimization selects designs that are good enough rather than optimal when evaluation is expensive and the budget is small. The alignment probability measures the chance that the selected set contains at least a prescribed number of truly good designs. We formulate quantum ordinal optimization as a class of problems that maximize this probability under a fixed oracle budget. We study exact, coherent pairwise comparisons with one selected design as a first instance, with the budget counted in comparison queries. For every classical comparison budget smaller than the number of designs, we prove that a knockout among uniformly sampled designs attains the optimum. The sample is drawn without replacement and contains one more design than the number of comparisons. For a uniformly random order, the selected design's rank has a polynomial probability law. At the same comparison budget, the maximum quantum degree is at most twice the classical maximum, a factor attained whenever there are more than twice as many designs as comparisons, so a quantum algorithm can realize rank laws that no classical algorithm with the same budget can. We determine the exact quantum optimum with one comparison for every number of designs and every good-enough set. For selecting the best of n designs, the optimal success probability with one quantum comparison is approximately 3.30/n for large n, compared with 2/n for one classical comparison. When the best design is sought, one quantum comparison gives a higher alignment probability than two classical comparisons whenever there are more than nine designs.

Optimization and Control.title: Learning linear dynamical systems under convex constraints
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider the problem of finite-time identification of linear dynamical systems from $T$ samples of a single trajectory. Recent results have predominantly focused on the setup where either no structural assumption is made on the system matrix $A^* \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, or specific structural assumptions (e.g. sparsity) are made on $A^*$. We assume prior structural information on $A^*$ is available, which can be captured in the form of a convex set $\mathcal{K}$ containing $A^*$. For the solution of the ensuing constrained least squares estimator, we derive non-asymptotic error bounds in the Frobenius norm that depend on the local size of $\mathcal{K}$ at $A^*$. To illustrate the usefulness of these results, we instantiate them for four examples, namely when (i) $A^*$ is sparse and $\mathcal{K}$ is a suitably scaled $\ell_1$ ball; (ii) $\mathcal{K}$ is a subspace; (iii) $\mathcal{K}$ consists of matrices each of which is formed by sampling a bivariate convex function on a uniform $n \times n$ grid (convex regression); (iv) $\mathcal{K}$ consists of matrices each row of which is formed by uniform sampling (with step size $1/T$) of a univariate Lipschitz function. In all these situations, we show that $A^*$ can be reliably estimated for values of $T$ much smaller than what is needed for the unconstrained setting.
Optimization and Control.comment: 31 pages; corrected typos and added additional explanations at certain places; minor corrections in proofs of Corollary 4 and Theorem 2

Optimization and Control.title: Controllability of finite-dimensional linear fractional systems under uncertain parameters
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper investigates the controllability of finite-dimensional linear fractional systems involving an uncertain parameter. We establish new results on the simultaneous and average controllability. In particular, we show that average controllability can be characterized by the so-called average Kalman rank condition and the average Gramian matrix. Moreover, using the average Gramian matrix, we design an open-loop control with minimal energy. These results can be seen as a natural generalization of the classical results known for systems with integer-order derivatives. Finally, numerical simulations are provided to robustly validate the theoretical findings, with a focus on the fractional Rössler system for a damping parameter following either a Gaussian or a uniform distribution.

Optimization and Control.title: Fast Trainable Multilinear Bases for Image Compression
Optimization and Control.summary: The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), and their block-wise variants underpin most deployed image and video codecs. Their effectiveness rests on three properties: their runtime is near-linear (up to a polylogarithmic factor) in the image size, they are exactly invertible, and they carry few to no parameters. We generalize these transforms to dataset-adaptive isometric multilinear bases that keep all three properties at the cost of a polylogarithmic number of parameters, by parameterizing each basis as an isometric tensor network, inspired by quantum many-body theory, and training one shared basis per image dataset with Riemannian optimization. Because the family contains the DFT and the DCT-IV (a variant of the DCT) as exact points, training can start from these transforms, and it improves on its starting point at the compression level it is trained for. We evaluate the bases on natural photographs and line drawings. On photographs, which the cosine basis already fits well, the best trained basis leads the DCT only under aggressive truncation. On Quick Draw line drawings, under a common codec at matched quality, the best trained basis stores each image in about 20% fewer bytes than the 8x8 block cosine transform of the Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPEG) format, not counting the one-off storage of the basis.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: DiffNash: Finding Nash Equilibrium in High-Dimensional Continuous Action Spaces with Diffusion Policies
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Computing equilibria in high-dimensional continuous games requires learning and representing rich, multi-modal strategy distributions, something conventional neural policies struggle to achieve. Diffusion models offer a natural solution, but standard diffusion training requires direct samples from a fixed target distribution, which are generally unavailable under iterative game-solving updates. We propose a diffusion-based framework for equilibrium computation that enables diffusion-based variants of Online Mirror Descent (OMD) and Fictitious Play (FP). Our approach derives a reweighted score-matching objective that trains diffusion policies without requiring direct samples from each updated policy. Our main method, DiffNash, combines the fast convergence of OMD with the sample efficiency of FP by reusing past actions through a replay buffer. To correct the resulting distribution shift from sample reuse, we derive an unbiased estimator of the difference between current and past policies' Evidence Lower Bounds, whose exponential provides a tractable proxy for the corresponding importance weight without evaluating diffusion likelihoods. We evaluate our approach on forest protection games and continuous Colonel Blotto games, reducing the Nash gap over the strongest baseline by 35.6% and 24.7%, respectively, with minimal hyperparameter tuning.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 41 pages, 11 figures

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Sample-Optimal Multi-Group Learning with an ERM Oracle
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: In multi-group learning, a single predictor must perform nearly as well as the best hypothesis in a class on every group in a rich, possibly infinite and overlapping, collection of subpopulations. The known algorithms with the optimal sample complexity keep track of every pair of a group and a hypothesis, which is impossible for the large classes of interest, and the known oracle-based algorithms have a worse rate. We ask whether the optimal rate can be attained by a learner that accesses the classes only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples and polynomially many calls to a weighted ERM oracle over pairs of a group and a hypothesis, where $d_G$ and $d_H$ are the VC dimensions of the group and hypothesis classes and $\varepsilon$ bounds the excess risk on every group, weighted by its probability. We also show a matching lower bound of $Ω((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples for every learner even with unlimited computation, so oracle efficiency costs no additional samples. We also consider a natural special case in which every input belongs to at most $k$ groups and these groups can be listed. In this case, an ERM oracle for the hypothesis class alone suffices, with $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples in the agnostic setting and $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon)$ samples when every group has a hypothesis that is correct on it.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Entropy-Regularized Mean-Field Games with Average-Reward Criterion: Span-Seminorm Contractions and Model-Free Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study stationary discrete-time mean-field games with finite state and action spaces under the average-reward criterion, with an entropy-regularized objective and population-dependent dynamics and rewards. Under a minorization condition, the soft Q-operator is a span-seminorm contraction for the full transition kernel, so relative value iteration does not require the minorizing measure. When the Lipschitz constant of the kernel is below the minorization mass and the temperature exceeds an explicit threshold, the equilibrium fixed-point operator is a contraction: an equilibrium exists, its population distribution is unique, and a fixed-point iteration converges to it geometrically. We then learn the equilibrium model-free from a simulator, combining soft Q-learning at a fixed population distribution with an empirical transition kernel. We prove a finite-sample bound for soft Q-learning in the span seminorm, with temperature-independent constants, and derive convergence rates for the learned population distribution and policy. A congestion-aware routing game illustrates the results.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Fair Allocation with Dichotomous Preferences over Item Complements
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the problem of fair allocation when agents have dichotomous submodular preferences over groups of, rather than individual, items. These preferences naturally extend existing models, and have a natural interpretation in settings such as course allocation. We show that this seemingly minor extension results in computational intractability barriers: computing a utilitarian or Nash-optimal allocation with item complements is NP-hard. However, when agents' complementary bundles have size at most $k$, there exist poly-time algorithms that compute $\frac1k$-\maxUSW allocations and approximate Nash-welfare-maximizing allocations. While PO+EF-1 allocations may not exist in the complementary preference setting, it is possible to compute $\frac1{k+1}$-approximately \maxUSW EF-X allocations in polynomial time; furthermore, these allocations offer each agent $i$ a utility of at least $\frac{\MMS_i - k}{k+1 + \frac1n}$, where $\MMS_i$ is agent $i$'s maximin share guarantee.
  While the standard dichotomous binary submodular setting admits simple sequential techniques for computing fair and efficient allocations, our results for the complements setting require more complex tools from combinatorial optimization.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Inverting Top Trading Cycles: Characterizing the Endowments that Implement a Pareto-Optimal Allocation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: In one-sided matching with strict ordinal preferences, the Top Trading Cycles (TTC) mechanism maps every initial endowment to a Pareto-optimal (PO) allocation, and many distinct endowments converge to the same outcome. We study the \emph{inverse} problem: given a PO allocation $σ$, characterize and enumerate its preimage $f^{-1}(σ)$, the set of endowments from which TTC produces $σ$. We characterize $f^{-1}(σ)$ via ordered partitions of the agents and present a sound and complete enumeration algorithm, invTTC. The preimage carries direct economic meaning: $|f^{-1}(σ)|/n!$ equals the probability that random serial dictatorship selects $σ$, and $f^{-1}(σ)$ is the basin of attraction of $σ$, quantifying robustness to the assignment of initial property rights. We analyze the enumeration's complexity and report experiments on preimage structure.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted at PRIMA 2026 (https://www.prima2026.org/)

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Improving the Bounds on Approximating Weighted Maximin Share for Chores
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We investigate the problem of allocating indivisible chores among agents with arbitrary positive weights and additive nonnegative cost functions. An allocation is said to be $α$-weighted-maximin-share (WMMS) fair if the cost incurred by each agent is at most $α$ times her weighted maximin share. We establish that every instance admits a $4.124234528$-WMMS allocation. Moreover, for instances in which all weights and costs are rational numbers represented in binary, we give an algorithm that computes a $4.12424$-WMMS allocation in time polynomial in the number of agents, the number of chores, and the total binary encoding length of the input. Complementing these upper bounds, we construct a family of instances with strictly positive, identically ordered costs for which the optimal WMMS approximation factors converge to $e$. Together, our results substantially narrow the previously best-known gap of $[2,12]$ established by Li et al.~\cite{LWX26} to $[e,4.12424]$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Robust Proportionality Axioms for Additive Utilities
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the model of participatory budgeting, in which a subset of candidates is selected subject to a budget constraint. Voters express their preferences by assigning a numerical utility to each candidate. Our focus is on formal analysis of proportionality, a central notion of fairness in multi-winner elections. Intuitively, proportionality means that each group of voters should influence the election outcome roughly in proportion to its size. Recent "plus" axioms of proportionality are particularly appealing notions: they are verifiable in polynomial time, and they provide strong representation guarantees without requiring groups of voters to have cohesive preferences. However, their existing formulations are restricted to approval-based preferences. We generalise extended justified representation plus (EJR+), and Core plus (Core+) to general additive utilities. Our approach builds on a payment-based interpretation of proportionality: candidates' costs are shared among their supporters, with the aim of balancing voters' total payments.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Lasso Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study games on finite graphs with labelled or weighted edges in which plays end as soon as the first loop is formed. The resulting play has a lasso shape: a path (head) followed by a cycle (loop). We consider two semantics for determining the winner: the loop semantics, where only the loop matters, and the lasso semantics, where the entire play is taken into account. We show that adopting the lasso semantics may have a dramatic impact on both the complexity of the game and the memory required to play optimally. Mean-payoff games with lasso semantics are no longer positionally determined, and the threshold problem â deciding whether the value of the game is at least 0 â is PSPACE-complete. In contrast, lasso parity games are equivalent to weak parity games, remain positionally determined and are solvable in polynomial time. Furthermore, we show that if a positionally determined winning objective is closed under cyclic permutation and both the objective and its complement are closed under concatenation, then it is equivalent to the parity objective. Finally, we consider mod-k games, where the winner depends on the length of the path modulo k >= 2. We show that these games, in both semantics, are PSPACE-complete. Alongside computational complexity, we analyze the memory required to play optimally. We establish that for any game positionally determined in loop semantics, memory of size 2^n is sufficient in lasso semantics. We complement this by showing exponential memory lower bounds for lasso mean-payoff and mod-k games.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: In Proceedings GandALF 2026, arXiv:2610.08898

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Representation Theorems for Actual Powers over Two-Agent General Concurrent Game Frames
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: One of the most well-known connections between logic and games is Pauly's representation theorem: the induced powers of individuals and coalitions in concurrent game frames correspond, in a precise sense, to a certain class of neighborhood frames. The precise sense here is what is called alpha effectivity (or alpha power): the power of a coalition is characterized by the sets of states in which it can ensure that the outcome lies by taking some joint action. This definition is inherently monotonic, and, as pointed out by van Benthem, Bezhanishvili, and Enqvist (2019), that fact can obscure relevant information about the power structure in the game: we do not know whether two sets that a coalition has the power to enforce correspond to the same joint action or to different joint actions. An alternative is to characterize the power of a coalition by its actual power (called basic power by van Benthem, Bezhanishvili, and Enqvist (2019)): the collection of sets of states, each of which corresponds to one joint action by the coalition and all possible joint actions by the other agents. It has recently been argued by Li and Ju (2025, 2026) that standard concurrent game frames rely on three assumptions that may, in some cases, be too strong: seriality, independence of agents, and determinism. This yields a total of eight different classes of general concurrent game frames. In this paper, assuming two agents, we prove that, in terms of actual powers, the eight classes of general concurrent game frames are represented by eight corresponding classes of neighborhood frames. This generalizes a result by van Benthem, Bezhanishvili, and Enqvist (2019).
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: In Proceedings GandALF 2026, arXiv:2610.08898. Corresponding author: Fengkui Ju

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Randomized Algorithm for MMS Allocation of Chores with Online Agent Arrivals
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the fair allocation of $m$ indivisible chores among $n$ agents in the agent-arrival model against an oblivious adversary. The chore set and the number of agents are known in advance. When agent $i$ arrives, her nonnegative additive cost function $c_i$ is revealed, and the algorithm must immediately and irrevocably assign her a subset of the unallocated chores. We focus on the notion of maximin share (MMS) and measure the fairness of the realized allocation $X$ by the ex-post MMS approximation ratio $ρ(X)$. We measure an algorithm's performance by its expected ratio, and also the guarantees that hold with high probability.
  For binary additive costs, we achieve an expected ex-post MMS ratio of $3/2+o(1)$, and show that every randomized online algorithm has an expected ratio of at least $3/2-o(1)$. For every $n$, the expected ratio is at most $1.755$. A variant of our algorithm guarantees an approximation ratio of $2$ with high probability, which is optimal. % For general additive costs, we present a weighted-rounding algorithm that achieves an expected ratio of $2+o(1)$, which also holds with high probability. The expected ratio is at most $2.594$ for every $n$. We also show that similar algorithms extend to additive goods, achieving a constant expected ex-post MMS ratio and guaranteeing every agent an $x$-fraction of her MMS with probability at least $1-85x^2$ for every $x\le1/15$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Polynomial Algorithms for Simultaneous Share-Based and Envy-Based Guarantees
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the simultaneous achievement of share-based and envy-based fairness in the allocation of indivisible goods with nonnegative additive valuations. The AnyPrice share (APS) is a strengthening of the maximin share (MMS). A polynomial-time algorithm is known to guarantee a $2n/(3n-1)$ approximation of APS, but without an accompanying envy-based guarantee. Separately, allocations simultaneously satisfying minimum EFX share (MXS) and envy-freeness up to one less-preferred good (EFL), and subsequently the stronger requirement of residual maximin share (RMMS) together with EFL, have been shown to exist. However, the known constructions do not provide pseudopolynomial-time guarantees.
  We develop algorithms that combine these share-based and envy-based fairness requirements. First, for every $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we give an algorithm that computes an allocation satisfying exact EFL, $(1-\varepsilon)$-MXS, and $2n/(3n-1)$-APS. Its running time is polynomial in the binary input length and $1/\varepsilon$. Thus, we match the previously established polynomial-time APS approximation while simultaneously guaranteeing exact EFL and an arbitrarily close approximation to MXS.
  Second, we provide a pseudopolynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously guarantees exact MXS, exact EFL, and $2n/(3n-1)$-APS. Third, for every fixed number of agents, we obtain a pseudopolynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact RMMS and exact EFL.
  Finally, we establish that computing a numerical threshold between MXS and RMMS is weakly NP-hard, even for additive valuations. This identifies a computational barrier to extending our polynomial-time approach to exact MXS through independently computed residual-valid share thresholds.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Equilibrium Computation in Extensive-Form Games with Stochastic Action Sets
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Extensive-form games (EFGs) are a standard model for sequential decision-making in games. A fundamental and typically implicit assumption in EFGs is that players always have access to all of their actions at every decision point. However, in many settings, certain actions might be unavailable during game-play due to exogenous stochasticity. Given a base EFG, we formalize a model that allows for actions to be stochastically restricted, leading to a corresponding Extensive-Form Game with Stochastic Action Sets (EFGSAS). In EFGSAS, we derive an expansion procedure that results in an equivalent EFG, thus showing that standard strategy formalisms could require exponentially large representations. However, under an appropriate independence assumption, we show that approximate compact strategy representations polynomial in the size of the base EFG exist. Computationally, we introduce an algorithm called CAT-CFR, which minimizes ranking regret and whose averaged induced sequence-form strategies converge to approximate Nash equilibria with high probability in two-player zero-sum EFGSAS. Finally, we utilize a stochastic approximation procedure to recover compact representations of approximate Nash equilibria, utilizing the iterates of CAT-CFR and additional action availability samples.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 50 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Game-Theoretic Understandings of Multi-Agent Systems with Multiple Objectives
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Agents in many multi-agent systems must balance several, possibly conflicting, objectives, and the trade-offs an agent can achieve depend on how the other agents behave. We study this setting through the Multi-Objective Markov Game (MOMG), a Markov game in which each agent receives a vector of rewards, and adopt the Pareto-Nash Equilibrium (PNE) as the solution concept: at a PNE, no agent can unilaterally improve one of its objectives without sacrificing another. We show that PNEs always exist and coincide with the Nash equilibria of the linearly scalarized games with strictly positive weights, so standard single-objective Markov-game solvers suffice to compute them. We further define the Weak Pareto-Nash Equilibrium (WPNE), which excludes only unilateral deviations that strictly improve all objectives at once. The associated gap (WPNG) is zero exactly at WPNEs and never exceeds the Nash gap of any linearly scalarized game; hence an approximate Nash equilibrium of a scalarized game is also an approximate WPNE. When the preference profile is known in advance, learning in an MOMG therefore reduces to learning in a single scalarized Markov game, for which we provide a sample-efficient algorithm. When preferences are revealed only after data collection, we design a two-phase algorithm that first explores without any preference information; with high probability, every Nash equilibrium of the learned scalarized game is then an approximate WPNE for every queried preference profile, and the WPNG of any policy can be estimated accurately from the learned model. Experiments on tabular games and four multi-objective multi-agent environments illustrate the theory and show the effect of preference-free exploration.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Do Rollups Self-Organize? Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in the EIP-4844 Blob Fee Market
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: EIP-4844 gave Ethereum rollups a separate fee dimension for data, governed by a multiplicative update rule that targets three ``blobs'' per block. Whether this target is reached depends on how many independent, self-interested rollups choose to post data, a question that closed-form models address only for a single agent under exogenous prices or in a static equilibrium. We propose a calibrated multi-agent reinforcement learning environment for the blob fee market in which the blob base fee is endogenous, set by the EIP-4844 rule on the aggregated decisions of heterogeneous rollups fit to post-Dencun Ethereum data. After confirming that the environment reproduces the known single-agent analytical optimum, we show that independent learners, with no convergence guarantee, still settle near the target without coordination ($3.32\pm0.01$ blobs per block over five seeds). Over a fiftyfold demand range ($10\times$ to $500\times$), supply stays at the target from $10\times$ to $200\times$ and rises above it at higher demand, where the fee can no longer hold it. Posting frequency increases with rollup size, an emergent analog of the size threshold predicted by prior theory. A costless layer-1 calldata outside option pushes the fee down by roughly an order of magnitude while aggregate supply stays at the target, so the fee rule acts as a negative-feedback controller on decentralized supply.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE 4th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain, and Internet of Things (AIBThings 2026)

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Thompson Sampling for Learning in Zero-Sum Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Thompson sampling (TS) achieves logarithmic and asymptotically optimal regret in classical stochastic bandits, but its behavior in multi-agent learning remains less understood. We study TS in an unknown finite two-player zero-sum matrix game with Gaussian bandit feedback. Under centralized self-play, TS samples a single payoff matrix from the posterior and plays a Nash equilibrium of the sampled game. For every fixed zero-sum game with a unique Nash equilibrium, we show that the expected cumulative duality gap is $O(\sqrt T)$. The rate improves to $O(\log T)$ for pure equilibria. We then identify the exact coefficient of the $\sqrt T$ term, which depends only on the equilibrium strategies and the noise level. We also establish a minimax lower bound matching the square-root dependence on $T$ and an instance-dependent lower bound matching the logarithmic dependence on $T$ for a class of games with a unique pure equilibrium. Experiments support the predicted rates and coefficient.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Mechanomyography-Based Integrated Sensing-Stimulation System for Fatigue-Aware Neuromuscular Therapy
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Muscle fatigue limits the effectiveness of functional electrical stimulation (FES), yet fatigue monitoring during active stimulation remains challenging because electromyography (EMG) is severely contaminated by stimulation artifacts. To address this issue, this study proposes an integrated mechanomyography-based sensing framework (MMG-FES) for artifact-resistant fatigue monitoring during stimulation. Fatigue states were first characterized during voluntary movement using established EMG spectral indicators, including median frequency (MF) and mean power frequency (MPF), and then linked to MMG-derived features, including high-frequency energy ratio (HFER) and spectral bandwidth (BW), for fatigue recognition under stimulation conditions. Experimental results showed consistent fatigue-related trends, with EMG spectral features decreasing and MMG features exhibiting coordinated spectral redistribution across repeated contractions. Using these features, the proposed framework achieved fatigue-state recognition accuracies of 0.93 and 0.96 with logistic regression and random forest, respectively. These findings support MMG as a physiologically meaningful and stimulation-compatible modality for fatigue-aware closed-loop neuromuscular stimulation.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 12 pages, 14 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Vision: "What Don't I Know About User's Preferences?" How Uncertainty Estimation Improves Proactive Assistant Alignment
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Proactive Smart Assistants (PSAs) increasingly use general knowledge, learned patterns from group-level data, patterns from individual user's data, and recent sensor observations to anticipate which action a user may prefer. Existing systems typically select actions from predicted user preference likelihoods, but these likelihoods alone do not reveal how reliable the prediction is, which evidence supports it, or why ambiguity remains. In this vision paper, we argue that uncertainty estimation can provide this missing information and substantially change appropriate downstream behavior. Using the example of a home assistant, we introduce the questions that uncertainty estimation aims to answer, i.e. how sure is the assistant about the predicted preference likelihood, whether the confidence come from group-level assumptions or individual's data, and whether likelihood ambiguity reflect the user's intrinsic preference variability or insufficient data for the particular situation. We further introduce uncertainty estimation applications in neighboring domains, such as human trajectory prediction, personalized activity recognition, information-collection, and model-based control. Finally, we draw on insights from neighboring domains to envision how future uncertainty-aware proactive assistants may address key challenges in proactive interaction.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Published in Companion of the 2026 ACM International Joint Conference on Pervasive and Ubiquitous Computing (UbiComp Companion '26) PEACE Workshop

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Navigating the Conceptual Multiverse
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: When language models answer open-ended questions, they implicitly make decisions that shape their answers. However, the models do not show these decisions to the user, so users cannot contextualize answers: they cannot see the assumptions an answer rests on or the alternatives to it. Drawing on multiverse analysis from statistics, we introduce the conceptual multiverse, a representation in which language models express answers as the result of intermediate conceptual decisions. We build a system that generates such decisions explicitly, organizes them into a space of answers that users can see and change, and checks them against the norms of a specific domain. In a user study across three domains - philosophy, AI alignment annotation, and poetry - participants say that our system helps them see the decisions leading to an answer, explore the space of answers, and understand the decisions structuring this space.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: FreeBrush: Motor Signals-Based Toothbrushing Monitoring System for Electric Toothbrushes
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Oral health is vital for overall well-being, yet many users brush different tooth surfaces for insufficient or excessive durations. Toothbrushing monitoring systems can help improve brushing habits by reminding users of under-brushed and over-brushed surfaces, but existing approaches often rely on external sensors, increasing cost and reducing practicality. We observe that the intrinsic motor signals of electric toothbrushes can reflect the brushing surfaces and durations. When brushing different tooth surfaces, the brush head experiences different constraints from the surrounding oral cavity, changing the motor's driving currents and position feedback. Based on this observation, we propose FreeBrush, a toothbrushing monitoring system that uses the intrinsic motor signals of electric toothbrushes to recognize brushed tooth surfaces and estimate brushing durations without any external sensors. We prototype the system on a commercial off-the-shelf electric toothbrush and conduct a comprehensive evaluation with 18 participants. FreeBrush achieves 92.8% accuracy for 16-surface recognition and 92.0% accuracy for brushing duration estimation. The system further shows robustness across different toothpastes, brush heads, vibration modes, usage scenarios, and long-term use, and is capable of running on edge devices. By recognizing brushed tooth surfaces and estimating the brushing duration, FreeBrush can help users identify under-brushed and over-brushed surfaces and build balanced brushing habits.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 15 pages. Includes a 2-page supplementary document as an ancillary file. Extended version of our workshop paper "BrushSense: Toothbrushing Region Recognition Using Motor Signals" (UbiSense 2026)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Configuring AI for Exploratory Learning: Educator Perspectives on Inference, Persistence, and Disclosure
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI (GenAI) can support open-ended learning through generation, personalization, and learner modeling, yet educators need ways to shape these capabilities around educational goals. Through interviews and design activities with 15 U.S. educators, we examined educator configuration of GenAI using K-12 career exploration as an exploratory context. Educators configured not only AI-generated experiences, but also when student activity became an inference, whether learner information persisted, who could access it, and how it informed subsequent human action. They also faced challenges translating teaching needs into configurations: recognizing possibilities for control beyond familiar uses of GenAI, decomposing general-purpose AI into understandable functions and responsibilities, and identifying useful information through intended teaching actions. We discuss how GenAI systems can support educators in expressing and testing configurations, while establishing boundaries around personalization, inference, persistence, disclosure, and action to keep AI-supported learning aligned with evolving learner needs.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 32 pages

Human-Computer Interaction.title: COSI-Lab: Conference Living Lab for Modeling Multi-Perspective Multimodal Social Intention
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: COSI-Lab presents a multimodal multi-sensor dataset of a real interdisciplinary scientific workshop with 32 academics at an international conference. It captures ecologically valid social interactions in a weakly scripted setting consisting of two 30-minute mingling sessions with real professional and social consequences. We argue that intelligent systems could better handle subjective perceptions by modeling their multiplicity not as label noise but as an explainable perspective-driven reasoning process. We focus on the Apparent Intent Inference (AII) problem as determined by ex-situ observers and conceptualize intentions to be independent of the future. We contribute a novel annotation process for AII that accounts for a perceiver's own interpretative tendencies, quantitative and qualitative analyses of intent narratives with respect to diversity, plausibility and grounding, benchmark tasks for AII and relevant contextual factors, speech quality audio for all participants as well as privacy-preserving multi-modal environmental and wearable sensor data, enabling lexical and nonverbal behavior analysis; and the coupling of self-reported participant goals (30 minute to 3 hour) with annotated AII (seconds).

Human-Computer Interaction.title: CoBG: Learning from Player Reviews to Design, Critique, and Revise Board Game Rulebooks
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Board game design alternates between thinking as a designer and experiencing as a player, over repeated cycles of prototyping, critique, and revision. This loop is cognitively demanding: without knowing how players will receive a rule, a designer cannot tell what to revise. We present CoBG, a design assistant that supports this workflow end to end with four modules that learn from 2.2K structured rulebooks and 180K player reviews: BG-Ideator turns multi-turn dialogue into a structured design draft; BG-Realizer writes a rulebook and revises it with BG-Critic, a review-grounded critic that localizes flaws along the Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics chain and accepts a revision only when it prefers it; and BG-Persona previews feedback from 150 profiled reviewers. On 207 held-out games, CoBG localizes flaws in rulebooks and revises them better than general-purpose LLMs, and iterative revision brings their rating close to that of published rulebooks. Blind readers prefer CoBG's rulebooks to GPT-5.4's in 38 of 50 new design intents under the same revision budget. In a 30-participant user study and paper-prototype playtests, designers using CoBG report less blank-page anxiety and catch flaws they would otherwise miss, and the resulting rulebooks hold up at the table with few rule breakdowns.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Co-Located MMG-FES Wearable Interface for Action-Updated State-Gated Stimulation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Functional electrical stimulation (FES) assists movement, but fixed schedules cannot track how a repeatedly activated muscle changes, and surface electromyography (EMG) near the stimulation electrodes is often obscured by artifacts. Prior work recorded mechanomyography (MMG) passively during closed-loop FES cycling and estimated FES-induced fatigue or predicted fatigue for FES control, without gating stimulation with stimulated-site MMG. In this study, we present VG-FES, a wearable module co-locating microphone-based MMG, programmable charge-balanced biphasic stimulation, and embedded state-gated control at one on-skin thigh site. After each action, we compare rectus femoris (RF) mean power frequency (MPF) with an early-session baseline of the same direction, giving a relative state. A threshold on its window means enables fixed-duration bursts separated by rest periods. During onboard stimulation, MMG remained recordable, whereas near-site EMG was artifact-dominated. Under prolonged external stimulation, cycle-wise MMG tracked an independent local-pressure reference (Spearman rho = 0.968). In leave-one-session-out evaluation on 2284 squat actions (11 sessions, eight participants), MMG-based action segmentation reached an event-detection F1 of 0.923 and direction classification a balanced accuracy of 0.925. Online, over 15.69 min of self-paced squats, one participant received four bursts while MMG acquisition and action monitoring continued. Mechanical feedback from the stimulated site offers wearable FES and assistive robotics a per-action basis for state-gated stimulation.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 9 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Side-Vent Design for Microphone-Based Mechanomyography Sensors: Modeling and Experimental Evaluation of Contact Dependence
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Wearable muscle sensing for rehabilitation, assistive robotics, and electrical-stimulation feedback needs mechanomyography sensors less sensitive to fit changes during wear. In microphone-based mechanomyography, cavity pressure depends on rim contact, a dependence housing design has rarely targeted. This study evaluates a side-vented housing, whose vent opens a pressure-relief path in parallel with the rim to lower contact dependence, and quantifies the acoustic-gain cost. Thermoviscous finite-element simulations compared twenty cavity configurations under prescribed source motion. Paired bench sweeps over 10-200 Hz on both housings compared direct contact with a Gap-ring spacer, a radially grooved spacer ring. At 100 Hz, side venting reduced the simulated acoustic-gain variation across 0.10-0.50 mm rim clearances from 25.8 to 10.0 dB and cost 5.5 dB of gain at 0.20 mm clearance. Velocity fields and branch-flow calculations identified this path. At the higher speaker drive level, the Gap-ring spacer caused median attenuations of 13.6 dB (vented) and 30.1 dB (unvented) relative to direct contact. In this front end, a 35.9-dB signal-gain increase at 100 Hz raised the calculated operational-amplifier voltage-noise gain by 1.6 dB. A single-participant demonstration of paced elbow flexion and extension compared envelope timing and spectra between housings, finding similar envelope timing (correlation 0.935) and broadly similar spectra (correlation 0.956). Vent area trades acoustic gain against contact dependence and can therefore serve as a housing design parameter.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 10 pages, 9 figures, 1 table. Submitted to IEEE Sensors Journal

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Benchmark for Spatially Grounded Gesture Generation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Communication in shared space interweaves verbal and non-verbal signals, and pointing gestures anchor language to the environment: "put the cup on that one" is uninterpretable without the gesture that fixes the referent. Yet no common framework exists for evaluating whether generated gestures indicate their intended referent; distributional metrics reward a gesture aimed at the wrong object as long as it looks natural. We introduce a benchmark for spatially grounded gesture generation, comprising ~2K pointing-annotated clips from naturalistic VR dialogue with ground-truth 3D referents, a task in which systems must decide when, how and where to point within conversational speech, and a protocol that separates temporal alignment, spatial grounding and perceived naturalness. We also provide a flow-matching baseline, MM-Conv-Flow. Evaluating it alongside an independent retrieval-based system and captured human motion, we find that geometric grounding can exceed that of human pointing without any gain in perceived naturalness, showing that referential gesture quality must be measured along separate dimensions.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 13 pages, 9 figures. Benchmark of the Referential Gesture Challenge at the HSI Workshop, ECCV 2026. Data and video: https://huggingface.co/datasets/hsi-workshop/referential-gesture-challenge, v2: corrected references

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AuthScribe: Supporting Agency and Authorship in LLM-Assisted Reflective Journaling
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Large language models are increasingly used in reflective journaling, where articulating an experience is part of interpreting it. This raises questions about how writers retain authorship, exercise agency, and assess personalized assistance. We present AuthScribe, an LLM-assisted reflective journaling system that combines contextual anchors, writer-steered AI support, Autobiographical Citations, and read-only Provisional Drafts that require re-expression before AI-generated suggestions enter the journal. Retrieval and LLM inference run on-device. In a 14-day field deployment with 14 participants, grounding shifted from situating current experiences to reconnecting them with prior self-authored interpretations. Perceived agency remained stable through Week 1 and shifted during Week 2. Participants described authorship through transforming AI-generated suggestions into personally meaningful expression, and trusted personalized prompts when they could trace them to prior writing. We discuss design implications for adoption friction, longitudinal agency, and traceable personalization in AI systems for personal reflection.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: "We Need a Standard": Toward an Expert-Informed Privacy Label for Differential Privacy
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The increasing adoption of differential privacy (DP) leads to public-facing DP deployments by both government agencies and companies. However, real-world DP deployments often do not fully disclose their privacy guarantees, which vary greatly between deployments. Failure to disclose certain DP parameters can lead to misunderstandings about the strength of the privacy guarantee, undermining the trust in DP. In this work, we seek to inform future standards for communicating the privacy guarantees of DP deployments. Based on semi-structured interviews with 12 DP experts, we identify important DP parameters to communicate privacy guarantees for transparency and trust. We further elaborate why and how these parameters should be disclosed according to expert consensus.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 13 pages, 5 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: ArguScale: Evidence-Grounded Human-AI Sensemaking Across Concurrent Live Conversations
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Monitoring concurrent classroom collaborative reasoning discussions is challenging because instructors have to track collaboration-relevant behaviors across multiple ongoing conversations at once. Existing Human-AI conversational sensemaking systems can scale monitoring upward through summaries and visual abstractions, but these representations may distance users from underlying conversational evidence, e.g., relevant audio and transcript segments, needed to forage downward. Through our formative study, we developed ArguScale, an evidence-grounded Human-AI sensemaking system that organizes interactional signals into temporally aligned representations linked to transcript and audio evidence. A temporal signal-density view provides temporal context and supports rapid cross-group comparison, while selective evidence access allows instructors to inspect audio and transcript. We evaluated ArguScale in a mixed-design study with 20 participants. Compared to other conditions, ArguScale improved participants' ability to efficiently and accurately identify collaboration-relevant cues. We further identify strategies participants used to forage for and make sense of conversational evidence under live time constraints.

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Application based Evaluation of an Efficient Spike-Encoder, "Spiketrum"
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Spike-based encoders represent information as sequences of spikes or pulses, which are transmitted between neurons. A prevailing consensus suggests that spike-based approaches demonstrate exceptional capabilities in capturing the temporal dynamics of neural activity and have the potential to provide energy-efficient solutions for low-power applications. The Spiketrum encoder efficiently compresses input data using spike trains or code sets (for non-spiking applications) and is adaptable to both hardware and software implementations, with lossless signal reconstruction capability. The paper proposes and assesses Spiketrum's hardware, evaluating its output under varying spike rates and its classification performance with popular spiking and non-spiking classifiers, and also assessing the quality of information compression and hardware resource utilization. The paper extensively benchmarks both Spiketrum hardware and its software counterpart against state-of-the-art, biologically-plausible encoders. The evaluations encompass benchmarking criteria, including classification accuracy, training speed, and sparsity when using encoder outputs in pattern recognition and classification with both spiking and non-spiking classifiers. Additionally, they consider encoded output entropy and hardware resource utilization and power consumption of the hardware version of the encoders. Results demonstrate Spiketrum's superiority in most benchmarking criteria, making it a promising choice for various applications. It efficiently utilizes hardware resources with low power consumption, achieving high classification accuracy. This work also emphasizes the potential of encoders in spike-based processing to improve the efficiency and performance of neural computing systems.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: Under review in "IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computational Intelligence"

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: How Shared Representations Become Specialized: Formation, Maintenance, and Latent Susceptibility
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: When several predictions use the same internal representation, information about some targets can remain easier to recover than information about others. We study how this specialization forms, persists, and changes in minimal artificial learners. With reconstruction errors weighted equally during learning, changing which target is observed precisely selects the favored target and redirects an already specialized learner. Removing current support can reduce a formed bias, whereas state-following update feedback can maintain it. We then compare learners formed through different observation and update conditions but matched on specified reconstruction measurements. Both change under the same brief opposing intervention, yet their responses differ. Resetting Adam largely removes the ten-update difference; exchanging its second moment reverses which route is more susceptible. New interventions show that equalizing the mean second-moment scaling reduces but does not remove the difference: its coordinate-wise pattern also matters. With fresh Adam or calibrated SGD, smaller route differences emerge later, whereas 500 common opposing updates bring the selected allocation endpoints close. A further control produces response differences with identical acquisition and equal mean loss weights but jointly different weight variability and realized sequence. Acquisition-selected formation also extends to a symmetric three-target setting. These interventions distinguish specialization's formation, present support, and time-dependent latent susceptibility.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: 23 pages including appendices; 5 figures

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Learned Structure Shows Up Earlier in the Task's Own Basis: A Controlled Look at a Synchronisation Precursor in Grokking
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Analyses of grokking usually read hidden activations in one basis, most often the Fourier basis modulo $p$. We ask how much the answer to "has the network organised yet?" depends on that choice. The measure FSD$_{\rm gen}$ averages each unit's activation over inputs with the same answer and counts how many units share the same strongest irreducible representation. For modular multiplication we read one answer-averaged profile in three orders: discrete-logarithm order, in which the characters of the multiplicative group become Fourier modes; natural order; and random orders. Across 60 networks at $p\in\{59,97,113\}$, the discrete-log reading reached a fixed threshold before both other readings in 60 of 60 networks (59 of 60 when it had to hold 500 steps). Because untrained networks already score higher in discrete-log order, we also required an equal rise above each reading's untrained level; the discrete-log reading was still first in at least 16 of 20 networks at every prime. At $p=59$ and $p=97$ this happened during the memorisation plateau in 35 of 39 networks; at $p=113$ in 12 of 20. Memorisation preceded grokking in all 179 runs that grokked, by more than any synchronisation signal on average, so a lead over grokking is not by itself evidence of a detected circuit. Synchronisation time is only weakly related to grokking time (pooled $ρ=0.18$). On six finite groups, read with the same measure in every basis, the irreducible-representation reading came before random element orders on all six; with equal-rise thresholds this held in every case on four groups, in 7 of 10 on $\mathbb{Z}_5\times\mathbb{Z}_5$ and in none on $D_{16}$, where about half the profile power lies in one-dimensional representations the measure leaves out. We also correct a conjugate-pair artefact that roughly halves the measure on abelian groups. This version withdraws the causal and predictive claims of v1.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, 9 tables. Replaces v1: the causal and predictive claims of v1 are withdrawn; see Appendix A

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Neuromorphic Computing Based on Parametrically-Driven Oscillators and Frequency Combs
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Parametrically driven oscillators exhibit distinct dynamical regimes that strongly influence their computational capability as physical reservoirs. Here, we demonstrate reservoir computing in a two-mode system exhibiting 2:1 parametric resonance using Mackey--Glass, Rössler, and Lorenz chaotic time-series prediction tasks. Mapping the normalized mean squared error over parameter space reveals that the lowest prediction errors consistently occur within the parametric resonance regime, where nonlinear interactions are activated while temporal coherence is preserved. In contrast, although frequency-comb states increase spectral dimensionality, prediction performance degrades in the chaotic comb regime due to loss of phase coherence. We further show that the modulation depth $Δ\text{F}$, detuning $κ$, damping ratio $γ_{21}$, and input data rate systematically reshape the accessible dynamical regimes and thereby control the reservoir performance.
