First, with relative position measurements over attack-free links, resilient formation tracking laws are designed for leaders with constant velocities and with time-varying velocities comprising translational, rotational, and scaling motions. These laws guarantee asymptotic tracking and finite-time recovery of tracking, respectively, when the duration of localizability-broken attacks is suitably bounded. Second, with only angle measurements and communications, a resilient simultaneous localization and formation control (RSLAF) scheme is developed. It combines a finite-time distributed observer, which estimates the exosystem matrices and states under asynchronous DoS attacks, with a perturbation-based localization law that prevents localization from getting stuck at degenerate configurations. The theoretical results are rigorously proved and illustrated by numerical simulations.

Systems and Control.title: On composition and decomposition operations for vector spaces, graphs and matroids
Systems and Control.summary:
In this paper, we study the ideas of composition and decomposition in the context of vector spaces, graphs and matroids. For vector spaces $\V_{AB},$ treated as collection of row vectors, with specified column set $A\uplus B,$ we define $\V_{SP}\lrarv \V_{PQ}, S\cap Q= \emptyset, $ to be the collection of all vectors $(f_S,f_Q)$ such that $(f_S,f_P)\in \V_{SP}, (f_P,f_Q)\in \V_{PQ}$. An analogous operation $\G_{SP}\lrarg \G_{PQ}\equivd \G_{PQ}$ can be defined in relation to graphs $\G_{SP}, \G_{PQ},$ on edge sets $S\uplus P, P\uplus Q,$ respectively in terms of an overlapping subgraph $\G_P$ which gets deleted in the right side graph (see for instance the notion of $k-sum$ \cite{oxley}). For matroids we define the `linking' $\M_{SP}\lrarm \M_{PQ} \equivd (\M_{SP}\vee \M_{PQ})\times (S\uplus Q)$, denoting the contraction operation by '$\times$'. In each case, we examine how to minimize the size of the `overlap' set $P,$ without affecting the right side entity. In the case of vector spaces, there is a polynomial time algorithm for achieving the minimum, which we present. Similar ideas work for graphs and for matroids under appropriate conditions.
  Next we consider the problem of decomposition. Here, in the case of vector spaces, the problem is to decompose $\V_{SQ}$ as $\V_{SP}\lrarv \V_{PQ},$ with minimum size $P.$ We give a polynomial time algorithm for this purpose. In the case of graphs and matroids we give a solution to this problem under certain restrictions.
Systems and Control.comment: Newer version titled "free products" (arXiv:2610.14111) has been uploaded

Systems and Control.title: Mixed-Reality Feedback Control: Towards Blending of Control and Digital Twinning
Systems and Control.summary: Technologies, such as co-simulation, in particular, digital twins (DTs) are used for comprehensive and reliable prototyping, verification and validation (V&V) of control systems. There, the combination of feedback loops across multiple realities (e.g., simulations, physical setups) enables various forms of experimentation with robots and autonomous systems. However, the handling of multiple realities requires a more specific support by the modelling techniques used in control engineering. To streamline the latter in the system life cycle, we propose a framework for mixing (i.e., fusing, defusing) control input and feedback signals (i.e., stimuli, responses) in simultaneously operated plants for multiple realities.
Systems and Control.comment: 19 pages, 7 figures

Systems and Control.title: Iteratively Convex Frequency Data-Driven Synthesis of Structured MIMO Controllers
Systems and Control.summary: Frequency-response-function-based controller design enables synthesis directly from measured data, avoiding the need for accurate parametric plant models. This paper presents a generalized IQC-based approach for convex synthesis of structured MIMO feedback and feedforward controllers from frequency response function data. The framework supports flexible controller parametrizations, multiple performance objectives, and both singular-value and element-wise performance shaping of MIMO controllers within a unified frequency-domain formulation. To facilitate practical deployment, the synthesis approach is embedded within a bootstrapped controller design methodology that progressively increases controller flexibility while refining the performance specifications. The resulting approach is validated experimentally on the motion stage of an industrial wirebonder, where clear performance improvement is demonstrated through MIMO $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ synthesis, element-wise feedback shaping, and dynamic feedforward design. The results demonstrate that high-performance multivariable controllers can be synthesized directly from measured FRF data in a practical and systematic manner.
authors: Maurice W. P. M. H. Heemels
Systems and Control.comment: 16 pages, 11 figures, TCST paper

Systems and Control.title: Severity-Aware Minimum Security Sets for Accelerated Preventive SCOPF Using Machine Learning
Systems and Control.summary: This paper proposes a severity-aware machine learning framework for reducing the computational burden of preventive AC security-constrained optimal power flow (PSCOPF). The central idea is to identify a compact minimum security set (MSS) containing only the non-dominated contingencies and associated post-contingency constraints that materially influence the preventive operating point while satisfying a prescribed severity tolerance. An offline procedure combines AC security assessment, severity-based ranking, non-dominated screening, and iterative reduced PSCOPF. After each reduced PSCOPF solution, exhaustive security assessment over all credible contingencies identifies additional contingency--constraint pairs whose residual severity exceeds the specified threshold. Severity is characterized using the normalized number, accumulated magnitude, maximum magnitude, and average magnitude of post-contingency violations. The resulting operating-point-dependent MSSs are used as labels for a supervised multi-label learning model that predicts the security elements required to construct the reduced PSCOPF directly from the pre-contingency state. The proposed framework therefore focuses the optimization on the contingencies and constraints that affect preventive control decisions, reducing problem size and computation time while explicitly controlling residual post-contingency severity. Results on the IEEE 60-bus and 118-bus systems, the latter having an approximately seven-times-larger PSCOPF formulation, demonstrate substantial computational reductions with limited impact on the preventive operating solution.

Systems and Control.title: Runtime Monitoring of Supermartingale Certificates
Systems and Control.summary: Supermartingale certificates formally guarantee temporal properties of discrete and continuous-time stochastic dynamical systems. However, these guarantees rely on a mathematical model of the world, leaving a sim-to-real gap that can invalidate them for the deployed system. We formulate the runtime monitoring problem for supermartingale certificates, in which a monitor observes a single system trajectory and raises an alarm when there is sufficient statistical evidence that the supermartingale certificate has been violated during execution. We present an algorithm to automatically construct a monitor using betting-based sequential tests that bound the probability of ever raising a false alarm at a user-specified level. Within this betting framework, we formulate strategies that allow the monitor to exploit spatial regularity to improve detection power while preserving this statistical guarantee. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on supermartingale certificate benchmarks from the literature.

Systems and Control.title: Bearing-based Circumnavigation with Collision Avoidance in Time-varying Graphs under Limited Target Information
Systems and Control.summary: In this paper, we study distributed circumnavigation of a stationary target by a heterogeneous team of agents. Each agent is modelled as a disk rather than a point mass to account for its physical dimensions. The target location is assumed to be accessible only to a small subset of agents, called leaders. The rest, called followers, therefore use only local information available from their designated out-neighbour in the interaction graph characterised by the selection of nearest neighbours. By controlling only angular speeds, we develop a distributed guidance law to circumnavigate a stationary target. The proposed guidance law works for both static and time-varying interaction graphs. Inter-agent collision avoidance is enforced through a logarithmic Barrier Lyapunov (BLF) Function, which guarantees forward invariance of the collision-free set. We show that every follower converges to circumnavigation about the same target as the leader at the end of its directed path in the interaction graph, provided the initial conditions are admissible. Numerical simulations illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for both static and time-varying topologies.
Systems and Control.comment: 13 pages, 27 figures

Systems and Control.title: Real-Time GPU-Accelerated Monte Carlo Evaluation of Safety-Critical AEB Systems Under Uncertainty
Systems and Control.summary: Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB) systems represent a safety-critical national interest, with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS No. 127) requiring AEB in all new light vehicles sold in the United States by September 2029. However, production implementations frequently rely on deterministic stopping-distance or Time-to-Collision (TTC) thresholds that fail to capture uncertainty in sensing, road conditions, and vehicle dynamics. This paper presents a GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo framework for stochastic evaluation of emergency braking performance using a longitudinal vehicle model incorporating aerodynamic drag, road grade, brake actuator dynamics, and weight transfer effects. A one-thread-per-sample execution strategy exploits the independence of Monte Carlo rollouts, while deterministic CPU-generated sampling ensures bit-exact numerical consistency between CPU and GPU implementations. The framework is evaluated across four hardware platforms: two laptop GPUs (GTX 1650, RTX 5070) and two automotive-grade embedded platforms (Jetson Orin Nano, Jetson AGX Orin). Peak speedups of 54.57x are achieved. Real-time feasibility analysis with a complete AEB timing budget demonstrates that the Jetson AGX Orin can execute approximately 25,000 Monte Carlo samples within a 530 ms budget, enabling real-time probabilistic AEB evaluation as part of a complete embedded pipeline. Collision probability analysis demonstrates that a threshold set at the mean stopping distance of 79.2 m leaves a collision probability of approximately 47%, while the conservative 1% risk threshold requires a minimum safe headway of 111.1 m, an additional 31.9 m (40%). These results provide quantitative guidance for risk-aware AEB threshold selection under the NHTSA final rule.
Systems and Control.comment: 11 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE journal for possible publication; under review

Systems and Control.title: Identifiability-Guided Composite Load Modeling of AI Data Centers
Systems and Control.summary: The rapid growth of AI data centers introduces large, workload-dependent loads whose protection and reconnection behavior can affect power-system transient stability. Calibrating dynamic models of such loads is challenging because treating all associated elements as freely estimable may lead to weakly identified or physically confounded parameterizations. This paper proposes an identifiability-guided calibration framework for a composite load model with separate IT, cooling, and auxiliary branches. A nuisance-projected Fisher-information criterion characterizes the local identifiability of the cooling-motor composition, while a workload non-equivalence result shows that voltage-only recalibration cannot reproduce workload-dependent responses. Guided by these results, a grey-box estimator trained with branch-level supervision learns the workload-to-power relation and the cooling composition, while retaining a prescribed UPS protection law and an externally anchored reconnect-ramp duration. The learned workload relation is then distilled into a closed form for transient-stability simulation. Evaluation using 300,000 MIT Supercloud GPU power-utilization samples and 12,600 IEEE 39-bus fault scenarios yields an aggregate active-power $R^2$ of 0.948, compared with 0.856 for an LSTM baseline. Removing branch-level supervision preserves relatively high aggregate accuracy but substantially degrades cooling-component recovery. Under unseen deep voltage sags, the proposed model achieves a transient $R^2$ of 0.750, compared with 0.033 for the LSTM. Closed-loop simulations further show that cooling composition and protection behavior can affect retained-load states and voltage responses near protection thresholds.

Systems and Control.title: Distributed Optimization with Nesterov Momentum and Finite-Time Quantized Consensus
Systems and Control.summary: In modern large-scale networked systems, rapidly solving optimization problems while utilizing communication resources efficiently is critical for addressing complex tasks. In this paper, we consider an unconstrained distributed optimization problem in which information exchange among nodes is governed by a directed communication graph. In our setup we focus on two key challenges. The first is the zigzag phenomenon caused by the objective functions of individual nodes having significantly different curvature along different directions. The second is that the communication channels among nodes are subject to limited bandwidth, which motivates the use of compressed (quantized) messages. To address both challenges simultaneously, we propose QANM, a distributed optimization algorithm that combines Nesterov momentum with a distributed finite-time quantized consensus protocol. Under strong convexity and smoothness assumptions, we show that our proposed algorithm converges linearly to a neighborhood of the optimal solution. Finally, we evaluate QANM on a distributed sensor-fusion problem. With each method's step size tuned separately, QANM exhibits the fastest initial error reduction among the tested methods, including QAGD, Acc-DNGD-SC, and MSDA. Comparisons with QAGD under the same quantized averaging framework illustrate the empirical benefit of momentum, while experiments at two quantization levels demonstrate quantization-dependent error floors.

Systems and Control.title: Heterogeneous Services in Multi-UAV Networks with No-Fly Zone and User Mobility
Systems and Control.summary: In this paper, we investigate a wireless communication network supported by multiple uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs). To ensure reliable connectivity, UAVs are desired to approach the boundaries of designated no-fly zones (NFZs) without violating them when mobile users (MUs) enter NFZs. To support heterogeneous communication services, MUs are assigned different priority levels based on their individual communication types. Considering the practical constraints arising from user mobility, heterogeneous communication requirements, and NFZs, the objective is to maximize the weighted sum of MU communication rates, where weights correspond to MU priorities. This is achieved by jointly optimizing trajectory planning, UAV transmission power control, and the binary association factor between UAVs and MUs. To address this challenging optimization problem under dynamic constraints, we develop a soft actor-critic algorithm with prioritized experience replay, which learns an adaptive control policy. Numerical results show that the proposed algorithm outperforms benchmark schemes in terms of convergence speed and stability. Moreover, it effectively meets diverse communication requirements, satisfies UAV energy constraints, and ensures reliable operation under NFZ constraints.
Systems and Control.comment: 12 pages, 10 figures

Systems and Control.title: Constrained coalition games for USV swarm confrontation
Systems and Control.summary: This paper formulates unmanned surface vehicle (USV) swarm confrontation as a constrained coalition game, capturing cooperation within swarms and competition between swarms. Local task costs are aggregated into coalition objectives to account for tradeoffs among target approach, interception, and formation maintenance, subject to individual geographic constraints and supply line limits shared within each swarm. For prescribed formation sizes and task assignments, explicit linear matrix inequalities in the task weights are derived to establish strong monotonicity of the coalition pseudogradient, thereby guaranteeing the existence of a unique Nash equilibrium (NE) whenever the joint feasible set is nonempty. A distributed robust NE seeking strategy is then developed by integrating gradient tracking and action estimation with projected primal-dual dynamics using local information and neighbor communication. Adaptive compensation addresses unknown hydrodynamic parameters and bounded time-varying disturbances. The disturbance compensation gains are adjusted through local error feedback without requiring disturbance measurements, prior knowledge of disturbance bounds, or a prescribed disturbance generation model. Under the derived weight conditions, the stated dynamics and communication assumptions, and suitable gain conditions, the physical states of all USVs are shown to converge asymptotically to the unique feasible NE. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

Systems and Control.title: Traffic State Prediction and Control Using a Koopman Operator Framework with Polynomial Observables
Systems and Control.summary: In this paper, we develop a Koopman operator framework for modeling and control of traffic flow governed by the Lighthill--Whitham--Richards (LWR) conservation law. We show that the nonlinear dynamics induced by the Greenshields flow--density relation naturally motivate a dictionary of polynomial observables, while the controlled dynamics become bilinear in the lifted Koopman coordinates. A reduced-order Koopman model is identified from spatio-temporal traffic-density snapshots and used as the prediction model in a model predictive control (MPC) framework for ramp metering. The resulting Koopman-MPC is compared with two predictive control baselines that use, respectively, a fixed linearized LWR model and the nonlinear finite-volume LWR model. In a one-hour freeway experiment, the Koopman-based controller maintains the traffic density below the critical Greenshields value and closely reproduces the behavior of the nonlinear PDE-based MPC, with a maximum-density difference below 1%. The Koopman predictor also reduces the mean online model-evaluation cost by approximately one order of magnitude relative to the nonlinear PDE predictor. In contrast, the linearized LWR predictor is computationally cheaper but exhibits substantially larger prediction errors and yields a more conservative metering policy. These results demonstrate that the analytical structure of the nonlinear traffic conservation law can be exploited to construct an interpretable data-driven surrogate for efficient traffic prediction and control

Systems and Control.title: Comprehensive Comparisons of Reinforcement Learning Algorithms in Autonomous Driving
Systems and Control.summary: This paper presents a comprehensive comparison of four representative reinforcement learning (RL) methods in autonomous vehicle (AV) decision-making, including: Fitted Value Iteration (FVI), Rollout Classification Policy Iteration (RCPI), Deep Q-Network (DQN), and a discrete-action adaptation of Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (D-DDPG). The four methods are applied to the same AV decision-making problem at an unsignalized intersection and are compared in terms of optimality and safety, training stability, and training and decision cost. RCPI is the closest to a reference solution and has the most stable training process. However, it is the least data-efficient. D-DDPG reaches the second-smallest gap to a reference solution with the highest data efficiency, but has the least training stability. DQN is the most stable model-free method but has the highest collision rate. FVI achieves a lower collision rate than DQN, but is less data-efficient and less stable. Based on these results, we provide suggestions for selecting a method according to whether a model is available, the budget for training, and whether stable training is required.

Systems and Control.title: Optimistic Distributed Submodular Coordination with Applications to Multi-Target Tracking with Multiple Robots
Systems and Control.summary: We provide a distributed online algorithm for multi-agent submodular coordination in bandit environments, i.e., environments whose evolution is unknown a priori and may even adapt to the agents' actions. We are motivated by multi-robot tasks such as target tracking, where the optimal actions change over time and the agents must track them rather than a single fixed optimum. To address such problems, we provide the Optimistic Distributed Online Greedy (O-DOG) algorithm, that leverages predictions about the environment's behavior and improves regret guarantees. The agents select actions simultaneously over arbitrary, possibly time-varying, network topologies, and each agent acts optimistically, i.e., leveraging predictions of its upcoming rewards, e.g., from forecasts of the targets' motion and of its neighbors' actions. We bound O-DOG's tracking regret in terms of the agents' prediction error and the bound never exceeds its prediction-free counterpart. Particularly, it is sublinear even when the optimal action changes at every time step, provided the predictions are accurate enough. We further quantify the suboptimality due to decentralization as a function of the network structure, and show that accurate predictions accelerate convergence. We validate O-DOG in simulated multi-robot target tracking.
Systems and Control.comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, under review for the American Control Conference (ACC 2027)

Systems and Control.title: Multiscale distributed MPC for Optimal Transport
Systems and Control.summary: In this paper, we present a novel multiscale formulation for the Optimal Transport (OT) of large swarms. The scheme is divided in two levels, a top-level OT formulation with a terminal penalty cost to handle time-varying densities, and a low-level, Model Predictive Controller (MPC) that allows agents to track the nominal velocity under control affine dynamics and rejects external disturbances. We show that the terminal-penalty dynamic formulation reduces to a regularized static dual, which agents solve in a distributed way to compute the nominal velocity.We also prove distributional input-to-state stability in the $1$-Wasserstein metric of the density flow with respect to the mismatch that the low-level and the target motion introduce, so that the tracking error only perturbs the macroscopic flow by a bounded, quantifiable amount. Finally, we demonstrate via simulations the effectiveness of the proposed method handling time-varying targets and state perturbations.
Systems and Control.comment: 9 Pages, 1 Figure, Submitted to American Control Conference 2027, under review

Systems and Control.title: A Critical Review of Grid Integration Challenges and Flexibility Opportunities for Large-Scale Data Centers
Systems and Control.summary: The rapid proliferation of cloud computing and artificial intelligence workloads is fundamentally reshaping the magnitude, spatial concentration, and electrical characteristics of data center power demand. Data centers differ from conventional commercial loads because they combine high rack densities, converter-dominated interfaces, thermally coupled cooling, uninterruptible power supplies, programmable workloads, and increasingly complex behind-the-meter generation and storage within a single facility. This review examines their grid integration from utility and sustainable-energy perspectives across resource planning, large-load interconnection, distribution feeders, market operation, real-time dynamics, power quality, and asset management. Particular attention is given to distribution-level issues that receive limited treatment in broader energy reviews: bidirectional operation on renewable-rich feeders, harmonic propagation and resonance, ride-through and reconnection, transformer derating, cable ampacity, neutral-conductor heating, protection, and measurement. Static, composite, physics-based dynamic, calibrated, impedance, electromagnetic transient, and hybrid load models are compared according to study purpose and data requirements, and utility coordination platforms, uninterruptible power supply and battery control, workload flexibility, renewable co-location, cogeneration, fuel cells, thermal storage, and clean firm supply are assessed. The central finding is that requested peak demand and annual energy matching alone cannot establish reliable or sustainable integration. Credible assessment must consider hourly and locational supply, network deliverability, marginal emissions, lifecycle and water impacts, backup obligations, rebound, asset health, and verified operating capability.

Systems and Control.title: Probe Sets for Nonlinear Kalman Filtering: Multi-Center Gains and Covariance Recalibration
Systems and Control.summary: Kalman filters (KFs) choose the gain as the product of the state-measurement cross-covariance and the inverse of the innovation covariance. In nonlinear systems, the predictive distribution generally changes shape, and these covariances require approximation. Conventional nonlinear KFs approximate them around a single center, the predicted state. They can produce inaccurate gains and overconfident covariance estimates when one local approximation does not represent the measurement geometry across the uncertainty region. To address this issue, we introduce probe sets, small covariance-scaled collections of states at which the filter repeats its local approximation. We then select the gain that minimizes the average covariance reported by these local approximations. The same construction is used in our previously proposed covariance recalibration step to improve covariance consistency. The construction applies to different KF variants without requiring a specific approximation rule. For quadratic measurements, we derive conditions under which probing yields lower normalized true error variance than the corresponding single-center gain when prediction uncertainty is sufficiently understated. We apply the framework to four KF variants and compare the resulting filters with multiple baselines across 300 randomized setups for each of two systems. The results show that probing preserves typical accuracy while substantially reducing covariance inconsistency and the rare large-error trajectories that dominate the root mean square of per-run errors. The code is available at https://github.com/Shida-Jiang/Probe_KF.

Systems and Control.title: Adaptive Dead-Zone Dual Sliding Mode Observer for Reliable Electrochemical Model-Based SOC Estimation
Systems and Control.summary: Accurate state-of-charge (SOC) estimation is essential for safe and efficient lithium-ion battery operation. Electrochemical models provide physically grounded SOC estimates, but nonlinear voltage dynamics and coupled state-parameter errors can destabilize online adaptation. This paper proposes an adaptive dead-zone dual sliding-mode observer (ADZ-DSMO) based on an improved extended single-particle (IESP) model. A state SMO estimates SOC-related states, while a parameter SMO updates dominant model parameters. An online-computable, Lyapunov-guided adaptive boundary selectively gates parameter updates while the state observer remains active at every sampling step. Validation on a Panasonic NCR18650PF cell under 1C and 3C constant-current discharge and the Urban Dynamometer Driving Schedule (UDDS) and New European Driving Cycle (NEDC) profiles shows lower SOC estimation errors than conventional dual SMO and the IESP-based dual extended Kalman filter (DEKF). Compared with DEKF, the proposed observer provides faster recovery from a 30% initial SOC bias. Selective parameter updating reduces the average per-step computation time compared with the always-updating dual SMO. Temperature tests and capacity-based, model-generated aging cases further assess robustness. These results support adaptive gating as a means of reducing error propagation and computational overhead in electrochemical-model-based joint state-parameter estimation.
Systems and Control.comment: 45 pages, 8 figures, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306261926016995

Systems and Control.title: Integer-Free Control Synthesis for Signal Temporal Logic via Ranked Implicants
Systems and Control.summary: This paper proposes an integer-free method for control synthesis of nonlinear discrete-time systems under finite-horizon Signal Temporal Logic (STL) constraints. Instead of introducing integer variables, we consider the discrete choices of the specification in a ranked order and solve a standard nonlinear program for each selected choice until a satisfying trajectory is found. We first define implicants as sets of timed atomic constraints whose joint satisfaction is sufficient to satisfy the specification. A reference trajectory obtained from a smooth approximation of the STL robustness is used to rank these implicants. Fixing one implicant turns the problem into a standard nonlinear program with no auxiliary weights or bilinear terms. If the solution does not satisfy the specification, the next implicant will be considered. We prove soundness and completeness of our method relative to the nonlinear programming solver. Numerical evaluation on nonlinear multi-agent systems shows that our proposed method identifies satisfying trajectories where the exact continuous reformulation fails, and moreover, it is faster than a mixed-integer formulation of the same specification.
Systems and Control.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures

Systems and Control.title: Adaptive Prescribed Performance Trajectory Tracking for Uncertain Autonomous Underwater Vehicles With Input Saturation
Systems and Control.summary: Accurate trajectory tracking is essential for autonomous underwater vehicles operating with uncertain hydrodynamics and limited thruster authority. This paper develops a low-complexity adaptive prescribed performance controller for uncertain underwater vehicle dynamics with coupled and saturated inputs. The proposed method adapts the performance functions directly through the mismatch between the requested and saturated control inputs, enlarging the performance funnels only when the available actuation cannot meet the nominal specifications. A coupled invariant-set analysis establishes boundedness of all closed-loop signals, prescribed bounds on the filtered tracking errors, and explicit feasibility conditions. Comparative simulations on a BlueROV2 underwater vehicle show that the adaptive design maintains prescribed performance during a figure-eight maneuver, whereas conventional prescribed performance control loses feasibility under input limits. A real-time pool experiment further demonstrates stable trajectory tracking and the practical implementation of the proposed method on an underwater robotic platform.
Systems and Control.comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Supplementary video included as ancillary material

Systems and Control.title: Congestion Price Uncertainty From Interconnection Queue by Monte Carlo Sampling
Systems and Control.summary: The generation interconnection queue adds discrete uncertainty to power grid congestion price estimates on the project planning timescale. The conventional approach to this uncertainty is to make an informed guess of the single or few most likely configurations of generators that interconnect. In this paper, we show that Monte Carlo sampling is a more effective alternative. Given an estimate of the joint probability distribution of generator interconnections, a small number of samples yields good estimates of the congestion distribution. Crucially, this problem is not about rare events, but rather about the expected congestion over the worst times of the year, which makes congestion a common outcome over the distribution of interconnection events. We give empirical results on a 2000-bus network, averaging price outcomes from security-constrained DCOPF over eight different loading scenarios. For each line and contingency of the network, we estimate the full distribution as well as mean price and probability of exceeding a price threshold. Single-point estimates are unreliable and can be misleading about whether a line is likely to be congested. Combining the top k probability configurations yields improved estimates; however, sampling the same number from a distribution gives a more robust result of similar accuracy, as well as error estimates. Including correlation in the distribution model introduces small changes, showing that standard Bernoulli distributions suffice in most cases. The sampling approach is also applicable to large-load interconnection and should be of interest for planning both generation and large-load projects.
Systems and Control.comment: 8 pages, 9 figures

Systems and Control.title: Objective-Aware Policy Orchestration for O-RAN Service Provisioning
Systems and Control.summary: O-RAN enables the deployment of heterogeneous control and provisioning algorithms through open interfaces and programmable intelligent controllers. However, most existing intelligent O-RAN solutions rely on a single optimization strategy designed for a fixed operational objective, limiting their ability to adapt when network conditions or operator priorities change. This paper proposes an objective-aware policy orchestration framework that selects the most appropriate provisioning policy for each control window based on the current network context and operator objective. The framework orchestrates a portfolio of heterogeneous provisioning experts using contextual-bandit learning. Two policy selectors, Linear Thompson Sampling and a Bootstrap Tree ensemble, are evaluated against static provisioning policies and a deterministic rule-based orchestrator. Experimental results show that learning-based policy orchestration can effectively adapt policy selection to varying operating conditions, improving overall objective-aware performance while preserving the modularity of existing provisioning algorithms.

Systems and Control.title: From Global to Local: Hierarchical Probabilistic Verification for Reachability Learning
Systems and Control.summary: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides formal safety guarantees for nonlinear systems. However, it becomes computationally intractable in high-dimensional settings, motivating learning-based approximations that may introduce unsafe errors or overly optimistic safe sets. In this work, we propose a hierarchical probabilistic verification framework for reachability learning that bridges offline global certification and online local refinement. We first construct a coarse, conservative under-approximation of the reach-avoid safe set using scenario optimization, providing an efficient global probabilistic certificate. We then introduce an online local refinement module that is structurally anchored to the global certificate and recovers regions excluded by the global verification. This refinement reduces conservatism while focusing computation on critical regions of the state space. Integrated with a condition-based switching mechanism between a learned reachability policy and a model-based controller, the proposed framework improves success rates in goal-reaching tasks with safety constraints, as demonstrated in drone-racing simulation experiments.
Systems and Control.comment: This paper has been accepted by the IEEE Control Systems Letters (L-CSS) and jointly by the IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC), 2026

Systems and Control.title: Planning to Learn: Real-Time Robust Adaptive Control on the GPU with Guaranteed Future Learning
Systems and Control.summary: Robust adaptive control is vital for keeping robots safe while actively reducing uncertainty in unfamiliar settings. However, traditional methods are often conservative since they fail to account for guaranteed future parameter learning during planning and struggle to scale to high-dimensional systems. In this work, we present A-SLS, a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework based on system-level synthesis. A-SLS forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations between process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tight, guaranteed reachable sets that account for future information gain. We also develop a GPU-accelerated A-SLS solver to enable real-time performance. Across nonlinear robotic systems, A-SLS reduces reachable-tube conservativeness, maintains real-time performance, and scales to whole-body control for a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs. We further demonstrate the approach on hardware, where a physical Crazyflie drone learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online to stabilize on the fly.

Systems and Control.title: Co-designing a Layered Control Architecture
Systems and Control.summary: Layered control architectures (LCAs) are ubiquitous in complex engineering systems. However, in practice they are largely designed ad hoc and mostly dictated by the experience of the designer. This is because there is currently no systematic and practically applicable theory available to holistically design LCAs. Hence, systematically reasoning about the optimality, stability, and feasibility of the LCA design is not possible. We set a first step toward such a theory by presenting a framework for co-designing a two-layer LCA for a linear time-invariant plant. The resulting co-design problem optimizes over architectural design variables (e.g., reduced order model dimension and sampling ratio between the layers) and tuning-based design variables (e.g., the numerical values of the feedback gain or the matrices of the reduced order model), all subject to constraints that ensure stability, feasibility, and compute properties of the closed-loop LCA. The proposed formulation allows to make informed tradeoffs along the Pareto front traced over different axes of optimality, e.g., speed, accuracy or computational effort. We demonstrate the effect of making various tradeoffs in a simple numerical example.
Systems and Control.comment: 19 pages, extended version

Systems and Control.title: Optimally Trading Energy for Information through Speed Trajectory Optimization of Sustainably Powered Mobile Robots
Systems and Control.summary: Sustainably powered mobile robots enable long-duration observational missions by harvesting energy from the environment. However, effective autonomy requires the robots to make decisions as to how to allocate this energy to maximize information quality over time. In this paper, we study a persistent (infinite-horizon) speed trajectory optimization problem that is posed as a periodic optimal control problem in which a robot repeatedly traverses a fixed closed path, coupling a super-linear propulsion cost with dynamic information gain and decay. Using the information-theoretic quantity of clarity as an information metric, we first derive the necessary conditions for optimal control. We then derive a number of specialized follow-on properties, which characterize (i) the nature of the optimal control when points on the path are of varying importance and when they are of equal importance, along with (ii) a high-speed information limit that is approached when energy reserves approach infinity. We illustrate the information-optimal speed trajectories on a simple example in order to showcase key trends that are followed under the optimized speed profile. This is followed by a simulation study based on the persistent characterization of salinity in the Chesapeake Bay, illustrating the practical merit of applying the results from this work.

Systems and Control.title: Clarity-Driven Adaptive Mission Planning for a Solar-Powered Autonomous Surface Vessel
Systems and Control.summary: This paper presents a comprehensive methodology, backed by simulation and experimental results, for an adaptive mission planning strategy that is mathematically grounded in the maximization of the information-driven quantity of clarity. In particular, the methodology introduced in this work addresses the use of sustainably powered autonomous surface vessels (ASVs) to perform scientific missions that prioritize locations of maximum interest. Because these locations of maximum interest are not known a priori but are rather identified based on in-situ measurements, online adaptation is essential for mission planning. Furthermore, the reliance on a limited-power renewable resource requires an adaptation strategy that maximizes information gathering subject to mobility restrictions imposed by the renewable resource. Our approach addresses these challenges through a clarity-driven ergodic search, where clarity represents a mathematical quantity that has been rigorously linked to differential (information) entropy. In our approach, a target clarity map is adapted online to reflect the prioritization of certain areas based on in-situ measurements, and an ergodic path planner continually re-plans based on the target clarity map and ASV speed limitations (driven by the renewable propulsion source). Focusing on a solar-powered ASV, we present simulations and experiments conducted at Jordan Lake, North Carolina, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Systems and Control.title: A Response to the Reply Presented in "A Fair Comparison of Sliding-Mode and Immersion-and-Invariance Observers"
Systems and Control.summary: In response to the reply presented in [Muñoz-Vázquez and Sánchez-Torres(2026)], this technical report extends the experimental evaluation of position-feedback velocity observers and adaptive tracking controllers for a pendular system with nonlinear friction reported in [Cervantes-Pérez et al.(2026)]. The immersion and invariance (I&I) adaptive control scheme proposed in [Romero et al.(2025)], whose gains are tuned according to the guidelines presented in [Ortega et al.(2025)], is compared with a control scheme employing the adaptive modi?ed super-twisting observer of [Dávila et al.(2006)], whose observer gains are selected according to the guidelines proposed in [Muñoz-Vázquez and Sánchez-Torres(2026)]. Although these "tuning guidelines" attenuate chattering in certain scenarios, the experimental results reported here show that they do not eliminate it in general.

Systems and Control.title: Navigation by Skylight Polarization via Rayleigh Model Optimization on a Road Vehicle
Systems and Control.summary: Reliable absolute heading estimation is critical for road-vehicle navigation, particularly when magnetic, inertial, or GNSS-based references are degraded. This paper presents a skylight polarization navigation method that estimates vehicle heading by globally optimizing a Rayleigh sky model against measurements from a division-of-focal-plane polarimetric camera. The proposed framework combines a pinhole camera model, a single-scattering Rayleigh polarization model, and a solar position algorithm to synthesize the expected full image angle of polarization distribution for candidate vehicle states. A degree of polarization weighted root mean square error objective function compares measured and simulated polarization patterns, allowing the estimator to use all available sky information while attenuating low confidence pixels caused by clouds, buildings, foliage, and other depolarizing occlusions. Experimental evaluation is performed using three urban road vehicle trajectories collected with a roof mounted polarimetric camera and a high precision dual-antenna GNSS/INS reference system. Results show sub-degree RMS yaw error across all trajectories, ranging from $0.718^{\circ}$ to $0.889^{\circ}$. Compared with representative feature-based and model-based polarization navigation methods, the proposed approach reduces RMS heading error by up to 87% and demonstrates improved robustness to partial sky occlusion.

Systems and Control.title: Electrical Power Grid Reliability Assessment Exposed to Straight Line Winds
Systems and Control.summary: Maintaining the resilience and reliability of electrical power grids under weather driven disturbances is a critical challenge for modern power system planning and operation. Among weather driven hazards, tornadoes and hurricanes are mostly considered for research purpose overlooking straight line winds despite its significant contribution to transmission line outages and cascading effects. Accurate modeling of these events is essential for operational decision making, and long term infrastructure planning and investment. This research explores the probabilistic risk assessment of transmission lines under straight line winds and their impacts on system level performance. The approach examines the probability of transmission towers failure, transmission lines outages, cascading effects, and identify critical transmission lines. The IEEE 118 bus system was utilized to validate the proposed approach and to demonstrate how wind induced component failures propagate throughout the network, affecting power grid reliability.
Systems and Control.comment: Accepted at the 2026 North American Power Symposium (NAPS)

Systems and Control.title: Optimal Demand Response-Based Energy Management for Campus Buildings with Battery Energy Storage Systems: A Case Study of the ELB Building
Systems and Control.summary: Buildings account for a significant portion of global electricity consumption, making demand response (DR) an effective strategy for reducing energy costs and improving grid flexibility. This paper presents an optimal energy management framework for a campus building that integrates demand response and battery energy storage systems (BESS) to minimize electricity costs while satisfying operational constraints and occupant comfort requirements. The proposed optimization model schedules building loads and battery charging/discharging based on time-varying electricity prices and building demand profiles. The framework is validated using the Engineering Laboratory Building (ELB) at the University of Michigan-Dearborn as a real-world case study. Four operating scenarios are investigated: (i) baseline operation, (ii) demand response without battery energy storage, (iii) battery energy storage, and (iv) demand response with battery energy storage. Simulation results demonstrate that demand alone reduces the building's electricity cost by approximately 12% compared with conventional operation. When battery energy storage is incorporated, the total electricity cost reduction increases to approximately 26%, highlighting the significant economic benefits of coordinated demand response and energy storage scheduling. The results demonstrate that integrating battery energy storage with demand response substantially enhances the operational flexibility of campus buildings and provides an effective solution for cost-effective and sustainable building energy management.

Systems and Control.title: LOOP-MAC: Learning-Based Multi-Agent Coordination with Guaranteed Local Feasibility in a Virtual Power Plant
Systems and Control.summary: By aggregating distributed energy resources (DERs) into a single dispatchable resource, virtual power plants (VPPs) enable the grid to use the flexibility of numerous small-scale DERs. Delivering an aggregate VPP commitment requires multi-agent coordination, where agents manage local DER models and operating constraints while jointly meeting a power commitment within limited communication rounds. Classical distributed optimization is computationally intensive, requiring iterative local optimization and repeated communication to reach consensus. Learning-based methods can accelerate coordination but often lack guarantees of local feasibility and accurate commitment tracking. This paper proposes LOOP-MAC (Learning to Optimize the Optimization Process for Multi-Agent Coordination), a fully decentralized learning-based framework that ensures local feasibility by construction while efficiently reducing the aggregate commitment gap. LOOP-MAC employs a two-stage decision process. Learned coordination uses neural optimizers equipped with a gauge layer to produce locally feasible schedules through a few rounds of message exchange. Local adjustment then rebalances each schedule toward feasible flexibility extremes using a commitment-gap estimate inferred from messages already received. The adjusted schedule remains locally feasible as a convex combination of feasible schedules, and the adjustment requires no additional communication round. On a 100-agent VPP, five communication rounds followed by local adjustment reduce the mean commitment gap from 5.1% to 0.75% of the agents' aggregate absolute power and the optimality gap from 3.93% to 3.07% relative to learned coordination alone. Per-agent online computation takes approximately 1.1 ms, including the adjustment.

Information Theory.title: What Does a Discrete Diffusion Model Learn? One Reverse Process in Three Coordinates
Information Theory.summary: What does a discrete diffusion model actually learn? The literature trains denoisers, bridge plug-ins, and concrete scores, each deriving its own ELBO objective under different conventions. This fragmentation makes the object being learned unclear and ELBO values difficult to interpret and compare. All three methods learn the same object in different coordinates: the exact time-reversal of the noising process. We first prove the Oracle Distance identity: for any noising process, the negative ELBO is not just a bound on the likelihood; it equals the data entropy plus the path KL divergence from the reversed noising process to the learned one. Next, for token-factorizing noise, we show that denoiser, bridge plug-in, and concrete score are three coordinates of this reverse process, derive exact conversions between them, and identify the probability distribution learned by each. In particular, contrary to its standard interpretation, the bridge plug-in learns not a denoiser but the cavity distribution: the clean token given the noisy sequence excluding its own position. We confirm the theory by training all three coordinates with masked, uniform, and GIDD kernels on OpenWebText under a shared recipe, and by training uniform-diffusion solvers on four logic tasks. The learned coordinates agree after conversion, while confusing the cavity with the denoiser can severely degrade sampling quality. Together with exact boundary-term formulas, closed-form NELBO calibrations at initialization, and a clock interpretation of time schedules, these results provide a conceptual framework and a mechanical recipe for deriving, implementing, and comparing discrete diffusion processes.
Information Theory.comment: 48 pages, 10 figures. v2: revised and extended; accepted as an oral at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop Diffusion Language Models: Foundations, Efficiency, and Reasoning

Information Theory.title: On Constructing and Decoding Quantum Triorthogonal Codes
Information Theory.summary: Triorthogonal codes are a basic ingredient in magic-state distillation, as they enable transversal implementation of logical $\mathsf{T}$ gates. As a non-Clifford operation, the $\mathsf{T}$ gate enables universal fault-tolerant quantum computation when combined with Clifford operations. We derive an existence criterion for even-weight triorthogonal generator matrices with a target dual minimum distance. The criterion combines triorthogonality constraints with MacWilliams identities via Krawtchouk-polynomial conditions on the dual weight distribution, yielding an integer linear programming formulation for the construction problem. We find novel nontrivial triorthogonal codes (degenerate and non-degenerate) that are not necessarily constructed from triply even binary linear codes. By imposing automorphism-group constraints, the formulation also recovers the known [[49,1,5]] and [[95,1,7]] triorthogonal codes. We also evaluate the performance of the obtained high-distance triorthogonal codes over the dephasing channel using different decoding methods, showing that automorphism ensemble decoding (AED) and guessing random additive-noise decoding (GRAND) are promising options.
Information Theory.comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. v3: Added the proof of Theorem 2 (Appendix A)

Information Theory.title: Performance Analysis of Pinching Antenna Systems Enabled NOMA Communications
Information Theory.summary: Pinching antenna systems (PASS) have the advantages in the perspective of flexible antenna reconfiguration, line-of-sight (LoS) creation, and scalability features. To highlight the ascendancy of PASS, we survey the integration of PASS into non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) networks. The locations of nodes are randomly distributed within a circular coverage region. The influencing factors of LoS and none-line-of-sight (NLoS) propagation links from PASS to non-orthogonal nodes are taken into consideration. To characterize performance of PASS-NOMA, we deduce the outage probability and ergodic data rates expressions of two nodes over LoS/NLoS fading channels. In light of these theoretical results, the formally unbounded diversity gains are also characterized with node n under ideal successive interference cancellation (ISIC) and node f over LoS links, when the SNR exceeds a finite threshold. The slopes of ergodic data rate for node n with ISIC equals to one and that of node f presents a zero slope. In addition, the PASS-NOMA system throughput are evaluated in different transmission modes. It is shown from the numerical results that: 1) The outage behaviors of PASS-NOMA networks under LoS/NLoS conditions outperform that of PASS aided orthogonal multiple access (OMA) networks and that of conventional antenna systems (CASS) aided OMA/NOMA networks; 2) The employment of PASS enables the larger ergodic data rates relative to PASS-OMA and CASS-OMA/NOMA networks; and 3) As the quantity of communication radius and PASS' height rises, the performance of PASS-NOMA networks are declined at a certain extent.
Information Theory.comment: Fixed the Abstract that was not updated in v2. The actual content of the paper and the TeX source are identical to v2

Information Theory.title: Exact Joint MAP Decoding for Unknown Load and Message Counts in Orthogonal Unsourced Random Access
Information Theory.summary: We study joint recovery of the load (the number of active users) and message-count vector in type-based unsourced random access with very short messages. Each user's $k$-bit message activates one of $M=2^k$ orthogonal resources; coherent collisions therefore produce a noisy, unnormalized histogram of the transmitted messages. For arbitrary load and message priors, we propose an exact joint maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoder. Known-load allocation is separable and convex; our contribution is to show that the solutions for all candidate loads are nested prefixes of one greedy chain. Scoring these prefixes with the Bayesian posterior terms jointly estimates the load and message-count vector in $O(M+K_{\max}\log M)$ time. We compare the proposed joint MAP decoder with marginal MAP, three scalar-count two-stage receivers, oracle-load MAP, a sum-only receiver, and a soft-pilot receiver. For $K\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{0{:}60\}$ at 2 dB, the proposed decoder cuts the no-activity false-alarm probability from $25.9\%$ to $3.5\%$ relative to the Bayesian-count two-stage receiver and, conditioned on $K\ge1$, reduces normalized count error by $21.4\%$. The advantage concentrates under idle or sparse uncertain activity, whereas support-count processing approaches joint MAP when the possible loads are well separated. We also prove that the sum-only statistic is insufficient and quantify prior and amplitude mismatch. The model targets synchronized, power-controlled, very-short payloads rather than general URA.

Information Theory.title: Cache-Aided Linear Function Computation
Information Theory.summary: We study cache-aided linear computation in distributed systems where each source generates and stores its own data. An external receiver requests a linear combination of these data, and the sources use information cached before the request is known to reduce the communication needed to recover the requested result. In our model, each of the $N$ sources stores its own independent file over a finite field and has an additional cache of normalized size $M$. The receiver must recover any requested linear combination with zero error from the messages sent by the sources over separate noiseless links. We establish a lower bound on the worst-case communication rate over any finite field by analyzing several requests under the same cache placement. This bound determines the optimal rate when no additional cache is available. For binary files, we propose parity-aided placement (PAP), a coded-placement scheme that combines cached parities with uncoded symbols. For every $N\geq3$, we characterize its communication rate for each request and optimize its placement parameters to obtain a closed-form worst-case rate. The resulting achievable rate meets the lower bound for $0\leq M\leq1/(2N-1)$ and $M\geq(N-1)/N$, establishing the optimal memory--rate tradeoff in these two ranges.
Information Theory.comment: 11 pages, 2 figures. A shorter version has been submitted to the 2027 IEEE Information Theory Workshop (ITW)

Information Theory.title: Exact Cap Response and Aperture Selection for Molecular Communication under Aligned Drift
Information Theory.summary: Spatial reception under directed molecule transport requires balancing useful molecule capture against intersymbol interference (ISI). To characterize this balance, we study a fully absorbing spherical receiver that counts absorption events only within a prescribed cap. Using the known joint first-hitting law under aligned drift, we derive exact cap impulse, cumulative, and eventual responses. We perform stable cumulative evaluation. We then assess the derived responses through particle simulations and time-step comparisons, and demonstrate that our conditional-timing analysis explains when opposite drifts of equal magnitude can favor the same wider aperture. We also show that for the studied geometry and a symbol duration of $0.15$ s, the aperture that maximizes the signal-to-interference difference (SID) increases from $29.13^\circ$ at zero drift to $61.86^\circ$ at a drift magnitude of $40$ $μ$m/s. These results (i) connect joint arrival-time and location statistics to spatial reception design, (ii) characterize the tradeoff between useful molecule capture and ISI, (iii) support SID-based aperture selection for a given drift and symbol duration, and (iv) quantify the SID loss incurred by retaining the zero-drift optimal aperture for the same symbol duration.
Information Theory.comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Full version including two appendices. A shortened version omitting Appendix A is being prepared for submission to IEEE ICC 2027

Information Theory.title: Entropic Inequalities and Limit Theorems in Boolean Probability
Information Theory.summary: We study Boolean entropy and Fisher information in information inequalities and the Boolean central limit theorem. We prove a fractional Stam inequality for the Boolean Fisher information associated with arbitrary fractional partitions of subset sums, and derive an entropy power inequality for sums of Boolean independent random variables and its weighted version. We then establish a Boolean analogue of Barron's entropy convergence result along the Boolean central limit theorem: Boolean entropy converges to the entropy of the Rademacher law if and only if the initial entropy is finite. Furthermore, under a finite fourth moment, in the Boolean central limit theorem, we obtain \[ Γ(μ_n\mid\mathbf b)= \frac{m_4(μ)-1-m_3(μ)^2}{2}\frac{\log n}{n} +o\!\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right), \] with an explicit example showing sharpness. For symmetric laws with finite fourth moment and finite Boolean Fisher information, \[ Ψ(μ_n\mid\mathbf b) =2\bigl(m_4(μ)-1\bigr)\frac{\log n}{n} +o\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right). \] Our approach is based on the Nevanlinna representation of Cauchy transforms.

Information Theory.title: Binary Cyclic Gradient Coding: Exact Recovery and Robustness to Compression
Information Theory.summary: We introduce binary cyclic gradient coding (BCGC), an exact gradient coding scheme for $n$ workers and up to $s$ stragglers. Its encoding matrix is binary, circulant when $(s+1)\mid n$ and nearly circulant otherwise, and the master decodes by a single summation. Like the fractional repetition coding scheme (FRC) and its generalized version (GFRC), BCGC splits the workers into $s+1$ classes that each cover the whole dataset, but it assigns the data through cyclic supports. Its encoding matrix has rank $n-s$, and $n-s-1$ workers keep the balanced load $s+1$, which is the largest possible number. We prove that encoding matrix of BCGC is not permutation-equivalent to those of FRC and GFRC schemes. Moreover, We also prove that a binary coded scheme with compression is equivalent to an uncoded compressed scheme on a coarser partition of the data. This explains why binary schemes remain stable under compression, whereas the large decoding coefficients of MDS codes amplify the compression error and lead to divergence in our experiments. For every contractive compressor, the standard convergence guarantee of compressed gradient descent holds on each coarse partition. FRC, GFRC and BCGC therefore share the same convergence guarantee and differ only in their partitions, with one partition for FRC, two for GFRC and $s+1$ distinct partitions for BCGC. Choosing among these partitions can recover the exact gradient in cases where FRC and GFRC cannot. Experiments on four datasets confirm the theory. BCGC matches GFRC, keeps its accuracy under top $κ$ sparsification while the MDS codes diverge, and on heterogeneous data its partition diversity reduces the compression error and improves the accuracy.

Information Theory.title: Minimax Binary Counting under Shuffle Privacy: Poisson Limits and Randomized-Response Optimality
Information Theory.summary: We study estimation of a deterministic binary count from the shuffled outputs of a common single-message local channel. Privacy is required for every neighboring composition at fixed global parameters $(\varepsilon,δ)$, and estimators may be biased. We obtain uniform critical Poisson and Skellam approximations and characterize the limiting minimax risk as an infimum over finite observed-mark Poisson experiments. Let $Λ$ be the noise intensity required by the boundary Poisson-shift profile and let $λ_{\min}$ be the intensity required by the full composition-maximized randomized-response profile. Binary randomized response is asymptotically minimax optimal if and only if $Λ=λ_{\min}$. When $Λ<λ_{\min}$, the minimax value lies strictly between $(Λ+λ_{\min})/2$ and $λ_{\min}$, and a randomized-response construction with observed rare marks strictly improves on binary randomized response. We give a finite-sample certified example. Binary randomized response is strictly suboptimal at $\varepsilon=0$ for every $0<δ<1$, and this persists for sufficiently small positive $\varepsilon$ at each fixed target. For every fixed positive $\varepsilon$, strict suboptimality also occurs along a sequence of fixed privacy targets tending to zero. The variational characterization permits approximation by finite marked channels; it does not assert that a finite optimizer exists.

Information Theory.title: Undirected Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
Information Theory.summary:
Network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages, whereas routing only forwards them. The Li-Li conjecture asserts that network coding and fractional routing have the same capacity region in undirected multiple-unicast networks. We give a counterexample to this conjecture and apply it to external-memory integer sorting. Since Aggarwal and Vitter posed the question in 1988, whether integer sorting can beat the external-memory comparison bound has remained a central and extensively studied open problem.
  We give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $Θ(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is $O\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon}\right]\right)$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is an absolute constant. In a range of parameter regimes, this bound is asymptotically smaller than the classical comparison-sorting bound. We also use Lean 4 to verify the sorting algorithm's correctness and complexity bounds, and the strict advantage of coding over routing.

Information Theory.title: List Size of Random Linear Codes: Optimality and the Limits of Average-Radius List Decoding
Information Theory.summary:
Guruswami, Li, Mosheiff, Resch, Silas and Wootters conjectured that, for every fixed prime power $q$ and $p\in(0,1-1/q)$, random linear codes of rate $1-h_q(p)-\varepsilon$ have list size $\frac{h_q(p)}{\varepsilon}\cdot(1+o(1))$ as $\varepsilon\to0$, both for list decoding and average-radius list decoding. The conjecture was known for $q=2$ and remained open for larger alphabets.
  We prove the conjecture for list decoding for every prime power $q$, with the sharper bound $L=\frac{h_q(p)}{\varepsilon}+O_{p,q}(1).$ In contrast, we disprove the conjecture for average-radius list decoding. We show that the required list-size leading constant is at least $p\left(1+\log_q\frac{(q-1)(1-p)}{p}\right)$, which is strictly larger than $h_q(p)$ whenever $q^p(1-p)>1$. Moreover, for $p=1-λ/q$ with fixed $λ>1$, the required leading constant can be as large as $\left(\frac{\logλ}{eλ}+o_q(1)\right)\frac{q}{\log q}.$

Information Theory.title: Nonlinear fixed-distance codes via real lifts of moment configurations
Information Theory.summary:
Let $A_q(n,d)$ denote the largest size of a code of length $n$ and minimum Hamming distance $d$ over an alphabet of $q$ symbols. For fixed $q\ge2$ and $d\ge4$ we construct codes with redundancy $n-\log_q A_q(n,d)\le(d-3)\log_q n+O(\sqrt{\log n})$ for all large $n$. No algebraic structure is imposed on the alphabet, and the codes are not linear. For $d=4$ and $d=5$ the coefficient of $\log_q n$ matches the Hamming bound, so the redundancy is determined up to lower-order terms. At distance four the codes are provably better than every linear code: by the polynomial-method bound for cap sets, $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear codes with $q>2$ require a strictly larger coefficient in front of $\log_q n$.
  The construction imposes moment checksums over an auxiliary finite field, as BCH codes do, but one fewer than the distance would normally require. The affine-line theorem from prior work describes the dependencies left by these checks. We exclude them by placing the code positions inside a specially structured subset of the field, built from Behrend's sphere construction with the help of algebraic number theory.

Information Theory.title: Generative Actor-Critic with Soft Bridge Policies
Information Theory.summary: Expressive generative policies such as diffusion and flow models are appealing for maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) online reinforcement learning because of their ability to model multimodal and highly non-Gaussian action distributions. However, training effective soft generative policies faces two obstacles that often arise together. First, marginal action densities are often unavailable, so existing methods typically rely on entropy bounds, heuristic proxies or approximations. Second, iterative shared-parameter samplers raise inference cost and require backpropagation through time over repeated network evaluations, increasing memory cost and potentially destabilizing policy optimization. These obstacles motivate us to seek a generative actor-critic method that exposes a tractable soft objective while generating each action in just one network evaluation. To this end, we propose soft generative actor-critic (SoftGAC), whose actor is a single stochastic feedforward network with internal Gaussian bridge layers. This explicit bridge structure allows us to lift the soft objective to path space, yielding an analytical path-KL regularizer against a high-entropy reference process for both actor improvement and the soft Bellman bootstrap, without estimating the endpoint entropy. Crucially, the actor generates each action in only one network evaluation under a total parameter budget comparable to strong baselines, substantially reducing inference cost relative to the existing iterative diffusion and flow policies. It also avoids long unrolled backpropagation through time. Across challenging continuous-control benchmarks, our method achieves competitive or superior returns compared with strong diffusion and flow policies, demonstrating a clear advantage in the compute-return tradeoff.

Information Theory.title: Bilinear Compressive Security with Finitely Many Samples
Information Theory.summary:
Bilinear Compressive Security (BCS) is a lightweight encryption scheme that combines compressed sensing with a fresh random convolution filter to improve resistance against key-recovery attacks under key reuse. Previous work derived information-theoretic guarantees for BCS by relating key identifiability to phase retrieval under the assumption that an adversary has access to the full ciphertext distribution induced by the random filter. In practice, however, an adversary only observes finitely many encryptions, leaving the security of BCS in the finite-sample regime largely unexplored.
  In this paper, we study key recovery from only finitely many observations. We first develop a covariance-based attack that estimates the linear measurements from repeated encryptions of the same plaintext and subsequently recovers the secret measurement matrix. We analyze the estimation procedure and derive finite-sample guarantees together with corresponding sample-complexity bounds. We further investigate the complete attack experimentally and compare its observed recovery behavior with the previously established information-theoretic identifiability results.
  Our experiments show two qualitatively different recovery regimes on the structure of the measurement matrix. For dense matrices, including Gaussian matrices, the number of measurements required for successful recovery appears to grow linearly with the signal dimension. This differs from the worst-case behavior suggested by information theory. In contrast, for matrices with sparse rows, we observe a quadratic growth consistent with the theoretical bound.
  These results suggest that the sparsity structure of the measurement matrix plays an important role in the security of BCS and should be taken into account when selecting parameters and designing practical instances of the scheme.

Information Theory.title: Global and Local Entropy Tests for STL Files Under IEEE-754 Validity Constraints
Information Theory.summary: Shannon entropy is a standard measure of ciphertext randomness, evaluated either globally over the byte histogram of the entire ciphertext or locally as the average over non-overlapping blocks of ?xed size. While the global statistic captures only the overall byte distribution, the local statistic is also sensitive to non-randomness that is con?ned to parts of the ciphertext. Both measures are commonly assessed against reference values derived under the assumption of independent uniform bytes. However, STL encodes most numerical data as single-precision IEEE-754 ?oats, and format validity requires them to be ?nite, causing nonuniform byte probabilities and dependence between the two bytes of each exponent pair. We derive the exact mean and variance of entropy under the valid-STL (VSTL) distribution, which assigns equal probability to every admissible sequence of triangle records, and provide second-order expansions that keep the global reference values practical to compute at large ?le sizes. Using these expansions, we establish a two-sided hypothesis test for the global entropy statistic, whose limiting value is lowered from 8 to 7.99991479609 bits. The format constraints also change the local entropy reference: applying the capacity energy criterion to triangle records selects a block size of 1950 bytes instead of 1936 bytes, with an exact reference mean of 7.903106732975 rather than 7.902469316647 bits. Although small, these shifts are su?cient to place the VSTL reference means outside the conventional 95% acceptance intervals at practical ?le sizes, making unadjusted entropy tests prone to falsely rejecting ideal VSTL ciphertexts. Monte-Carlo simulations con?rm all reference values within sampling error. We therefore recommend using the format-speci?c reference values derived here to evaluate STL ciphers.

Information Theory.title: The Cross-Correlation Distribution of the Niho-Type Decimation $d=4(2^m-1)+1$
Information Theory.summary: The cross-correlation problem is a classical problem in sequence design. In this paper, we determine the cross-correlation distribution of the Niho-type decimation $d=4(2^m-1)+1$ over $\mathbb F_{2^{2m}}$ for every positive integer $m$. With $q=2^m$, this is equivalent to determining the distribution of the number of roots in $U_{q+1}$ of $f_a(x)=x^7+ax^4+\bar a x^3+1$ for $a\in\mathbb F_{q^2}$, where $U_{q+1}=\{x\in\mathbb F_{q^2}:x^{q+1}=1\}$. The main difficulty is to count the four-element subsets of $U_{q+1}$ that may occur as root sets of $f_a$. We normalize such subsets by their product and study the resulting condition through the associated resolvent. This reduces the required enumeration to several equations over $\mathbb F_q$, which are evaluated by character sums and Kloosterman sums. The remaining mixed Kloosterman sum is related to a Kloosterman sum over $\mathbb F_{2^{2m}}$ and is evaluated using a theorem of Carlitz. Consequently, we obtain explicit formulas for all the frequencies in the cross-correlation distribution.

Information Theory.title: Joint Identification, Transmission, and Sensing over State-Dependent Channels with Noiseless Feedback
Information Theory.summary: We consider a discrete memoryless state-dependent channel with noiseless feedback, where the transmitter uses randomized encoding to jointly perform message transmission, identification, and state sensing. In this setting, the transmitter sends a conventional transmission message and an identification message while estimating the unknown channel state sequence under an average distortion constraint. We establish a single-letter characterization of the randomized identification-transmission-sensing capacity-distortion region. The result reveals a single-letter separation structure: the communication rates are determined by the averaged channel, subject to the sensing-induced constraint on admissible input distributions. Specifically, the transmission rate is characterized by mutual information, while the identification rate is characterized by output entropy under the same distortion constraint. The achievability proof combines constant-composition transmission coding, output partitioning, and combinatorial identification coding, while the converse follows from an averaged-channel reduction, distortion lower bounds, and feedback-identification converse arguments.

Information Theory.title: Directional and Quasi-Omnidirectional Indoor Channel Measurements at Upper 6 GHz
Information Theory.summary: This paper presents wideband indoor channel measurements and measurement-based statistical modeling of channel parameters in the upper 6 GHz (U6G) band using directional and quasi-omnidirectional antenna pairs. Measurements span 6.425-7.125 GHz at 32 matched positions per configuration in an open hall and an L-shaped corridor. System calibration and frequency-dependent peak-gain normalization retain antenna radiation-pattern weighting. Close-in and floating-intercept models are fitted to line-of-sight (LOS) and non-LOS (NLOS) path loss, respectively. Shadow-fading residuals, RMS delay spread (DS), and equivalent K factors derived from power delay profiles are characterized. LOS exponents range from 1.98 to 2.14. Despite similar attenuation slopes, directional links exhibit smaller LOS residuals and DS and higher equivalent K factors. Hall DS medians are 1.78 and 36.52 ns for directional and quasi-omnidirectional links. Corridor NLOS slopes are -1.12 and 2.54, respectively, while DS ordering varies by position. These results characterize antenna-dependent parameters for U6G indoor channels.

Information Theory.title: Vectorized Generalized Nearest Neighbor Decoding for In-block Memory Channel
Information Theory.summary: This work extends the generalized nearest neighbor decoding (GNND), originally developed as a receiver architecture for memoryless channels, to a vectorized GNND (Vec-GNND) suitable for in-block memory (IBM) channels. Leveraging the generalized mutual information (GMI) as an operational lower bound on the mismatch capacity, an analytical characterization of the optimal Vec-GNND is obtained for general IBM channels with Gaussian codebooks. The formalism further provides closed-form optimality conditions and achievable GMIs for restricted variants of the receiver architecture. Furthermore, we formulate a GMI-based joint design viewpoint for Gaussian codebook covariance and decoding metrics. Since the metric optimization admits a closed-form solution for each fixed covariance, the joint design is reduced to an input-covariance optimization problem; for the diagonal covariance family, we derive first-order self-consistent optimality conditions. Numerical evaluations on block noncoherent AWGN and phase-noise channels demonstrate consistent GMI gains over conventional scaling-based GNND schemes, suggesting potential performance advantages of Vec-GNNDR in practical communication systems.

Information Theory.title: Capacity Bounds for Optical Interference Channels Subject to Average Power Constraints
Information Theory.summary: Accurate information-theoretic analysis of multiuser wavelength-division multiplexed (WDM) optical links is complicated by Kerr nonlinearity and chromatic dispersion. Existing capacity bounds for first-order regular perturbative (RP) channel models have relied on per-symbol peak power constraints to simplify the underlying extremal analysis. In this paper, we replace these peak constraints with the more practically relevant average input power constraints and study the resulting RP WDM interference channel.
